Simulations showed that temperature‐minimizing or oxygen‐maximizing strategies resulted in constant depth selection, whereas fish that balanced temperature and oxygen exhibited diel vertical movement. Most fish exhibited diel vertical movement that matched simulation; however, the movement extent was smaller than expected as fish endured hypoxic conditions in exchange for colder temperatures. We show that diel vertical movement exploits temperature and oxygen asynchrony to soften the trade‐off between these variables. These findings likely apply to other aquatic systems where asynchronous stressors constrain habitat use.

title: Stoichiometric imbalance affects competitive superiority in marine herbivorous zooplankton communities
content:
Abstract
Traditionally, abiotic drivers and predator–prey interactions have been considered critical to shaping the taxonomic composition of a marine zooplankton community, whereas the role of indirect biotic processes, such as exploitative competition, remains unexamined. The competitive performance of a zooplankton taxon can be limited by biochemical mismatches between its requirements and available prey, known as stoichiometric imbalance. Such imbalance impairs zooplankton growth and reproduction, thereby reducing their competitiveness. Stoichiometric imbalance is known to shape zooplankton communities in freshwater systems; however, its role in marine systems has largely been examined only at the species or individual levels under experimental conditions. To fill this gap, we measured the family‐level taxonomic composition and carbon : nitrogen : phosphorus ratios (C : N : P) of herbivorous zooplankton and quantified their stoichiometric imbalance relative to their prey in the southern East China Sea. We examined three hypotheses: Hypothesis 1—Intra‐family stoichiometry of zooplankton is independent of and less variable than phytoplankton; Hypothesis 2—Zooplankton show interfamily variation in stoichiometry; and Hypothesis 3—A higher degree of stoichiometric imbalance reduces the relative abundance of a zooplankton family in the community. Our results showed zooplankton stoichiometry was stable within but variable among families. Family‐level relative abundance was significantly associated with phosphorus imbalance. Despite seasonal shifts in dominant families, the negative relationship between stoichiometric imbalance and relative abundance remained consistent, suggesting that stoichiometric imbalance is an important factor modulating zooplankton community composition across seasons. Notably, phosphorus excess did not negatively affect relative abundance, a pattern that contrasts with the traditional stoichiometric knife‐edge hypothesis.

title: Intestinal molecular siphoning by engineered bacterial spores for non-systemic treatment of nicotine addiction
content: Eradicating toxic small molecules from the body typically requires the administrations of therapeutic agents for systemic circulation and tissue distribution, resulting in inevitable adverse events from off-target effects. Here, we propose a intestinal molecular siphoning approach for treating diseases caused by toxic substances, in which enzymatic degradation of a toxic substance in the intestinal lumen serves as a driving force for the diffusion of the toxic substance from blood to gut, and continuous elimination of the toxic substance in the gut could effectively ease substance dependence. Using nicotine as a model substance, a live bacterial system was constructed by displaying a trypsin-resistant nicotine oxidase on the surface of Bacillus subtilis spores, and encapsulating in enteric-coated microspheres for gastric protection and targeted intestinal release. After oral treatments with the live bacterial system in mice, peak concentrations of nicotine in blood and brain were remarkably reduced compared to controls. Moreover, the live bacterial system could effectively attenuate nicotine addiction by suppressing dopamine reward surges to reverse withdrawal hyperalgesia, preventing the upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and alleviating anxiety-like behaviors. These findings show the potential of intestinal molecular siphoning as a target-independent therapeutic strategy for lowering circulating toxic substances through non-systemic enzyme reprogramming.

title: Photographic age gap is associated with frailty and predicts survival in laboratory mice
content: Ageing studies in mice need biomarkers that are cheap, non-invasive and repeatable. We asked how much of a mouse's age can be read from an ordinary photograph, and whether the part that cannot be explained by age carries biological information. We assembled 2,846 photographs of 1,292 mice (four strains, 1 to 34 months old) from seven facilities and predicted age with a frozen self-supervised vision model (DINOv2) and a ridge regression, always tested on facilities the model had never seen. Absolute age transferred poorly between facilities (median absolute error 138 days), because each facility's photographs carried an offset. Relative age transferred well: among mice photographed in the same session, the older mouse was predicted older in 65% of pairs, rising above 95% for age differences over 500 days, and the later photograph of the same mouse was predicted older in 63% of repeat pairs. Sex, in comparison, was inferred more reliably (87%). Mice predicted older than their age were frailer (+0.12 SD per 100 days) and had shorter survival (hazard ratio 1.14 per 100 days), and fourth generation (G4) telomerase-deficient mice looked 151 days older than their wild-type controls. Routine photographs therefore carry a real biological age signal that can be read at no extra cost, best used to compare mice photographed together.

title: ExPert infers causal perturbations from cell states across biological and clinical contexts
content: Pooled single-cell CRISPR screens have driven substantial effort toward models predicting the response to a perturbation. We posed the inverse question: which perturbation produced an observed cell state? Here we developed ExPert (Extracting Perturbations), which learns one prototype per perturbation in a latent space shared by 12 cellular contexts, trained on 8,964 perturbations and 19.5 million cells, and ranks 19,895 candidate genes per query, over half absent from training. ExPert more than doubled held-out-context recall over the best existing method with 1,000-fold less compute, and transferred without retraining to drugs, protein degradation and combinations. In alcohol-associated liver disease it implicated mRNA export, unchanged in expression, and we experimentally confirmed nuclear poly(A) retention and isoform switching. In primary mitochondrial disease it recovered the affected complex from blood, localized the signal to monocytes, and flagged a misdiagnosed control. Perturbation atlases can thus be queried in reverse, from state to likely driver.

title: Ultrasensitive Regulation in the Tryptophan System in Escherichia coli Provides Effective Noise Mitigation
content: The tryptophan system in Escherichia coli maintains intracellular concentration of tryptophan in a narrow band regardless of the nutritional status and uncertainty in its environment. The system is characterized by three distinct regulations namely, genetic regulation, mRNA attenuation and enzyme inhibition, that use the tryptophan concentration as a feedback signal. It has been shown previously, that the multiple feedback loop design is responsible for rapid synthesis of tryptophan when faced with starvation. It is well known that a design with rapid response to external signals also implies poorer noise mitigation properties. This work investigates the design elements that limit the adverse impact of the multiple feedback loop architecture on noise propagation in the tryptophan system using a frequency response analysis. Specifically, we use sinusoidal input describing functions to approximate the transfer characteristics of the ultrasensitive regulators and then obtain the frequency response of the closed-loop feedback system. The study suggests that the tryptophan system of E. coli has evolved to simultaneously satisfy the two properties of rapid response and noise mitigation. Particularly, the multiple feedback loop is responsible for the rapid response, while the nonlinear regulation provides effective noise mitigation.

title: Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs) spreading antimicrobial resistance, host-adaptation factors and defense systems, a novel satellite family of nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae
content: Phage satellites are mobile genetic elements that depend on helper bacteriophages to promote their own dissemination. Here, we identified a novel family of large satellites, named Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs), that are widespread in Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica among diverse hosts, worldwide. These largest satellites to date (71.6 {+/-} 15.8 kbp) are specifically transduced by the persistent jumbo bacteriophage Goslarvirus of the nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae family. Furthermore, PICJIs carried numerous accessory genes associated with clinically relevant antimicrobial resistances, host-adaptation, and several anti-phage defense systems.

title: Functional genomic characterization of anti-phage defense systems in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium
content: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a significant public health threat, demonstrating high rates of antibiotic resistance and frequently causing hospital-acquired infections. Bacteriophages (phages) are a promising adjunctive therapy to reduce bacterial load and manage VREfm infections. Many bacteria encode anti-phage defense systems--groups of genes that can counteract phage infection--but these systems have not been characterized in VREfm. Here we explored the diversity of anti-phage defense systems within clinical VREfm isolate genomes and examined their impact on phage susceptibility. We first used two available bioinformatic tools (DefenseFinder and PADLOC) to identify putative anti-phage defense systems in 21 hybrid-assembled VREfm clinical isolate genomes, and observed that most anti-phage defense systems were located on plasmids, defense islands, and prophages. Combining this information with functional testing of phage susceptibility did not reveal robust associations between specific defense systems and resistance to four VREfm-targeting lytic phages. Due to inherent limitations of phage susceptibility testing, we next developed an assay to assess phage survival after co-incubation with bacteria, and identified over two dozen genes associated with phage killing, including a potentially novel defense island. Lastly, we attempted to functionally validate 10 candidate anti-phage defense systems, only four of which were ultimately tested in enterococci. Expression of one of these candidates, AbiE, decreased bacterial susceptibility to two Enterococcus-targeting phages. As VREfm-targeting phage therapy becomes more widely available, identification of genes contributing to phage resistance can aid in streamlining the provision of phages to patients who could benefit from this new therapeutic modality.

title: The YjfJ protein is the effector of a second PspA/VIPP1 system that is widespread in the Gammaproteobacteria
content: Maintaining the integrity of the cytoplasmic membrane is essential for bacterial cell survival. Unsurprisingly, prokaryotes have evolved conserved mechanisms by which they sense, maintain, and repair membrane integrity in response to stress. The phage shock protein (Psp) is one such system, understood primarily through work undertaken in the Gammaproteobacterial species Escherichia coli and Yersinia enterocolitica. The system utilises an effector, PspA, alongside accessory proteins that sense stress and recruit PspA to damaged membranes. Homologues of PspA - part of the PspA/VIPP1 family - are found in a variety of bacterial phyla. Although most work in the Gammaproteobacteria has concerned the canonical Psp response, there have been descriptions of non-canonical PspA/VIPP1-containing systems that warrant further genomic analysis. By analysing the PspA/VIPP1 content of a diverse selection of Gammaproteobacterial genomes, we reveal the existence of two phylogenetically distinct subtypes of PspA/VIPP1 proteins, PspA- and YjfJ-like, which are found at similar frequencies. The YjfJ-like proteins are not only a novel subtype of PspA/VIPP1, having their own unique set of accessory proteins, but in some species, such as the ESKAPE pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, comprise the only PspA/VIPP1-containing system. Our study positions the YjfJ-like containing systems on equal footing with the PspA system in terms of their conservation and distribution in the Gammaproteobacteria. This suggests that studies into the biological functions of YjfJ-like proteins would be well-justified from their unique presence in some important human pathogens.

title: Lung Epithelial TLR7 is a Factor in Viral Replication and Pathogenesis
content: Respiratory virus infections are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality of infants and the elderly worldwide. Currently it is not known how Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccination of infants can cause enhancement of RSV disease, highlighting gaps in our understanding about how viruses like RSV interact with the immune system. Here we address this and show that ERK MAP kinase signaling from Toll-like Receptor-7 (TLR7) detection of RSV and influenza, but not human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3), infections in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) drives replication of the viruses. Virus infection is detected by pattern recognition receptors like TLR7 that bind to single stranded RNA (ssRNA) viral replication intermediates in late endosomes. Here we report that TLR7 is expressed in BECs and detects RSV ssRNA, causing ERK MAP kinase signaling. RSV and influenza use this detection and signaling in BECs to drive its replication and infection, a mechanism that counters TLR7s role in antiviral defence. Experimental blockade of TLR7 binding or downstream signalling through ERK MAP kinase decreased RSV and influenza replication, but had no effect on HPIV3. RSV viral loads in mouse and human females were higher compared to males, consistent with higher sex-dependent expression of the TLR7 gene from two copies of the X chromosome in females. In a TLR7 gain of function mouse model there was a significant enhancement of RSV replication and RSV eosinophilic and Th2 disease markers like interleukin-5 (IL-5). In summary, TLR7 is expressed in human lung BECs in the lungs where it acts as a factor in RSV and influenza replication and disease pathogenesis. We propose that this is a major factor in determining the sex-disparity of viral disease.

title: Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov. sp. nov., a new gut genus isolated from the stool of a healthy donor
content: Strain Marseille-QA0792 (=CSUR QA0792, CECT 31199) was isolated from the feces of a healthy person using the culturomics method. The fecal sample originated from leftover material collected for a fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) procedure, obtained during a routine screening in accordance with the guidelines of the French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety (ANSM). This strain is Gram-stain-negative, rod-shaped, non-motile, and non-spore-forming. It is strictly anaerobic, with optimal growth at 37{degrees}C. Strain Marseille-QA0792 presented its highest 16S rRNA identity, 96.2%, with ''Merdibacter massiliensis'' strain Marseille-P3254 (not validly published) (accession number LT598590) and ANI similarity of 75.0% with the same species. Among validly published species, strain Marseille-QA0792 showed its highest 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity (91.5%) with Faecalicoccus acidiformans strain 37-2a (accession number HQ452864), whereas all computed average nucleotide identity (ANI) values were below 75%. Genome sequencing revealed a genome size of 2.67 Mb and a G+C content of 50.01%. This species is classified within the Erysipelotrichaceae family in the Bacillota phylum. Thus, we isolated for the first time a novel genus named Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov., sp. nov., strain Marseille-QA0792. This discovery highlights the importance of continuing culturomics efforts to explore the human microbiome.

title: MoALE1, an ART-like effector, contributes to rice blast virulence through host immune suppression
content: Rice blast, caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is one of the most destructive diseases affecting rice production worldwide. During infection, M. oryzae secretes effector proteins that suppress host immunity and facilitate colonization. Here, we characterized MoALE1, a predicted effector that is structurally similar to members of the heat-labile enterotoxin/cholera toxin family. Using a yeast secretion trap assay, we demonstrated that MoALE1 contains a functional signal peptide. A MoALE1-GFP fusion localized to the biotrophic interfacial complex, indicating that MoALE1 is a cytoplasmic effector. Expression analyses revealed that MoALE1 is expressed during biotrophy, from 16 to 48 h post-inoculation. Transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana showed that MoALE1 suppresses BAX-mediated cell death, suggesting a role in host immune suppression. To investigate its contribution to pathogenicity, a{Delta} moale1 mutant was generated and evaluated in rice infection assays. Deletion of MoALE1 significantly reduced disease severity but did not affect fungal growth, stress tolerance, sporulation, appressorium development, host penetration, or early invasive growth. In contrast, infection by the {Delta}moale1 mutant resulted in enhanced host H2O2 accumulation and increased expression of ROS-associated defense genes. Together, these findings identify MoALE1 as a biotrophy-associated cytoplasmic effector that promotes rice blast pathogenicity by suppressing host immune responses and provide new insight into the function of ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART)-like effector candidates in M. oryzae .

title: Phosphate-responsive ornithine lipid biosynthesis remodels outer membrane composition and contributes to polymyxin tolerance
content: Bacteria frequently encounter environments in which essential nutrients are limiting. Phosphate limitation constrains phospholipid synthesis and challenges maintenance of the cell envelope. While many Gram-negative bacteria respond by producing phosphorous-free membrane lipids, the mechanisms and consequences of this remodeling remain poorly understood in Enterobacterales. Here, we characterize the genetic and physiological basis of ornithine lipid (OL) biosynthesis in the opportunistic pathogens Enterobacter cloacae and Klebsiella pneumoniae. We show that OL biosynthesis depends on OlsF, a bifunctional acyltransferase that catalyzes both acylation steps required for OL synthesis. Phosphate limitation promotes OlsF-dependent OL accumulation through the PhoBR two-component system. Membrane fractionation revealed that OlsF-derived OLs are present in both membrane compartments but are enriched in the outer membrane. OlsF-dependent OL production enhances polymyxin tolerance during phosphate limitation, linking nutrient availability to changes in antimicrobial susceptibility. Together, these findings identify OlsF-dependent OL synthesis as a phosphate-responsive membrane remodeling pathway that reshapes outer membrane composition and influences the physiological properties of the Gram-negative cell envelope.

title: Antibiotic-induced protein mislocalization drives hypervesiculation in Salmonella
content: The incorporation of cytosolic proteins into bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) has remained mechanistically unresolved, as these proteins are normally excluded from vesiculation sites by the inner membrane (IM) barrier. Here, we show that antibiotic-induced envelope perturbation compromises this spatial barrier, enabling an aberrant interaction between proteins that are ordinarily segregated across cellular compartments and thereby promoting MV formation in Salmonella. Exposure to non-lethal cephalexin (LEX) induced robust hypervesiculation, accompanied by inhibition of the essential division penicillin binding protein (PBP) 3 and accumulation of the PBP5. Under envelope perturbing conditions, PBP5 accumulated at lateral sites associated with MV emergence and promoted periplasmic crowding independently of its catalytic activity. A cytosolic acyl carrier protein (ACP) emerged as a PBP5 interacting partner under LEX exposure, coinciding with cryogenic electron microscopy detected IM perturbation and aberrant ACP mislocalization. Formation of the PBP5 ACP complex promoted PBP5 accumulation, resulting in periplasmic crowding, progressive weakening of outer membrane peptidoglycan tethering, and ultimately MV formation. Together, these findings uncover a mechanism whereby stress-induced disruption of subcellular compartmentalization enables a non-canonical interaction between normally segregated proteins, driving hypervesiculation in Salmonella.

title: High-throughput, single-cell-encoded colony imaging reveals infection-linked heterogeneity
content: Phenotypic heterogeneity within bacterial populations shapes adaptation, antibiotic tolerance, and infection dynamics, yet colony-level quantification remains difficult at scale and on dark/selective media. We present HeteroTyper, an automated, high-throughput time-lapse platform that measures colony phenotypes across >100 plates per run on both transparent and dark media. HeteroTyper includes a ready-to-use computational pipeline that can be deployed on common plate-imaging setups and across agar types, delivering appearance times as a proxy for lag times, growth trajectories, colony size, intensity, and morphology from routine image series. Automated counts closely matched manual counts, supporting accuracy and scalability. Using Yersinia pseudotuberculosis as a model, HeteroTyper resolves phenotypic heterogeneity in vitro, with early and late phases showing broader appearance time distributions than mid-log phases. It also reveals organ-specific heterogeneity in vivo, with mesenteric lymph node isolates displaying the broadest appearance time distributions compared to spleen and liver. Appearance time was negatively associated with final colony size and intensity, linking growth initiation to downstream colony outcomes. Together, these distribution-level measurements indicate that bacterial adaptation during infection is compartmentalized by tissue microenvironments and prior history, and establish HeteroTyper as a practical, generalizable route to quantify infection-relevant phenotypic diversity on solid media at routine, high throughput.

title: Rhizobia transform legume nodules via native T-DNA transfer systems
content: Agrobacteria can deliver transfer DNA (T-DNA) into plant cells, causing tumorous growth. This process, agrobacteria-mediated transformation (AMT), underlies plant genetic engineering and has been regarded as an evolutionary innovation specific to these pathogens. By screening 63,759 alphaproteobacterial genomes for T-DNA border sequences, we identify mini-T-DNAs in diverse rhizobial genera. Each typically encodes a single cargo, a RolB/RolC family protein or a distant rhizobial homologue. We show that native rhizobia-mediated transformation (RMT) systems deliver these mini-T-DNAs into the root nodules of common bean, pea, and chickpea, where the cargo genes are expressed, with no signal in adjacent root tissue. RMT systems share VirG-dependent activation of the core virulence regulon but respond to distinct upstream signals. Our genome screen identifies many additional candidate T-DNA transfer systems, and phylogenetic analysis places their genes into two of the many type IV secretion system (T4SS) clades. RMT systems occur in both clades, together with other systems unrelated to T-DNA transfer, and typically have an ancestral-like T4SS configuration. In contrast, AMT systems occupy a single subclade, consistent with later acquisition of their T4SS module. AMT and RMT thus represent two specialized outcomes of an older, more widespread capability for bacteria-to-plant DNA transfer.

title: A closed genome of Streptococcus agalactiae ST347/II reveals a composite integrative element coupling nisin P biosynthesis to erm(B) and tet(O) in Dominican group B Streptococcus
content: Clindamycin is the alternative for intrapartum prophylaxis against group B Streptococcus in penicillin-allergic women, and whether it works depends on which lineages carry the resistance and on the mobile element that moves it. No Dominican group B Streptococcus genome has been closed. A Streptococcus agalactiae isolate from residual diagnostic material was sequenced twice on Oxford Nanopore, annotated, and screened against 83 genomes from a published Dominican maternal colonisation survey. The assembly is one circular chromosome of 2,066,859 bp with all seven rRNA operons resolved: ST347/CC19, serotype II, carrying erm(B), tet(O), mef(J) and msr(I). Two integrative conjugative elements were delimited: one of ~34 kb related to Tn5252 carrying erm(B) and tet(O), another of ~35 kb at a tRNA-Lys gene carrying mef(J) and msr(I). An eleven-gene class I lanthipeptide cluster lies 96 bp from the first element, on the same strand and with no annotated feature between them; its precursor encodes a 31-residue core identical to nisin P. The complete operon was found in 12 of the 83 genomes, 13 of 84 (15.5%) with the isolate. tet(O) was present in all 12 carriers and none of the 71 others (Fisher p = 1.03 x 10^-14), erm(B) in 12 of 12 against 3 of 71 (p = 4.70 x 10^-12). All eleven ST1 genomes lack both the operon and the nisin resistance protein; all 15 ST1010/IV genomes carry aac(6')-Ie/aph(2'')-Ia. Clindamycin resistance is therefore tightly associated with a lantibiotic-encoding element and contiguous with it in the one closed genome; in the drafts the relationship is statistical, and co-occurrence is not linkage. The ST1 absence predicts lineage-wide susceptibility, testable by deferred antagonism.

title: Competence repression by the SPβ prophage in Bacillus subtilis revealed by transcriptomics across culture conditions
content: Prophages are near-ubiquitous in bacterial genomes, yet their effects on host physiology are typically assayed under a narrow range of laboratory conditions, mostly involving DNA-damaging agents or physical and chemical stress. This leaves open the question of which ecological and physiological conditions trigger prophage-host interaction, and whether the outcome benefits the host or the prophage. Here, we used publicly available transcriptomic data to investigate conditions promoting prophage-host interaction in Bacillus subtilis. This analysis identified that competence strongly induces prophage gene expression. To further investigate the role of competence, we used two sets of B. subtilis strains: a natural SP{beta} lysogen strain and its cured counterpart, and a natural non-lysogenic strain and the same strain lysogenised with SP{beta}. Under competence-inducing conditions, both lysogen strains showed lower expression of the competence genes compared with their non-lysogenic counterparts. This result was corroborated by transformation assays that showed consistently lower transformation efficiency in the lysogen strains, and by fluorescence microscopy using a transcriptional reporter for the late competence gene. Because competence is a principal route for horizontal gene transfer in B. subtilis, prophage repression of the competence programme constrains host DNA uptake and evolvability. More broadly, these results show that mining public transcriptomes for condition effects can guide experimental effort towards prophage-host phenotypes that conventional laboratory conditions would miss.

title: Tn-Seq-based identification of genes that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates
content: Microbial biofilms, whether surface-associated or in the form of aggregated microbes, cause a variety of persistent infections due to their inherent tolerance to antibiotic treatment. Current knowledge of the mechanistic basis of biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance is fragmented, and the relative importance of previously identified factors remains unknown. We developed a Tn-Seq-based workflow that enables simultaneous assessment of the relative antibiotic tolerance of thousands of individual clonal bacterial aggregates, each established by a single transposon mutant. Using this genome-wide Tn-Seq analysis approach, we identified several factors and pathways that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates. The majority of these factors are important for aggregate-associated tolerance to specific antibiotics, whereas some factors play a role in aggregate-associated tolerance regardless of the class of antibiotic. This methodology provides a framework that can be adapted to investigate aggregate-associated tolerance for other bacterial species and in response to different antimicrobial agents and stressors.

title: Particle-Associated Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
content: Free-living and particle-associated bacteria play distinct roles in the cycling of organic matter, but how these lifestyles are partitioned in the highly productive, rapidly warming Bering and Chukchi Seas is largely unknown. During the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, a period of anomalously warm sea surface temperatures, we collected 78 samples at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) at 12 process stations and sequentially filtered them onto 20 {micro}m, 3 {micro}m, and 0.2 {micro}m filters. Using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances, we resolved four sample clusters. Although pore size was not used to build the clusters, communities separated into a free-living cluster associated mainly with Anadyr Water (FL1; 0.2 {micro}m fraction) and three particle-associated clusters (PA1-PA3; 3 and 20 {micro}m fractions), several of which were enriched in Bacteroidia. Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia were present in all size fractions, with Gammaproteobacteria most biased toward the free-living fraction. Community structure did not differ with depth, consistent with the shallow, weakly stratified shelf, and distance-based redundancy analysis identified salinity as the sole significant environmental factor distinguishing communities. These results suggest that lifestyle and water-mass origin, rather than depth, structure size-fractionated bacterial communities on the Pacific Arctic shelf, and that freshening and changes in bloom dynamics could reshape particle-associated communities in this region.

title: Factors affecting microbial community composition in Split Lake, MB, Canada
content: Split Lake is a large freshwater lake in northern Manitoba, Canada, that receives major inflows from the Nelson River, Burntwood River, and Grassy River. In 1976, during the Churchill River Diversion (CRD) project, most of the water in the Churchill River was diverted into the Nelson River via the Rat River, and the Burntwood River, creating a large inflow pressure in the lower Nelson area, including Split Lake. Decades after its implementation, the Churchill River Diversion still influences ecological and environmental processes in the area. In this study, metabarcoding of the 16S rRNA gene was employed to characterize the microbial community structure of the lake. Environmental factors (temperature, pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen) and cyanotoxin levels were also assessed. The objectives of this study were to establish a baseline for microbiota across the lake and examine how environmental variables affect microbial population dynamics. The study was conducted in the summer of 2024, encompassing 14 sites on Split Lake and 2 sites on Assean Lake, an adjacent waterbody with minimal influence from hydroelectric infrastructure. Split Lake was found to harbor six distinct microbial clusters, with turbidity and dissolved oxygen levels correlating with different aquatic regimes within the lake. The predominant taxa in Split Lake included Actinobacteria hgcI clade and Cyanobium. Microcystin concentrations measured throughout the study were always below the Maximum Acceptable Concentration (MAC) set for Canadian federal drinking water standards.

title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
content: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state's first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78-0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of Culex annulirostris. Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.

title: Intrinsic timekeeping in Escherichia coli
content: Circadian clocks allow organisms to anticipate predictable environmental changes across the day-night cycle. Here we show that the bacterium Escherichia coli exhibits intrinsic timekeeping that anticipates daily temperature cycles. E. coli biofilms entrained to daily temperature shifts, producing 24-hour rhythms in curli plaque formation that persisted under constant temperature. Mechanistically, genetic analyses localized the autonomous timing machinery to the Rcs phosphorelay, which exhibits structural and conceptual parallels with other circadian systems. The BluFR sensory pathway, which acts upstream of the Rcs phosphorelay, linked temperature and blue-light cycles to rhythmic curli production. Flagellar promoter activity and curli production peaked at opposite times of day, suggesting daily coordination of adhesion and motility programs. These findings identify an intrinsic timing system in E. coli that expands our understanding of biological timekeeping.

title: A large, distinct family of RNase H fold nucleases associated with numerous defense systems in prokaryotes
content: During the last decade, systematic efforts aimed at the characterization of prokaryotic immunity resulted in the discovery of several hundred distinct defense systems in bacteria and archaea. This suggests that the common defense systems were already known and only rare ones remained to be identified. Here we present a genomic census and analysis of a vast family of bacterial and archaeal proteins (known as Domain of Unknown Function, DUF3800) that contain a distinct variant of the RNase H fold and are encoded in a striking 15% of the available complete prokaryotic genomes. Most of these proteins are encoded in defense islands, often in a close association with known defense systems, hence the designation WARD (Weaponized Antiphage RNase- dependent Defense). The WARDs display a broad variety of protein domain architectures and genomic contexts, including a strong link to restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas, retrons, and non-coding RNAs, suggestive of a substantial diversity in defense mechanisms. We experimentally tested 10 WARDs, mostly, encoded by standalone genes, and found that 9 of these conferred robust protection against diverse phages in Escherichia coli. Therefore, WARDs appear to represent the third most abundant defense system type in prokaryotes.

title: Non-homologous end-joining is implicated in rapid and efficient caspofungin adaptation in Nakaseomyces glabratus
content: Antifungal resistance in Nakaseomyces glabratus is a major clinical challenge, yet the cellular processes that shape its evolution remain poorly understood. Here, we used experimental evolution to investigate the role of the error-prone double-strand break repair pathway, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), in adaptation to fluconazole and caspofungin. Wild-type and NHEJ-deficient (lig4{Delta}) populations were evolved under antifungal selection for 25 days. Fluconazole resistance emerged rapidly in both genetic backgrounds and was associated with recurrent PDR1 mutations and aneuploidies. In contrast, caspofungin adaptation was delayed and less efficient in lig4{Delta} populations, with several lineages failing to survive. All wild-type caspofungin-evolved isolates carried canonical FKS2 hotspot mutations, whereas lig4{Delta} isolates predominantly acquired resistance through alternative genetic pathways. Caspofungin adaptation also frequently conferred cross-resistance to fluconazole and was accompanied by changes in the abundance of ergosterol-associated proteins. Together, these findings implicate NHEJ in promoting efficient evolution of FKS-mediated echinocandin resistance and demonstrate that DNA repair capacity can shape antifungal resistance trajectories in N. glabratus.

title: Metagenome-assembled genomes reveal water-mass-associated distribution ecotypes of marine Archaea in the Western Arctic Ocean
content: Archaea are important contributors to marine biogeochemical cycling, yet their ecology remains poorly characterized in the Arctic Ocean. The three dominant marine archaeal lineages, Marine Groups I, II, and III (MG-I, MG-II, and MG-III), are generally reported to have distinct, clade-consistent vertical distributions that are attributed to light penetration and temperature. Here, we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing of seawater collected during the 2015 U.S. Arctic GEOTRACES expedition (GN01) to recover archaeal metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from the Western Arctic Ocean and to relate their relative abundances to water mass structure. Temperature, salinity, silicate, and N* distinguished four water mass layers: the summer surface layer, the Polar Mixed Layer, Atlantic Water, and Arctic Ocean basin water. Of 155 MAGs recovered from a metagenomic co-assembly, 17 were archaeal and represented all three marine groups (four MG-I, eleven MG-II, and two MG-III). Abundance-based clustering of samples from two deep central Arctic stations separated microbial communities according to water mass. Mapping MAG relative abundance across several hundred samples revealed surface, mid-depth, and deep distribution ecotypes; members of every marine group displayed more than one ecotype, and ecotype was not consistent with MAG phylogeny. These results indicate that archaeal distributions in the Western Arctic Ocean are more closely tied to water mass stratification than to clade identity, and that previously reported clade-specific depth distributions of marine Archaea may partly reflect the limited resolution of amplicon-based surveys and shallow sampling.

title: Knockdown of fibrillarin reveals cell- and virus- dependent restriction of henipavirus replication and enhanced antiviral immune signalling
content: The henipavirus genus includes several highly pathogenic zoonotic viruses that lack medical countermeasures. The 2-O-methyltransferase fibrillarin (FBL) has been identified by genome-wide functional genomics studies as a henipavirus pro-viral factor. While FBL is a potential target for host-directed antiviral therapeutics, its impact on henipavirus replication in cell types relevant to henipavirus disease has not been explored. Here we demonstrate that depleting cellular FBL using short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) has varying impacts on henipavirus replication, depending on cell type and virus. FBL depletion in small airway epithelial cells (HSAEC1-KT) significantly impaired viral gene transcription for Hendra virus (HeV) genotypes 1 and 2 (HeV-g1, HeV-g2), and Nipah virus (NiV) Bangladesh strain (NiV-B), but not NiV Malaysia (NiV-M) strain or Cedar virus (CedV). Conversely, reduced FBL expression in bronchial epithelial (NuLi-1) cells, aortic endothelial (Telo HAEC) cells or neuroblastoma (BE(2)-M17) cells did not inhibit HeV-g1 replication. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that impaired virus replication in FBL knockdown cells was associated with enhanced activation of innate immune pathways and robust upregulation of interferon stimulated genes (ISGs). Together, these findings demonstrate a virus- and cell-type dependent impact of FBL on henipavirus replication and support a role for FBL in modulation of the antiviral innate immune response.

title: GMP-Cor: Quantifying Transcriptional Dysregulation in Antibiotic Tolerance and Persistence
content: When cells are exposed to stress, they typically activate stress-response pathways and enter a regulated growth-arrest. But what if the stress overwhelms these pathways? In such cases, cells may enter a disrupted growth-arrest - a poorly adapted, abrupt cessation of growth, characterized by a broad distribution of lag times upon stress removal. This distribution underlies antibiotic persistence during stress recovery. Therefore, gaining a deeper understanding of the disrupted growth-arrest is important for developing more effective antibiotic therapies. In this study, we perform single cell RNA-seq on bacteria in disrupted conditions. We develop GMP-Cor: a metric to quantify dysregulation and analyze gene-gene correlation patterns in sparse single-cell data. We find that gene-gene correlations are significantly reduced in disrupted cells compared to regulated cells, providing direct evidence that this tolerance-enhanced state, along with its increased membrane sensitivity, is associated with global-dysregulation. We demonstrate that GMP-Cor can extend to other biological systems, such as persistent cancer cells, where it separates proliferating from drug-arrested cells.

title: Description of Alternaria kierstenii sp. nov. from invasive garlic mustard highlights agricultural biosecurity risks of foreign weeds as pathogen reservoirs
content: Invasive weeds can increase agricultural biosecurity risks by serving as reservoirs for emerging or undercharacterized plant pathogens. Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata), an invasive brassicaceous weed in North America, occurs near agricultural landscapes and is susceptible to multiple crop pathogens. A previously undescribed Alternaria species was isolated from a diseased garlic mustard population in Maryland, USA, prompting investigation of its taxonomy, origins, and host range. De novo genome sequencing produced a near-chromosome scale assembly of 35.8 Mb comprising 17 contigs. Comparative genomic analyses with other crucifer-infecting Alternaria species revealed expanded repertoires of predicted CAZymes and peptidases, as well as unique effectors and biosynthetic gene clusters. Phylogenetic and comparative analyses supported recognition of this fungus as Alternaria kierstenii sp. nov., representing a distinct lineage within section Sonchi. Host range assays demonstrated that A. kierstenii was highly aggressive on diverse hosts in the Brassicaceae, including vegetable, ornamental, cover crop, and invasive species. The disease caused by this new pathogen manifested as foliar and stem lesions, chlorosis, necrosis, leaf death, and, in several hosts, rapid plant mortality. Amplicon sequence data from a nationwide garlic mustard microbiome study detected closely related taxa only in the plants from the eastern states of Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New York, suggesting a geographically restricted population consistent with expectations for a potentially emerging pathogen. The description of this phylogenetically unique, broad host range pathogen demonstrates the potential for widespread invasive weeds to harbor pathogens and pathogen genomic diversity with agricultural relevance, underscoring the hidden biosecurity risk of understudied invasive weeds.

title: Gut microbiome-associated adaptability of suckermouth catfish inhabiting the polluted Buriganga River: insights into heavy-metal-remediating microorganisms
content: The suckermouth catfish (SMCF), known for its pollutant tolerance and high invasiveness, is prevalent in the heavily contaminated Buriganga River in Bangladesh. This waterway, contaminated with a variety of pollutants, including heavy metals, has experienced the near-complete disappearance of native fish populations; however, the suckermouth catfish demonstrates remarkable adaptability in this environment. One objective of this study is to elucidate the role of the gut microbiome in SMCFs' adaptation to this severely polluted habitat. We performed next-generation sequencing (NGS) of gut contents from SMCFs to analyze the gut microbial profiles of the fish samples. The results indicated that the suckermouth catfish's gut is enriched with microbial communities, including Paraclostridium, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus, Bacillus, and Pseudomonas, which have the potential to remediate pollutants, including heavy metals. The subsequent aim of this research is to isolate and identify bacteria from the SMCF gut capable of remediating multiple heavy metals. We isolated three isolates with the potential to remediate multiple heavy metals and identified them as Staphylococcus pasteuri SD, Morganella morganii SAS1, and Sporosarcina saromensis SAS using partial 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and conventional techniques. All isolates showed distinct capabilities for remediating multiple heavy metals. Notably, S. pasteuri showed the highest lead (Pb) bioaccumulation (36.28%), S. saromensis showed the highest chromium (Cr) uptake (39.22%), and M. morganii showed the highest nickel (Ni) uptake (35.90%). Furthermore, these isolates exhibited remarkable metal-tolerance profiles, with maximum tolerable concentrations ranging from 125 ppm to 1000 ppm, and sustained healthy growth under metal-supplemented conditions throughout a 48-hour incubation period. This validates their potential to remediate multiple heavy metals. Collectively, the results underscore the ecological adaptability of suckermouth catfish in polluted aquatic environments, which is associated with their gut microbiome, and highlight the bioremediation potential of these gut-derived microbes as effective agents for mitigating heavy metal contamination.

title: Chromosomally-Encoded Hok/Sok Toxin/Antitoxin SystemsInhibit Phage Infection
content: The primary physiological role of toxin/antitoxin (TA) systems is phage defense; they are also used to stabilize mobile genetic elements. In the initial publication in 1996, plasmid-encoded Hok/Sok, a type I TA system (protein toxin, RNA antitoxin that inhibits toxin mRNA), was shown to inhibit T4 phage infection in Escherichia coli by reducing its efficiency of plating and burst size and by increasing the time for mature phage to form (latent period). This publication also identified that the mechanism of Hok/Sok inhibiting T4 was host transcription shutoff, arguably the most-general phage inhibition system since most phages impair host transcription. However, recently, the role of Hok/Sok in phage inhibition has been challenged. Therefore, here we investigated the role of four E. coli chromosomally-expressed, hok+/sok+ loci and the one orphan hok+ locus and found that the Hok proteins inhibit the infection of E. coli by BASEL phage 48, a Vequintavirus with myovirus morphology. Of the five Hok proteins, the greatest phage inhibition was by HokB, and infection by BASEL phages 34 and 39 were also inhibited by HokB. We also find BASEL phage 48 requires the WecB-generated receptor NGR for infection. Therefore, chromosomally-derived orphan Hok proteins, produced at physiological levels, are relevant for phage inhibition.

title: GENOME ASSEMBLIES FOR 28 PHAEOSPHAERIACEAE ISOLATES FROM CANADA
content: Glume blotch and Septoria Tritici Blotch (STB) are destructive crop diseases caused by fungal pathogens formerly classified under the genus Septoria. Recent taxonomical revisions have led to the reclassification and renaming of these fungi, some of which are now under the genus Parastagonospora, family Phaeosphaeriaceae, order Pleosporales, and class Dothideomycetes. In this study, we performed whole genome sequencing and assembly for 28 Phaeosphaeriaceae isolates from Canada. Sequencing was performed using a combination of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read and Illumina short-read sequencing platforms. Most of the genomes were very complete, BUSCO >99%, with the genomes assemblies derived from ONT sequencing having very few contigs that likely encompass entire chromosomes or chromosome arms. To determine the relationship between these isolates and similar fungi that have been previously characterized, we performed whole genome alignments to 2,668 other Dothidiomycete genomes obtained from NCBI using NUCmer. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that 27 of the isolates clustered discretely with either Parastagonospora nodorum, or Parastagonospora pseudonodorum (Parastagonospora avenae f. sp. tritici), with one genome having no other similar genome in NCBI which we hypothesize to be the first genome assembly of Phaeosphaeria pontiformis. Both P. nodorum and P. pseudonodorum species were isolated from wheat and barley and only the latter was isolated from durum, while the P. pontiformis was isolated from wheat. In summary, we sequenced and assembled the genomes of 28 isolates of Phaeosphaeriaceae spp. from Canada and the genomes add to our foundational knowledge of these plant pathogens and efforts to better understand their diversity.

title: Proteomic signatures of cold adaptation and sponge host adaptation in marine Archaea
content: Temperature shapes the biochemistry of microbial proteins, and several amino acid compositional indices have been proposed to detect cold adaptation in microbial proteomes. Whether these indices capture cold adaptation in Archaea, which are abundant in cold marine environments such as the Arctic Ocean, has not been tested. We calculated six amino acid compositional indices (arginine to lysine ratio, acidic residue proportion, aliphatic index, aromaticity, grand average of hydropathicity, and proline residue proportion) across global protein families for 142 Marine Group I (MG-I; Thaumarchaeota) and 146 Euryarchaeota genomes from the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), together with three MG-I metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) recovered from the Western Arctic Ocean. The Arctic MAGs fell within the range of index and phylogenetic distances of the wider MG-I population, and no signature of cold adaptation was detected. Instead, index values differed between the two main MG-I phylogenetic groups and between freshwater and marine genomes, and the Euryarchaeota formed five index-based clusters consistent with phylogeny. A group of 19 MG-I MAGs associated with sea sponges had significantly higher arginine to lysine ratios than other MG-I, differed in the usage of all amino acids except alanine and lysine, and had distinct codon usage and higher GC content; their anomalous placement in the MG-I phylogeny is consistent with long-branch attraction. These results indicate that amino acid compositional indices developed for Bacteria have limited power to detect cold adaptation in Archaea, but reveal strong proteomic signatures associated with host adaptation in sponge-associated Thaumarchaeota.

title: Defining nutrient dependencies of intestinal Klebsiella pneumoniae guides rational probiotic engineering
content: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major cause of antibiotic-resistant infections, yet the ecological determinants enabling its intestinal expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we combined in vivo transcriptomics and metabolomics to identify carbon sources exploited by K. pneumoniae during colonization of the antibiotic-disrupted gut across strains and dietary contexts. Despite its metabolic breadth, K. pneumoniae consistently exploited a restricted set of substrates, including arabinose, raffinose, oligogalacturonate, arabitol, xylose, and gluconate, that contributed to intestinal fitness, with related metabolic signatures also observed in antibiotic-treated human samples. Guided by these findings, we engineered Escherichia coli Nissle to enhance consumption of these nutrients and assembled a defined consortium, NICHE, designed to reinforce colonization resistance through nutrient competition. NICHE restricted intestinal expansion of multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae in preventive and therapeutic settings, with efficacy influenced by dietary nutrient availability. Together, this work defines exploitable K. pneumoniae nutrient dependencies and a framework for rational probiotic engineering.

title: Oil biodegradation and marine oil snow formation in Arctic seawater microcosms at 4 °C
content: Hudson Bay is a sub-Arctic inland sea characterized by seasonal sea-ice cover, which governs marine circulation, biological productivity, and ecosystem structure. In recent decades, the duration of sea-ice cover has declined, resulting in longer ice-free seasons that are expected to elevate marine activity and environmental exposure to anthropogenic disturbances. As such, the potential for oil spill incidents associated with increased marine operations is expected to rise. To understand microbial biodegradation dynamics associated with marine oil snow (MOS), seawater microcosms amended with diesel fuel were incubated at 4 {degrees}C for 6 weeks. We amended all our microcosms with UV-weathered Churchill diesel fuel at 1% (v/v). 16S rRNA sequencing of the incubations revealed a decline in overall microbial diversity and a dramatic increase in specialized oil-degrading taxa, with Pseudomonas and Pseudoalteromonas being the main taxa involved, as both effectively degrade hydrocarbons under ambient and stimulated conditions. Biostimulation with nutrients (NaNO3, KH2PO4) and an alternative dispersant at 0.1% (v/v) resulted in a greater abundance of MOS aggregates and rapid enrichment of oil-degraders. Simple n-alkanes exhibited the highest biodegradation loss relative to complex polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs); however, biostimulation did not substantially enhance their degradation. Additionally, UV weathering resulted in a 22% loss of PAHs, which is three times higher than the UV loss observed for n-alkanes. Biostimulated samples exhibited an elevated transfer of high molecular weight alkanes and PAHs from the oil into the aqueous phase, accompanied by a rapid enrichment of oil-degrading taxa.

title: Marine oil snow formation in microcosm incubations of artificial seawater at 4 °C
content: An oil spill in the Arctic would have far-reaching impacts on the environment, the biota, and the Inuit communities that depend on this unique ecosystem for their livelihoods. Due to the rapid retreat of sea ice in the region, the Arctic is becoming more vulnerable to oil spills. Since microorganisms are the first responders to oil contamination, understanding their behavior is critical for designing bioremediation approaches tailored to Arctic conditions. In this study, we conducted microcosm experiments at 4 {degrees}C in the dark to simulate an Arctic oil spill, using crude oil and diesel as hydrocarbon sources. Biostimulation was tested with the addition of nutrients NaNO3 and KH2PO4, and soy lecithin-Tween 80 dissolved in ethanol as an alternative dispersant. Microcosms were placed on tube rollers at 3 rpm to mimic natural wave action and run with appropriate controls to assess microbial community shifts. Our objectives were to characterize the early microbial succession associated with oil degradation and marine oil snow (MOS) formation, and to determine how nutrients, dispersants, oil type (crude vs. diesel), photochemical aging (fresh vs. weathered), and oil concentration influence these processes. We observed that the combined effect of nutrients and dispersant resulted in rapid MOS formation, occurring as early as 30 minutes after the initial setup. Microbial taxa exhibited varying tolerance to different concentrations of the same oil, and the dominant hydrocarbon degraders in fresh diesel treatments were distinctly different from those in weathered diesel. Furthermore, the nutrient-dispersant treatment promoted an earlier succession of oil-degrading taxa compared to nutrient-only or dispersant-only treatments. Together, these results highlight the importance of cold-adapted microbial communities in driving early oil degradation and MOS formation in Arctic waters, and they provide insights relevant to the development of Arctic-specific bioremediation strategies.

title: Social copying drives spatial allocation in gregarious herbivores
content: Resting patch selection in free-ranging social cattle (Bos taurus) inhabiting steep, rugged, mountain valleys is critical, because the recurrent use of flatter resting patches may reduce energetic costs and enhance fitness prospects. As these patches may constitute a limited resource, understanding their pattern of use dynamics may help explain resting patch selection. We therefore combine empirical data with a theoretical modelling framework to investigate the processes underlying resting patch selection. Using high-resolution GPS tracking data from 144 cows collected over three seasons, we identify several recurrently used resting patches located on significantly gentler slopes than expected in the valley. We then build a simple, memory-free agent-based model, which suggests that the dynamics of resting patch selection arise from social copying and, to a lesser extent, from individual heterogeneity. The model quantitatively reproduces three empirical observables: a slowing (sub-linear) discovery of new sites through time, heterogeneous occupancy across resting patches and similarity in patch use among individuals. These results suggest that collective dynamics in social species can emerge primarily from a simple social mechanism with weaker modulation from inter-individual heterogeneity, such as age, without explicitly incorporating individual memory to reproduce the aggregate patterns.

title: Atmospheric pollution contributed to destabilizing a small mammal community amid four decades of environmental changes
content: In the recent decades, climatic and land-use changes paralleled major decreases in atmospheric pollution, but unclear is how these concomitant changes shape ecological dynamics. We analyzed 39 years (1986-2024) of semiannual abundances for six small-mammal species in the Black Triangle of Europe (Czechia), a region historically-marked by acidic rains causing forest diebacks and toxic lead (Pb) deposition. We combined these small-mammal data with monthly time series of atmospheric pollution, vegetation index (NDVI), meteorology and soil moisture. We used Empirical Dynamic Modelling (EDM) to infer chaos, recover species-species and environment-species causal relationships, recover time-varying interactions, and perform out-of-sample forecasts. Small mammal populations were causally affected by atmospheric pollution, and its abrupt decline in the late 1990s likely triggered a delayed critical transition of community composition. Pollution primarily affected the dominant omnivores and strengthened the interactions among species, a hallmark of instability. We identified a second route to chaos with a role of vegetation dynamics and soil moisture that was especially strong on shrews. Our feedback-loop analysis suggests how pollution and other environmental changes favored destabilizing, positive feedbacks. Forecasting of these chaotic dynamics improved when adding the relevant environmental predictors, demonstrating that the unpredictability of chaotic systems can slightly improve when we identify the main drivers of interactions in a network, offering hope for anticipating the future of complex ecosystems. Our study offers a unique retrospective of the destabilizing effects of pollution, an overlooked macro-ecological driver.

title: Algal turf sediment dynamics across the Florida Reef Tract
content: Algal turfs and their associated sediments are dominant components of many degraded reefs, where they mediate key ecosystem processes. However, the quantification of algal turfs and their sediments across reef shelves is limited outside Indo-Pacific reef systems. We quantified algal turf length, sediment loads, and sediment grain size distribution across four reef positions (nearshore, inner, middle, and outer) at three locations along the northern Florida Reef Tract (FRT). Sediment loads were positively associated with algal turf length and generally declined moving offshore. Nearshore reefs supported algal turfs that were both 1.6-fold longer and contained 1.6-fold higher sediment loads than on outer reefs, while sediment composition shifted toward finer grain sizes offshore. Nevertheless, regardless of reef position, all algal turfs had high sediment loads ranging from 1,445 to 16,639 g m-2. Our findings suggest that cross-shelf patterns in algal turf sediment dynamics are present on Western Atlantic reefs and reveal that long sediment-laden algal turfs dominate on the FRT. These results highlight the pervasive nature of sediment-laden algal turfs on degraded reefs and emphasize the need to monitor and manage their expansion on reefs subject to chronic coastal development and climate-driven disturbance.

title: Plant-plant communication in tomato: mechanisms underpinning information transfer between plants
content: As evidences about plant-plant communication are mounting, we lack a mechanistic understanding of intricate events occurring inside and among pairs of plants. This is needed to untangle proximal causes explaining how volatiles emitted by herbivore-attacked plants can enhance plant defence in intact neighbouring plant. A comprehensive knowledge of these interactions may favour their integration in trait-based agroecological frameworks. Based on an original experiment set-up, we connected infested sender plants and intact receiver plants during 3 days. We monitored metabolomic reprogramming of sender plant and progressive adjustments in their volatile emissions. Plant-plant communication was tested according to metabolomic priming of receiver plant. Information transfer was tracked with kinetics of volatile profiles and chemodiversity metrics grounded in information theory. Our results show that sender plants infested with Phtorimae absoluta undergo deep reconfiguration of immune systems and balance their emissions of mono- and sesquiterpenoids over 3 days. These changes in airborne cues result in similar reprograming of immune system in receiver plants. Additionally, we observed herbivory-driven relationships between chemodiversity of volatile profiles produced by sender and receiver plants. Both metabolome and volatilome suggest that plant-plant communication operates as mirror effects with receiver plants matching up their defences on that of sender plants. From an adaptative standpoint, this supports the idea that information conveyed among plants is explicit enough to warn receiver plant against appropriate stress. More generally, this study points that information transfer could rely not only on composition but also on chemodiversity of volatile cues. We discuss implications related to cue detection at the molecular scale and cue propagation at the plant cover scale. Bridging composition and chemodiversity of volatile cues opens interesting avenues to study the efficiency of communication system in noisy environments.

title: Seeing danger? Visual constraints and collision risk in the Bearded Vulture Gypaetus barbatus
content: The Bearded Vulture, Gypaetus barbatus is highly vulnerable to collisions with human-made aerial infrastructures. Yet, its visual sensory system remains poorly understood, limiting the development of species-specific collision mitigation measures. To address this gap, we characterized its visual ecology across four complementary dimensions: visual fields, spatial resolution, contrast sensitivity and spectral sensitivity of cone visual rhodopsins. Bearded vultures have no blind area in the direction of travel during foraging flight, indicating that frontal visual-field limitations are unlikely to contribute to their risk of collisions. Their axial length predicts high spatial visual resolution, suggesting that insufficient spatial resolution is unlikely to be a primary cause of collisions. By contrast, Bearded Vultures display very low peak contrast sensitivity compared to other birds, which may limit their ability to detect objects when contrast with the background, or within the objects themselves, is low. Functional characterization of the four cone visual pigments indicated sensitivity spanning approximately 350-640 nm, with a potential chromatic-discrimination range from 400 to 602 nm. Together, these results identify that contrast sensitivity, rather than visual-field configuration or spatial resolution, is a key perceptual constraint to consider in collision mitigation of the Bearded Vulture. Visual markers should therefore maximize both internal contrast and brightness contrast against the surrounding environment. More broadly, our multidisciplinary approach highlights how birds differ substantially in how they perceive anthropogenic structures and illustrates the importance of incorporating species-specific sensory ecology into conservation efforts, especially in the design of collision-mitigation strategies.

title: Joint effects of climate change and urbanization accelerate plant biodiversity loss across urban green spaces
content: Urbanization and climate change are rapidly reshaping biodiversity worldwide, yet their combined impacts on ecosystems remain poorly understood. Urban green spaces (UGS) underpin urban biodiversity, but differ widely in their structure, management, and exposure to global change. Here, we examine how these two drivers jointly influence plant communities across five major UGS types (allotments, private gardens, residential green spaces, parks, and ruderal areas) in three socio-culturally distinct Swiss cities. By combining vegetation surveys from 180 sites (60 sites per city) with species-specific thermal niches, high-resolution projections of historical and future urban microclimates, and land-use change scenarios, we trace how climate-driven species loss interacts with the shifting availability of urban habitats to shape biodiversity outcomes by mid-century. We found that UGS types differed markedly in their contributions to biodiversity, with allotments and ruderal areas supporting disproportionately high compositional uniqueness. However, climate change alone was projected to drive substantial plant diversity declines across all UGS types, with 40-80% of species exceeding their thermal niches by mid-century based on climate change scenario and UGS type. Although allotments exhibited relatively greater tolerance due to broader community-level thermal preferences, this advantage was undermined by their rapid decline under urbanization. When considered jointly, climate change and urbanization generated widespread biodiversity losses through complementary mechanisms: climate change drove species declines, while urbanization amplified these losses by disproportionately reducing high-value habitats. These results reveal a consistent trajectory of biodiversity decline across urban landscapes and highlight the need to conserve high-diversity yet shrinking UGS, particularly allotments, while enhancing the ecological value and climate resilience of expanding UGS, such as parks and residential areas, to safeguard future urban biodiversity under global change.

title: Ecology of gene drives: Organism fitness under larval competition determines gene drive performance
content: Gene drives are a promising technology to control disease vectors, such as mosquitoes. However, as these interventions aim to modify and/or control the population of disease vectors, a full understanding of how gene drives interact with the ecology of the target species is essential. In this study, we explore how larval competition determines gene drive performance. We first extend an agent-based model of the larval behaviour of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to obtain detailed predictions for gene drive designs under realistic larval competition. Using Bayesian optimisation techniques, we explore the performance of different gene drive designs and find the Pareto frontier of optimal underdominant drives with different release thresholds. To understand what determines the structure of the Pareto frontier, we conduct both local and global sensitivity analyses to assess the role different parameters play in determining gene drive performance. We find that ecological parameters, which determine the behaviour of the organism, dominate over genetic parameters for much of the parameter space, although genetic parameters play an important role at the frontier. Finally, we develop stochastic and deterministic surrogate models to enable efficient comparison and simulation without imposing the computational costs of agent-based approaches.

title: A workflow to gather, clean, and standardize species occurrence records at scale for conservation applications
content: Biodiversity declines and pressing threats to wildlife necessitate data-driven approaches for conservation and management planning. Natural resource agencies, conservation practitioners, and researchers increasingly leverage digital species occurrence records. However, we still lack user-friendly and flexible tools to aggregate, clean, and standardize such data. These tools are particularly needed for speciose groups like invertebrates and plants whose natural histories are poorly or unevenly known. To provide such a tool and overcome limitations of existing options, we developed a workflow in R that encompasses the entire process of aggregating, cleaning, and standardizing occurrence records within one free software platform. It additionally can return information useful for assessing species' conservation status. Key features include user friendliness, flexibility in data sources and filtering, handling large volumes of data or multiple species, and high transparency. We demonstrate workflow functionality focusing on Texas native bees. We combined bee data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and several smaller datasets, then cleaned and standardized the combined dataset including removing duplicates. Processing 145,870 bee records took about an hour on a standard-configuration government computer. We used the resulting records in three case studies that demonstrated various uses conservation practitioners commonly implement. Case study 1 compiled a species list for Denton County, the second described phenology of bumble bees (Bombus genus) in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, and the third assessed conservation status of Bombus pensylvanicus. Our workflow greatly facilitates addressing a range of questions at various spatial and temporal scales from one vetted dataset that are tailored to the needs of a specific research objective, management question, municipality, or audience.

title: Predicting seabird-vessel interactions from bird-borne data alone
content: Seabirds often follow fishing vessels to scavenge discards and bait, benefiting from access to food but also facing the risk of bycatch. Exposure to bycatch is commonly assessed by analysing seabird-fishing interactions, typically through the spatiotemporal alignment of seabird and vessel tracking data. However, this approach may underestimate interactions when vessel tracking information is incomplete or unavailable. We tested whether seabird-vessel interactions could be identified using seabird telemetry alone and whether fishing and nonfishing vessels could be distinguished. We analysed GPS, wet-dry, accelerometer and pressure data from 273 Scopoli's shearwaters in the Northwest Mediterranean. We identified 779 vessel-attendance events using seabird GPS, Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and simulation-based tests to distinguish vessel attraction or following from chance encounters. We then trained random forest models to predict vessel-attendance from bird-borne movement and environmental metrics, testing different sensor combinations. Finally, we selected the GPS and environmental model for its performance and compatibility with GPS-only tracking data from 17 radar-equipped shearwaters, whose detectors identified nearby vessels independently of AIS. Models predicting vessel-attendance from seabird movement metrics derived from GPS, wet-dry sensors and accelerometers achieved classification rates above 90% during training. However, when tested on new individuals, 42% of their positive predictions were false-positives. Models combining environmental metrics with either GPS or GPS and wet-dry data achieved classification rates around 75% during training and generalised consistently across individuals, maintaining classification rates of 70% or above. Attendance events involving fishing (n = 482) and nonfishing vessels (n = 297) could not be reliably distinguished. Across 45 trips of radar-equipped shearwaters, the GPS and environmental model discriminated vessel-attendance in hourly bins against AIS detections (AUC = 0.85), supporting assessment of spatiotemporal attendance patterns. At the event level, only 17% of 227 predicted vessel-attendance events were supported by AIS or radar detections. However, radar detected nearby vessels during 19 predicted events lacking AIS support, highlighting the value of complementary vessel detection. This study presents a vessel-independent framework for assessing seabird-vessel interactions based solely on bird-borne data, complementing fisheries monitoring programmes, helping to identify gaps in vessel-tracking systems across poorly monitored marine regions, and informing future assessments of bycatch risk.

title: Long-term biodiversity responses to anthropogenic change are spatially and taxonomically heterogeneous across coastal wetlands
content: Coastal wetlands have undergone centuries of anthropogenic modification, yet their long-term biodiversity trajectories remain poorly understood because ecological monitoring rarely extends beyond recent decades. Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) offers a historical perspective for evaluating how biodiversity patterns vary across environmental contexts and timescales. We combined COI and 18S sedaDNA metabarcoding with 210Pb and radiocarbon chronologies, sediment geochemistry and stable-isotope records from eight coastal wetlands across four regions of the Iberian Peninsula. We reconstructed changes in eukaryotic amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness and taxonomic composition and examined their relationships with an Anthropogenic Enrichment Index (AEI) based on ten elements potentially associated with human activities. Richness-AEI relationships differed among sediment records and genetic markers. Higher enrichment was associated with lower richness for both markers in one Cadiz record, whereas COI richness increased with enrichment in the Ebro Delta. However, after accounting for calendar time, only the positive association in the Ebro Delta remained statistically significant, indicating that several initial relationships were partly explained by shared temporal trends. Exploratory rolling correlations further suggested that the direction of richness-enrichment associations varied across historical periods within individual records. Taxonomic profiles differed between markers and wetlands, while community composition was strongly differentiated among sediment records, highlighting ecological variation not captured by richness alone. Multiproxy changes also followed locally specific configurations rather than a common regional trajectory. Together, these findings show that long-term relationships between sedimentary enrichment and biodiversity are context-dependent and sensitive to the temporal perspective considered. Integrating molecular, geochemical and isotopic records can therefore improve the historical interpretation of biodiversity change and inform conservation approaches that account for taxonomic composition, environmental history and locally appropriate reference conditions.

title: Habitat degradation destabilizes complex metacommunities by disrupting dispersal
content: Habitat loss and fragmentation are rapidly reshaping ecosystems worldwide, yet their consequences for ecological stability remain unresolved. Classical theory, pioneered by Robert May, established rigorous criteria for stability; however, these apply to spatially well-mixed communities, limiting their relevance to habitat degradation. Here, we develop a metacommunity framework that integrates classical stability theory with spatial dynamics to determine how anthropogenic habitat degradation reshapes ecosystem stability. We show that metacommunities exhibit three distinct dynamical regimes following a perturbation (e.g., drought or forest fire): stable regime (perturbations decay and species persist), reactive regime (perturbations are transiently amplified, which increases extinction risk under repeated disturbances), and unstable regime (perturbations grow, causing extinctions even after a single disturbance). Dispersal fundamentally reshapes these stability transitions, converting unstable communities into reactive ones and reactive communities into stable ones. While homogeneous dispersal progressively stabilizes communities, heterogeneous dispersal maximizes stability at intermediate strengths. We further show that habitat loss and fragmentation can be comparably effective at driving species extinctions by shifting metacommunities from stable to reactive and ultimately unstable regimes, demonstrating that fragmentation per se can be as important as habitat loss. Our findings reveal that reactivity is both an early-warning signal of impending instability and a state of elevated extinction risk under recurrent disturbances.
