Gene regulatory architecture in antibiotic resistance is optimized for specific dynamic regimens
content: Cellular responses to antibiotics face a fundamental trade-off: resistance must be deployed quickly enough to prevent the accumulation of drug inside the cell, but expression of resistance genes is costly in the absence of the drug. Therefore, antibiotic responses are typically regulated, controlling not only whether resistance is expressed, but also when, how strongly, and for how long. These regulatory strategies are implemented through the strength and arrangement of promoters and operators. However, it is still not clear how the dynamics of drug exposure select for specific regulatory strategies. Here, we develop a dynamical model of a typical antibiotic response, where a transcriptional repressor senses the drug and regulates expression of a resistance protein, coupled to the effects of the drug on cell growth and gene expression. We define a cost function that weighs the different burdens imposed on the cell over the course of the response, and perform in silico optimization of the regulatory parameters under different selective pressures for three architectures of increasing complexity: constitutive expression of resistance, repression by a constitutively expressed repressor, and repression by a self-regulated repressor. We find that strong drug exposures favor constitutive expression of resistance, high costs of basal expression favor repression by a constitutive repressor, and self-regulation of the repressor is favored only when the response must provide protection while also restraining overexpression of resistance. Stochastic simulations further show that self-regulation of the repressor protects cells against fluctuations in repressor levels, which cause unnecessary induction of resistance before exposure and failed induction after exposure. This framework links the dynamics of the environment to the evolution of gene regulation, providing a basis to predict which regulatory strategies are expected to arise under specific selective pressures.

title: Dynamic allocation of MurJ coordinates bacterial growth and division
content: Rod-shaped bacteria grow by inserting peptidoglycan into the lateral cell wall during elongation and into the septal cell wall during division. These two modes of growth are driven by distinct peptidoglycan synthesis machineries that consume the shared precursor Lipid II and must be coordinated so that cell enlargement remains matched to division. However, how cells spatially allocate this shared precursor, and whether Lipid II translocation itself contributes to this coordi-nation, remain unclear. Here we show that the spatial distribution of the essential Lipid II flippase MurJ coordinates this balance in Escherichia coli. Increasing nonseptal MurJ abundance shifted cell-wall synthesis toward elongation and reduced septal synthesis. Single-molecule tracking revealed that MurJ diffuses throughout the membrane but is transiently captured at the division site, rather than stably incorporated into the septal synthesis machinery. This recruitment requires active septal cell-wall synthesis, but not ongoing Lipid II synthesis or flipping, indicating that MurJ recruitment is coupled to the active synthesis machinery rather than to substrate availability or transport. Thus, activation of septal synthesis creates transient MurJ capture at the division site, providing a mechanism to preferentially supply Lipid II for septal growth during cytokinesis. These findings reveal a capture-and-release mechanism that dynamically enriches MurJ at active division sites and thereby coordinates elongation and division in bacterial cells.

title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates
content: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous {beta}-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.

title: A Urinary Metabolomic Signature Associated with Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Children with Short Bowel Syndrome
content: Direct sampling of the small intestinal microbiome is challenging. Urinary metabolites may offer a noninvasive approach to studying microbial functional activity. We used clinically available gas chromatography/mass spectrometry to profile urinary organic acids in 94 children with short bowel syndrome, comparing those with clinically defined small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO; n=21) with those without SIBO (n=73). SIBO-associated metabolites included microbial fermentation products, dietary derivatives, and host metabolic intermediates. Metabolites enriched in SIBO mapped to aromatic amino acid metabolism, including tryptophan and tyrosine pathways, consistent with altered microbial fermentation. Many associations persisted after adjustment for intestinal anatomy, age, antibiotic exposure, and nutritional composition. These findings identified a urinary metabolic profile associated with clinically defined SIBO in children with short bowel syndrome and support further evaluation of urinary metabolomics as a noninvasive approach to studying small intestinal microbial function.

title: Second-site capsule-locus mutations, not Ade efflux disruption, determine phage susceptibility across an Acinetobacter baumannii transposon mutant panel
content: Resistance-Nodulation-Division (RND) efflux pumps have been implicated in phage adsorption in several Gram-negative bacteria, suggesting that AdeABC, AdeFGH and AdeIJK, the three characterised RND efflux systems of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, could play a similar role. We tested this hypothesis using five phages (Equilibrator, Taro, AT01, BB02, and AC03) and a panel of 13 A. baumannii strains, including nine AB5075 transposon mutants affecting AdeABC, AdeFGH, or AdeIJK. Host-range testing, efficiency-of-plating assays, capsule-associated density measurements, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing were performed to assess the relationship between genotype and phage infection. Overall, the data did not support a role for the Ade components as receptors. Phages Equilibrator, Taro and AT01 formed plaques on every strain, and the restricted host ranges of BB02 and AC03 did not correspond to disruption of a particular efflux system. Sequencing instead identified second-site mutations in the KL25 capsule locus in six of the ten AB5075 strains. These included a 1,998-bp deletion affecting wzc, substitutions in mnaA and mnaB, an ISAba13 insertion in a putative glycosyltransferase and a subpopulation-associated frameshift in wzx. AC03 formed plaques on all six strains with capsule-locus changes but on none of the five strains without them. Capsule dependence differed among the other phages: relative to the parental AB5075, infection by these phages, Equilibrator, Taro and BB02, was restricted on the capsule-deficient wzc::T26 strain, whereas AT01 efficiency was only slightly reduced. Insertion-site mapping also distinguished a near-terminal adeK insertion that retained the parental antimicrobial phenotype from an early adeK insertion associated with loss of AdeIJK function. Together, these findings identify capsule-locus variation as the strongest correlation with phage susceptibility in this panel and demonstrate the importance of verifying mutant genomes before assigning phenotypes to their annotated insertions.

title: A Staphylococcus phage recombination cassette that enables recombineering across distant bacteria
content: Modifying bacterial genomes with phage recombinases, a process termed recombineering, has enabled precise genome editing, but its reach is limited by host specificity: each new organism generally requires its own recombinase to be identified and optimized. Using known phage recombination genes as synteny anchors, we mined Staphylococcus genomes and recovered a diverse collection of phage recombination cassettes, spanning the RAD52-like annealase superfamily (Sak, Erf) and the RAD51/RecA-like Sak4 family. Functional testing of representatives in S. aureus identified several highly efficient systems that support recombineering. We engineered the most efficient of these into a single-plasmid tool that yields markerless editing in S. aureus in four days. Notably, where other recombineering systems rely on host-specific factors for nuclease evasion and ssDNA loading, this cassette encodes both activities itself: a predicted broad-spectrum nuclease inhibitor and a dedicated single-stranded DNA-binding protein. We therefore tested the cassette across phylogenetically distant hosts, and observed recombination in Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecium, Francisella novicida, and Escherichia coli. These results identify a self-sufficient class of phage recombination systems and provide a portable tool for

title: Higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals gate pathobiont expansion through succinate-driven pH modulation
content: Despite advances in defining microbiome shifts associated with inflammatory mucosal diseases, the ecological interactions that constrain or facilitate pathobiont expansion remain poorly understood. Using a six-species synthetic oral microbial community and factorial interaction screening, we identified a higher-order interaction governing the growth of the periodontal pathobiont Porphyromonas gingivalis. The core community member Veillonella parvula was the strongest positive determinant of P. gingivalis growth, but this effect was substantially reduced by the health-associated commensal Actinomyces oris. A. oris-mediated antagonism resulted from extracellular acidification and was enhanced under anaerobic conditions. Genetic dissection of A. oris fermentation revealed that lactate dehydrogenase (ldh1) contributes to anaerobic lactate production, but ldh1 deletion only partially relieved P. gingivalis inhibition. Instead, succinate, produced through a succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase pathway (sdh2), emerged as the principal driver of acidification and P. gingivalis suppression. At high cell densities, however, V. parvula consumed both lactate and succinate, reversing acidification and restoring conditions permissive for P. gingivalis growth. To assess the relevance of these interactions in vivo, we analyzed subgingival microbiome from 1,355 adults, including 555 with detectable P. gingivalis. Among these individuals, P. gingivalis abundance was negatively associated with Actinomyces abundance after adjustment for periodontitis severity, whereas this association was attenuated at high V. parvula abundance, consistent with the interaction observed in vitro. Together, these findings identify succinate as a previously unrecognized mediator of interbacterial antagonism and reveal how higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals regulate pathobiont expansion through pH modulation, with protective effects shaped by oxygen availability and metabolic cross-feeding.

title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
content: Background Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus) system comprising free-living mice (Wild:As), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like:As), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like:As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory Mus musculus (Lab-like:As). We compared these three Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory Mus musculus (Lab:Mm) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions. Results We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab:Mm and Lab-like:As than in Wild:As and Wild-like:As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild:As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like:As mice remained most similar to Wild:As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like:As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like:As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab:Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in [≥]90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild:As to 46 in Wild-like:As, 72 in Lab-like:As, and 138 in Lab:Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild:As and Wild-like:As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like:As shifted toward the Lab:Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct. Conclusions Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.

title: Bayesian phylogenetic inference accounting for recombination in whole bacterial genomes
content: Recombination is a major evolutionary force in bacteria, and ignoring it distorts phylogenies and can invalidate downstream analyses such as dating. We present ClonalFrame2, a new software for Bayesian phylogenetic inference from whole bacterial genomes that accounts for recombination. It replaces both ClonalFrame and ClonalFrameML while using the same evolutionary model, in which both mutation and recombination events occur on the branches of the clonal genealogy. The locations of recombination events are integrated out of the likelihood using a hidden Markov model, so the algorithm targets only the clonal genealogy and three recombination parameters. Ancestral sequences are recomputed whenever the tree changes and are used to propose efficient topology updates. We validated the method by analysing data-free datasets, which recovered the prior, and by comparing the approximated likelihood with the exact one on simulated data. Across 100 simulated datasets of 100 genomes each, the recombination parameters were accurately recovered, and trees inferred while accounting for recombination were many times more accurate than when ignoring it. In Staphylococcus aureus ST239, we showed that accounting for recombination gave a stronger temporal signal and a more robust dated phylogeny. In Neisseria gonorrhoeae, we identified interesting patterns of clustered recombination events happening repeatedly across the branches of the tree.

title: Orsay virus infection is associated with reduced locomotion and alters cue-dependent food choice in Caenorhabditis elegans
content: Behavioral responses are an important component of host defense; however, most evidence in Caenorhabditis elegans comes from bacterial pathogens. Here, we tested whether infection with Orsay virus (OrV) alters host dispersal and food choice and whether these responses involve the RNA-processing factor EOL-1. When measuring distance travelled over a certain period of time in control and infected wild-type animals, we observed that OrV infection was associated with lower locomotion. Moreover, when presenting infected and control animals with food choices, we observed that infected animals preferred OrV infected food sources only when the alternative was a pure food source, preferring a non-inoculated food source when both control and viral food sources contained a C. elegans filtrate. Moreover, loss of EOL-1 altered baseline locomotion and attenuated the infection-associated reduction detected in the earlier motility assay, while also modifying the food choice response, suggesting that eol-1 contributes to the motility and behavioral changes induced by OrV infection. Collectively, these results support an overall association between OrV infection and reduced host dispersal, whereas its effect on food choice depends on the sensory context. These findings extend infection-associated behavioral responses to a natural viral pathogen and identify eol-1 as a modulator of their expression.

title: Phenotypic and Molecular Characterization of Potentially New Shigella boydii Serotype in Bangladesh
content: Objective: Shigella is a major cause of bacillary dysentery among children under 5 years of age, especially in low- and middle-income countries. At Dhaka hospital of icddr,b, every year around 3% of Shigella isolates from patients with diarrhea are identified as Shigella-like organisms (SLOs). These isolates do not react with any of the existing and provisional Shigella antisera. The major aims of the present study were to characterize a unique cluster of SLOs using phenotypic and genotypic methods. Methods: A cluster of 6 SLOs was characterized using biochemical tests, serotyping, antimicrobial susceptibility, and virulence assay by using the Sereny test, PCR and compared their pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) patterns with known serotypes of Shigella spp. Antisera against the isolate were raised in a rabbit model to determine cross-reactivity with known serotypes. Results: All six SLOs were mannitol fermenting, have invasive properties, positive for ipaH and Shigella enterotoxin 2 gene along with possession of virulence plasmid of ~ 140 MDa. All isolates were resistant to ampicillin, tetracycline, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, but were sensitive to mecillinam, nalidixic acid, and ciprofloxacin. Plasmid and PFGE profiles showed that the genomic patterns of these isolates were identical but were different from all other S. boydii serotypes. Antiserum prepared against one of the isolates agglutinated with all isolates but did not cross-react with other Shigella and E. coli reference strains. Conclusion: This unique cluster of isolates might belong to a new provisional serovar of S. boydii and further analysis is required to incorporate it into the stereotypic scheme of Shigella.

title: The Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretome exerts antimicrobial activity against Burkholderia glumae by disrupting cell envelope homeostasis and impairing bacterial replication
content: The effectiveness of antimicrobials used to manage bacterial infections is increasingly threatened by the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Many conventional antimicrobials act on a single defined target that pathogens can circumvent through target modification or pathway adaptation. In contrast, antimicrobials that disrupt multiple cellular processes may impose greater fitness costs and reduce the likelihood of resistance development, making their discovery a priority for pharmaceutical and agricultural applications. We previously demonstrated that the environmental bacterium Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretes a complex mixture of molecules (secretome) with antimicrobial activity against several plants and human pathogens. However, the mechanism underlying this activity remained unknown. Here, we used the plant pathogen Burkholderia glumae to investigate the mode of action of the P. protegens PBL3 secretome. We showed that the P. protegens PLB3 secretome causes extensive cell envelope damage that results in cell death and interferes with bacterial multiplication. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed broad disruption of processes associated with cell-envelope biogenesis and homeostasis and bacterial replication. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the P. protegens PBL3 secretome acts as a multi-target antimicrobial that could be harnessed in the development of therapeutics to control bacterial infections of agricultural and medical importance.

title: Long-read shotgun metagenomics identifies distinct urogenital microbial community states associated with functional potential and urinary tract infection during pregnancy
content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections during pregnancy and are associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Although previous studies used enhanced culture, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and/or short-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize the urogenital microbiome of adult females, few have assessed the urogenital microbiome during pregnancy and thus this microbiome remains poorly understood. Here, we applied Oxford Nanopore long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize urogenital microbial composition, functional potential, metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), and the urogenital virome of pregnant females. Taxonomic profiling identified three distinct microbial community states predominated by Lactobacillus crispatus, Gardnerella species, and L. iners. The Gardnerella-predominated community was associated with a higher frequency of UTI during pregnancy. Functional profiles strongly reflected these community states, demonstrating that taxonomic differences were accompanied by distinct functional potential. Genome-resolved analysis recovered 415 MAGs, including 29 high-quality genomes, revealing substantial genomic diversity among urogenital microbes. Viral sequences, predominantly bacteriophages, also were detected in most samples, highlighting an additional component of the pregnancy-associated urogenital microbiome. These findings demonstrate that pregnant females possess distinct urogenital microbial community states and show that they differ not only in taxonomic composition but also in their functional potential.

title: Gut Roseburia hominis-derived 10-hydroxystearic acid alleviates metabolic disorder by restoring hepatic fatty acid metabolism
content: Metabolic disorders and health-promoting dietary interventions represent complementary contexts of metabolic impairment and improvement, providing an opportunity to identify gut microbial taxa associated with both disease status and dietary response. Here, we integrated five independent human cohorts spanning metabolic disorders and dietary interventions and identified Roseburia hominis as a gut microbial taxon that consistently decreased in metabolic disorders and increased after dietary interventions. Beyond species abundance, strain-level genetic variation in R. hominis provided additional information for distinguishing metabolic disorder status and stratifying cardiometabolic severity. Integration of phenotype-associated variants with circulating metabolomics prioritized ohyA, encoding an oleate hydratase, as a candidate functional determinant linking R. hominis genetic variation to host metabolic heterogeneity. An ohyA-based genetic burden score was associated with adverse cardiometabolic traits and changed longitudinally during dietary intervention, while circulating metabolites statistically accounted for part of the associations between ohyA variants and host phenotypes. Functional experiments demonstrated that R. hominis OhyA protein converts oleic acid to 10-hydroxystearic acid (10-HSA), whereas an OhyA carrying five prioritized missense substitutions showed markedly impaired enzymatic activity. In high-fat diet-fed mice, 10-HSA attenuated body-weight gain, improved glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, and reduced dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. Multi-omics profiling revealed limited remodeling of the gut microbiota but pronounced hepatic transcriptional and metabolic responses, characterized by activation of PPAR-associated lipid-metabolic pathways, altered fatty-acid oxidation and desaturation, and remodeling of hepatic lipid composition. Together, these findings establish a diet-responsive R. hominis-OhyA-10-HSA axis linking microbial variation to host metabolic dysfunction and show that 10-HSA can improve metabolic health in mice.

title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity
content: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina. Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2{Delta} complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, {beta}-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced {beta}-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2{Delta} mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1, RLM1, FKS2/GSC2, GFA1, CHS1, CRH1, SED1, and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1, GAS1, GAS3, and CHS2 expression. Expression of either Pjpgm2 or Pmpgm2 broadly shifted these responses toward wild-type levels. Selected transcriptional changes were further evaluated by qRT-PCR, which supported the major stress and cell-wall responses identified by RNA sequencing. FKS2/GSC2 showed the same directional pattern, although differences were not statistically significant by qRT-PCR. Despite this compensatory response, Pgm2-deficient cells were markedly more susceptible to sublethal caspofungin, whereas either Pneumocystis Pgm2 homolog restored tolerance toward wild-type levels. These findings link Pgm2-dependent glucose-phosphate metabolism with {beta}-1,3-glucan levels and cell-wall function. Given the importance of {beta}-1,3-glucan to the Pneumocystis cyst wall and its limited cell-wall biosynthetic pathways, these findings further support Pgm2 as an important component of Pneumocystis cell-wall biology and a potential antifungal target.

title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting
content: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase in vitro, type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets in vivo, suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference. These findings identify RNA polymerase backtracking as a key determinant of Cas10-Csm activity and support a model in which arrested transcription complexes generate substrates for DNA degradation, opening up new anti-CRISPR strategies against type III.

title: Temperature alters Culex tarsalis West Nile virus vector competence, tissue bottlenecks, and transcriptional responses
content: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Temperature is frequently the strongest abiotic factor impacting transmission in many virus-vector pairings, including WNV and Culex. However, it is unknown how temperature impacts WNV population bottlenecks and transcriptional responses to infection in Culex tarsalis. We found that elevated temperatures led to increased likelihood of transmission of rare virus variants due to increased vector competence and less stringent tissue barriers. Analysis of Cx. tarsalis transcriptional responses confirmed that WNV infection had minimal impacts on transcriptional activity. Temperature, however, induced significant changes to mosquito gene expression, whereas canonical immune gene expression minimally changed in response to infection. Thus, temperature impacts bottlenecks in the Culex-WNV system independent of known antiviral pathways, possibly by altering virus replication dynamics. While temperature had a dramatic impact on bottleneck stringency, this is likely independent of antiviral pathways and instead some other change to mosquito biology. Together, these results shed light on the relationships between temperature, virus evolutionary dynamics and antiviral immunity.

title: Replication-coupled maturation of readthrough late transcripts by a polyomavirus small T antigen
content: Productive polyomavirus gene expression requires the maturation of long, non-polyadenylated "wraparound" transcripts generated by late-strand readthrough of the polyadenylation signal on the circular genome, giving rise to structural protein mRNAs and microRNAs. In Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV), small T (sT) antigen, along with large T (LT) antigen-mediated DNA replication, drives this process. Deletion of sT (MCV{Delta}sT) attenuates late gene transcription, abolishes splicing, eliminates VP1 expression, and traps unspliced transcripts in the nucleus. Exogenous sT restored transcription and splicing in an aphidicolin-sensitive manner, requiring domains that activate DNA replication and bind chromatin. RNA sequencing revealed that sT promotes splicing and polyadenylation of wraparound transcripts, thereby increasing cytoplasmic VP1 and VP2 mRNA levels. A dual-fluorescence reporter confirmed that the leaky late poly(A) signal (LpA) was used more efficiently upon sT expression, indicating enhanced polyadenylation. Co-expression with LT abolished this effect, likely by overwhelming the capacity of the polyadenylation machinery. sT from HPyV7 and HPyV9 could similarly rescue this defect, indicating that this regulatory activity is conserved in a subset of sT proteins. Together, these findings define sT as a replication-coupled regulator of late transcript expression, splicing, and polyadenylation, revealing how a compact DNA virus converts readthrough transcription into productive gene expression.

title: RubisCO-encoding methanotrophs elicit a coordinated transcriptional response to carbon dioxide limitation.
content: The methanotroph Methylococcus capsulatus encodes the carbon dioxide (CO2)-fixing enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RubisCO), which, along with CO2 and methane (CH4), are required for growth of this bacterium. This unique, dual one-carbon metabolism is present in phylogenetically diverse methanotrophs and is likely widespread in nature, but the connection between organic and inorganic carbon metabolism in these methanotrophs is unclear. Here we used a systems approach to investigate the requisite role of CO2 in M. capsulatus metabolism and physiology. We show that atmospheric CO2 levels are sufficient for M. capsulatus cultivation, and that CO2 assimilation is linked to cellular redox balance. In the absence of CO2, M. capsulatus elicits a global transcriptional response that includes induction of RubisCO- and other inorganic carbon assimilation-encoding genes with a concomitant decrease in ribosome biogenesis and nitrogen assimilation genes typical of a bacterial stringent response. This CO2 starvation response balances biosynthesis with carbon availability. Genetic and biochemical evidence show that a LysR-type transcriptional regulator (CbbR) activates RubisCO and other CO2 assimilation gene transcription via direct promoter binding in response to elevated intracellular RubisCO substrate, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, in CO2-starved cells. These results offer insights into the essentiality of CO2 for M. capsulatus metabolism and establish a function for CbbR-family regulators in methanotrophs beyond their canonical association with CO2 fixation in autotrophic bacteria.

title: Hidden infections: Linking parasite ecology, fish health and stakeholder perceptions in Nile tilapia aquaculture in central Kenya
content: Parasite infections in farmed fish may remain unrecognised when fish-health assessment relies mainly on visible signs. We investigated metazoan parasite occurrence, parasite diversity and community composition, associations between gill-parasite burden and histological alterations, and stakeholder recognition of fish-health problems in Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) aquaculture in central Kenya. We examined 157 fish from 20 farms, assessed gill histology in 137 fish, measured water quality once per farm, and collected questionnaire and interview data from 48 stakeholders. Five metazoan parasite groups were recorded, with monopisthocotylans the most prevalent (36.3%). Higher monopisthocotylan burden was associated with a greater cumulative number of gill lesion types (odds ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.43-2.42, p < 0.001), whereas copepod burden was not. Parasite diversity was higher in the larger operational pond category across all three Hill-number orders (p = 0.006-0.008), and parasite-community composition differed between categories (PERMANOVA, p = 0.034), although these comparisons were exploratory because only four farms were in the larger category and farm category overlapped with county. Single-time-point water-quality measurements showed no clear associations with parasite burden, diversity or community composition after multiple-testing correction. Farmers and fisheries or extension officers recognised signs of poor fish health but rarely identified parasites as a specific cause, and routine diagnostic confirmation was uncommon. The findings reveal a gap between laboratory detection of parasite-associated gill alterations and farm-level recognition and diagnosis.

title: Human-caused ignitions and plant invasion drive fire-regime change in a dryland biodiversity hotspot
content: Dryland ecosystems cover much of Earths terrestrial surface and are increasingly affected by climate warming, land-use change, and biological invasion. The Sonoran Desert of western North America, a biodiversity hotspot that historically experienced infrequent fire, exemplifies how these global-change processes are driving ecosystem transformation through the emergence of novel disturbance regimes. Using records of more than 73,000 wildland fire events, we quantified anthropogenic and environmental controls on fire ignition, size, and spread across the Sonoran Desert. Human-caused ignitions accounted for 95.5% of all recorded fires since the early 1990s and were concentrated near roads, buildings, and other areas of human activity, particularly during late spring. In contrast, lightning-caused ignitions were rare within the Sonoran Desert and occurred primarily in adjacent montane forests during late summer months. Consistent with broader trends across the western United States, fires were typically largest when they ignited far from roads, where access is limited, and fire management often relies on indirect attack strategies. Pre-fire annual and perennial herbaceous vegetation both promoted fire spread, with detectable effects at cover values as low as 5%, while bare ground reduced fuel connectivity and constrained fire growth. Rather than exhibiting a distinct threshold response, fire spread increased linearly with herbaceous cover, suggesting that even modest increases in fine fuels can alter fire behavior in this historically fuel-limited ecosystem. Together, our results illustrate that human ignitions determine where fires occur, whereas herbaceous fuels determine whether those ignitions spread, driving fire-regime transformation across an iconic North American desert. Managing and adapting to this novel fire regime will require coordinated efforts to reduce human-caused ignitions, limit invasive herbaceous fuels, maintain bare-ground interspaces, and rapidly suppress fires. More broadly, our findings identify the mechanisms controlling fire regime change in dryland ecosystems and provide a framework for anticipating ecosystem transformation under ongoing global change.

title: High-density environmental DNA metabarcoding reveals fine-scale three-dimensional structure of a fish community in a semi-closed bay
content: Coastal fish assemblages are influenced by environmental heterogeneity across horizontal and vertical dimensions, yet their fine-scale three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. We investigated spatial variation in fish assemblages using environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding at 100 stations across three depth layers (300 samples) in Maizuru Bay, a semi-enclosed coastal bay in Japan. Concurrent hydrographic measurements were used to examine associations between fish assemblage composition and environmental conditions. We detected 216 fish species, with mean species richness decreasing from 28.4 at the surface to 16.4 at the bottom. Thirty-three species were detected exclusively below the surface. Fish assemblage composition differed significantly among depth layers and exhibited pronounced horizontal turnover along the bay axis. Although depth, geographic position, and measured environmental variables were associated with assemblage composition, they collectively explained only 13.0% of the variation. The independent contribution of spatial position (2.9%) exceeded those of depth (0.8%) and measured environmental variables (0.9%). These findings demonstrate substantial three-dimensional heterogeneity in coastal fish assemblages that cannot be fully explained by conventional hydrographic measurements. Our study highlights the importance of integrating horizontal and vertical sampling to characterize coastal fish biodiversity and improve marine ecosystem monitoring.

title: Virus coinfection in plants determined by ecological responses to environmental heterogeneity
content: Community ecology is acknowledged as a relevant causative agent of epidemiological processes of plant viruses and has consequences for coinfection and virus and host evolution. Plant virus coinfection is common, but factors that promote non-random virus interactions above the population-level are unknown. Here, we analyse intrinsic and extrinsic factors in virus-host and virus-virus interactions by eighteen generalist virus species of a diverse multi-host-multi-virus system. Coinfection among viruses with broad host ranges, diverse modes of horizontal transmission, and interspecific variation in responses to environmental heterogeneity is expected to be shaped by ecological as well as evolutionary constraints. We analyse patterns of coinfection from 1,931 individual plants in 94 species from multiple plant communities of distinct habitat types and show that above 50% of plants were coinfected by 2-8 viruses. To analyse the role of environmental variables on the observed virus associations we used Markov and conditional random fields modelling. Results showed that a large majority of coinfections were random interactions, consistent with ecological fitting, and only a minor fraction being non-random associations. Random field models underscored the relevance of common responses to environmental heterogeneity driving coinfection, and strongly suggest mode of horizontal transmission as a causal agent. Results highlighted a major role of between-host, rather than within-host processes in driving coinfection. This study is a considerable addition to the understanding of drivers of virus coinfection and, hence, of virus community ecology and epidemiology.

title: Social ties are maintained through sensory adaptations in green chromides
content: Sensory systems exhibit considerable plasticity in response to environmental changes, yet the functional implications of such plasticity remain poorly understood, particularly regarding how changes in visual gene expression influence social behaviour. To address this gap, we investigated how visual sensory plasticity relates to conspecific preferences in green chromides (Etroplus suratensis), an Indian cichlid that relies on vision for social preferences towards conspecifics. We first characterized retinal opsin and chromophore-related genes through transcriptomic analysis and subsequently examined behavioural and molecular responses under sequential white- and blue-light environments. We quantified visually mediated conspecific preferences, and the expression of rod and cone opsins and the chromophore-related gene Cyp27c1 at regular intervals. Green chromides retained stable conspecific preferences despite contrasting light environments. Opsins exhibited plasticity, with long wavelength-sensitive opsin (LWS) increasing under blue light, whereas short wavelength-sensitive opsins remained unchanged. Additionally, Cyp27c1 expression declined under blue light, suggesting a potential shift towards increased A1 chromophore utilization. Together, these findings suggest that green chromides undergo multiple molecular modifications under contrasting light environments, whereas maintaining stable social behaviours, demonstrating the cross-talk between the two is not straightforward. Overall, these results highlight that unraveling the underlying proximate mechanisms of behavior is highly intricate, involving multiple pathways, starting from perception (at the retinal level) to post-processing of the stimulus.
