title: Extratropical Forcing of Tropical Subsurface Oxygenation Under Future Warming
content:
Abstract
The global ocean overall is losing oxygen under climate warming, yet most climate models project increasing subsurface (100–1,000 m) oxygen concentrations in the tropical “shadow zones”—poorly ventilated low‐latitude regions of the Indian, eastern Atlantic, and eastern Pacific Oceans. Previous studies have attributed this projected oxygen increase partly to improved ventilation in the tropical subsurface, often explained by enhanced tropical stratification that suppresses upwelling. However, such local stratification changes cannot readily account for the basin‐scale reduction in tropical upwelling projected under climate warming. Here we show that the improved tropical subsurface ventilation arises primarily from remote extratropical forcing. Using climate model simulations and a suite of process‐based ocean experiments, we demonstrate that extratropical warming and freshening weaken subtropical water mass formation and induce cross‐hemispheric overturning adjustments that deepen isopycnal surfaces across ocean basins. This adiabatic deepening displaces well‐ventilated, oxygen‐rich shallow waters to greater depths, thereby improving the ventilation and oxygenation of low‐latitude subsurface waters. These results provide a dynamic explanation for the projected oxygenation response in tropical shadow zones and highlight the central role of ocean circulation and extratropical processes in shaping future ocean oxygen distributions.

title: Transcription of the uropathogenic Escherichia coli vat gene is driven by multiple promoters whose activity is modulated by the cyclic AMP receptor protein
content:
Abstract
Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC), a cause of urinary tract infections, expresses various virulence factors to enable it to infect and persist, overcoming host defences. One of these is the vacuolating autotransporter toxin (Vat), which causes vacuole formation and cellular damage in bladder epithelial cells. Bacteria tightly regulate transcript initiation of most virulence factor genes using either bespoke transcription factors, or, sometimes, global transcription factors, such as the cyclic AMP receptor protein (CRP), which regulates hundreds of bacterial genes, typically responding to nutritional stress. We report that CRP binds to the regulatory region of the vat gene and describe the complex nature of regulation of vat gene transcription in UPEC CFT073. In vivo and in vitro analysis revealed that whilst the vat regulatory region contains a CRP-activated promoter, P1, two additional promoters, P2 and P3, ensure that net promoter activity is not dependent on CRP. Functional -10 and -35 elements were identified for the P2 promoter, which is suppressed by CRP binding, blocking the -35 element. Expression from the P3 promoter is also supressed by binding of CRP over the transcript start site.

title: Biomolecular mechanisms of iron oxidation in prokaryotes: a protein focused review
content:
Abstract
Iron oxidation by prokaryotes is a fundamental biogeochemical process with broad environmental and biotechnological significance. Despite growing knowledge of iron oxidation pathways at the systems level, the structural and biochemical characterization of individual proteins directly responsible for ferrous iron [Fe(II)] oxidation remains limited. This review provides a critical survey of the molecular knowledge of proteins directly involved in Fe(II) oxidation across phylogenetically diverse microorganisms (including acidophilic bacteria and archaea and neutrophilic bacteria) spanning aerobic, anaerobic, and phototrophic metabolic strategies. For each protein (Cyc2, Cyt572, Cyc2PV-1, sulfocyanin, FoxC, PioAB complex, MtoAB complex, and Iro), we discuss structural features, cofactor binding and localization, and redox properties, integrating experimental biochemistry with structural predictions. We further provide an overview of how broader computational approaches, including molecular dynamics simulations and quantum methods, also for redox potential calculations, can complement experimental data to yield mechanistic insights into iron oxidation. Finally, we highlight existing knowledge gaps and outline biotechnological applications (including bioleaching, wastewater treatment, bioremediation, and bioelectrocatalysis) that stand to benefit from a deeper molecular understanding of these proteins.

title: Granuloma-like structures in tuberculosis a critical review of their biology, quantitative behavior, and translational use
content:
Abstract
Tuberculosis (TB) granulomas are complex multicellular structures central to disease pathogenesis and treatment challenges, notably due to bacterial persistence and immune modulation. Existing animal and in vitro models do not fully capture granuloma heterogeneity and immune complexity. Here, we review the biology and applications of granuloma-like structures (GLS) derived from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which recapitulate key features of early granuloma formation, including macrophage differentiation, lymphocyte involvement, and cytokine dynamics. Quantitative analysis identifies conserved bacterial growth trajectories and recurrent aggregate sizes, despite protocol diversity and donor variability. Furthermore, a minimal theoretical model illustrates how aggregate size may influence drug efficacy, through physical and biological mechanisms. Although underutilized in drug screening, GLS offer a promising intermediate platform by bridging simple cell monolayers to animal models, particularly for evaluating host-directed therapies. Standardized metrics and integration with computational models are needed to enhance reproducibility and translational relevance. GLS thus represent a valuable tool to investigate host–pathogen interactions and advance TB drug development under controlled immune conditions.

title: Tat-dependent protein translocation and its evolution
content:
Abstract
The Tat system is a general translocation machinery responsible for the transport of folded proteins across biological membranes that are energized by a proton or sodium motive force. Protein substrates are characterized by usually amino-terminal signal peptides harboring a conserved twin-arginine sequence motif. Phylogenetic analyses suggest that a Tat system was already present in the last universal common ancestor. Today, Tat systems are found in bacteria, archaea, and bacteria-derived organelles. Minimally, Tat systems are composed of one TatC-family component and one TatA/B-family component, with multiple copies of these components forming the functional translocon, while more complex Tat systems exist that require additional homologs of TatA/B or TatC. Due to its ability to translocate folded proteins with bound cofactors, the Tat system is essential for a wide range of important physiological pathways, such as many anaerobic respirations or photosynthesis. With a focus on evolutionary aspects, and by including recent structural and mechanistic insights, we herein review our current knowledge on this mechanistically unique translocation pathway.

title: From holobionts to habitats: opportunities and limitations of microbiome-assisted restoration strategies of marine ecosystem engineers
content:
Abstract
Marine ecosystem engineers such as corals, seaweeds, and seagrasses are foundational to coastal ecosystems, yet are declining at unprecedented rates due to accelerating climate and anthropogenic pressures. Microbiome-based approaches have attracted attention as a promising avenue to enhance the resilience and recovery of these organisms. Over the past decade, diverse marine probiotic microbes have been isolated and shown to positively influence key host life functions, including growth, development, reproduction, responses to environmental stressors, and pathogen defence. However, current research remains confined to laboratory settings, with few practical field applications tested or utilised, likely driven by practical and technological challenges and lacking communication between science and policy. To help close this gap, we propose a set of risk and success assessment criteria for microbiome-assisted restoration. This framework is built around four pillars: (1) ensuring environmental compatibility of candidate probiotics, (2) establishing scientific validation for their mechanisms of action, (3) securing legal clarity before application, and (4) implementing mandatory in situ monitoring to evaluate ecological outcomes. By integrating these pillars into a cycle of risk assessment, monitoring, and adaptive management, microbiome-assisted restoration could progress from an experimental concept to a practical application complementing existing conservation tools, strengthening the resilience of these ecosystems.

title: Links Between Environmental Quality, Gut Microbiota, and Host Performance in Nutrient‐Impacted Springs
content:
Gut microbiota and freshwater chemistry jointly shape host performance in least killifish, Heterandria formosa. Matching microbe inoculation to native habitat water chemistry nearly doubled reproduction, while nutrient enrichment reduced growth and altered metabolism. These findings highlight microbe and environment interactions as key contributors to freshwater fish resilience and conservation.

ABSTRACT
Microbial symbionts may enhance adaptation to environmental stress, yet their role in nutrient‐enriched freshwater habitats remains unclear. We conducted a full‐factorial laboratory experiment with least killifish, Heterandria formosa, manipulating water chemistry from four Florida springs and gut microbiota inoculations from conspecifics at those sites. Sequencing of 16S rRNA revealed that gut microbial richness was higher in fish reared in less nutrient‐loaded waters, but inoculation treatments, if successful, did not produce significant shifts in composition. Gut communities consistently differed from ambient water, with enrichment of Pseudomonadota and Planctomycetota. Females grew more slowly in the most polluted water. In a parallel result, males displayed higher mass‐specific metabolic rates in the most nutrient‐loaded water. Reproductive output per female nearly doubled when experimental microbiota and water originated from the same site, despite stable microbial diversity, though parentage and inoculation success were not verified; therefore, these results should be interpreted cautiously. These results indicate that environmental quality shapes gut microbiota and host performance, and that matching microbial communities to habitat conditions can boost reproduction. Such interactions may contribute to freshwater fish resilience and merit integration into conservation strategies.

title: Mycoviruses in the Genomic Era: Ecological, Evolutionary and One Health Perspectives
content:
High‐throughput sequencing and petabase‐scale data mining have transformed mycoviruses from isolated curiosities into ubiquitous components of the biosphere, revealing deeply divergent lineages across fungal hosts and environments. We compare discovery workflows and their biases and grade the evidence for cross‐kingdom viral transfer, separating experimental demonstration from phylogenetic inference. Within a One Health framework, hypovirulence‐based biocontrol is the best‐supported application, whereas mycovirus‐based antifungal therapy remains a long‐term hypothesis.

ABSTRACT
Mycoviruses are widespread and ecologically significant components of the biosphere, acting as hidden modulators of fungal diversity, metabolism and symbiotic interactions. This review synthesizes historical and technological advances in mycovirus discovery within an integrative One Health framework linking human, animal, plant and environmental health. We trace the transition from early dsRNA‐based detection and Sanger sequencing to modern metatranscriptomic, metagenomic and petabase‐scale data‐mining approaches that have dramatically expanded known mycovirome diversity, uncovering deeply divergent RNA virus lineages. We survey the major mycovirus families and their genomic architectures and compare the strengths and inherent biases of current discovery strategies. We critically assess evidence for horizontal viral transfer across kingdoms, distinguishing experimentally demonstrated cross‐host replication from phylogenetic inference alone and review mycovirus roles in modulating fungal virulence in agricultural and clinical settings, explicitly separating robust findings from preliminary or speculative reports. Hypovirulence‐based biocontrol of phytopathogenic fungi emerges as the only application currently supported by field‐validated evidence, whereas mycovirus‐based therapy for human fungal infection remains a long‐term hypothesis rather than a near‐term clinical strategy. We underscore the need to combine rigorous experimental and computational approaches to characterize mycovirome complexity and function and outline priority research directions for the coming decade.

title: Riverine organic matter dynamics in the headwaters of the Yellow River under climate change
content:
Riverine organic matter dynamics in the headwaters of the Yellow River under climate change
Xiaoxiao Wang, Jie Wang, Tianqing Ren, and Jun Zhou
Biogeosciences, 23, 7939–7954, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7939-2026, 2026
Organic matter dynamics in alpine rivers are highly sensitive to climate change, yet long-term trends in riverine organic matter (ROM) remain poorly. Using satellite and in situ observation data and machine-learning models, we discovered that midstream regions of the Yellow River's headstream show higher and increasing ROM linked to wetter conditions, richer soils, and greater vegetation, but climate change is projected to reduce ROM in the Yellow River's headstreams by the end of the century.

title: Tracking sulfate, magnesium and amorphous phases in cultured benthic foraminifera
content:
Tracking sulfate, magnesium and amorphous phases in cultured benthic foraminifera
Guillaume Paris, Caroline Thaler, Marc Dellinger, Jérôme Aléon, Smail Mostefaoui, Alice Aléon-Toppani, Claire Rollion-Bard, David Troadec, Guillaume Yangshu Wang, and Annachiara Bartolini
Biogeosciences, 23, 7911–7937, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7911-2026, 2026
To understand sulfate incorporation in the calcitic tests of foraminifera, we grew specimens with labeled sulfur. We documented sulfur, magnesium and calcium distribution across the cell, together with the ultrastructure of the test. S and Mg often co-occur and are particularly concentrated in amorphous blocks within organic linings . Strong biological control of those three elements likely plays a role in amorphous calcium carbonate formation and its evolution to calcite.

title: Microscale C-O-S isotope signatures record microbial sulfate reduction in ancient deep subsurface pyrite–calcite–barite assemblages
content:
Microscale C-O-S isotope signatures record microbial sulfate reduction in ancient deep subsurface pyrite–calcite–barite assemblages
Eric Runge, Vanessa Fichtner, Mikael Tillberg, Martin Whitehouse, and Henrik Drake
Biogeosciences, 23, 7893–7909, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7893-2026, 2026
We investigated past microbial processes in the deep continental subsurface by stable C-O-S isotope analyses of fracture-hosted pyrite-calcite-barite assemblages. These minerals show signatures of two different pathways of microbial sulfate reduction, linked to local hydrogeochemical conditions. We further suggest that these local conditions are also crucial in controlling the preservation of microbial biosignatures in deep subsurface mineral assemblages.

title: Salinity, Inundation, and Redox Gradients Shape Reactive Iron and Organic Carbon Spatial Patterns in Tidal Wetland Soils
content:
Abstract
Tidal wetland soils are important blue carbon reservoirs; however, how hydrological and redox gradients regulate reactive iron (Fe) pools and their relationships with soil organic carbon remain poorly resolved. We examined soils at five sites along the brackish‐to‐freshwater Elbe estuary, spanning salinity, inundation, and vertical redox gradients, to assess how operationally defined reactive Fe pools covary with soil organic carbon (SOC). Since recurrent reducing conditions complicate conventional interpretations of dithionite‐citrate (Fed) and acid ammonium oxalate (Feo) extractions, we complemented these single‐step methods with a sequential Fe extraction scheme and reference‐mineral tests. The latter showed overlapping extraction selectivity, confirming that the sequential fractions are operational rather than uniquely mineral‐specific. Large ascorbate‐ and HCl‐extractable fractions were consistent with substantial contributions from short‐range ordered Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides and Fe(II)‐bearing phases, particularly in frequently inundated and reduced soils. Reactive Fe and SOC varied among sites without a consistent directional response along the estuarine salinity gradient, whereas fine‐grained and vegetated soils generally contained more SOC and reactive Fe. Fed and Feo tended to be higher in less frequently inundated low‐ and high‐marsh soils and remained positively associated with SOC after accounting for fine fraction, depth, site, and inundation zone. In contrast, no individual sequential Fe fraction showed a robust independent relationship with SOC. These results demonstrate that hydrological and redox gradients reshape operationally defined reactive Fe pools that covary with SOC, underscoring the role of Fe transformations in the context of sea‐level rise and tidal wetland blue carbon dynamics.

title: Evolution of Potential Vorticity and Kinetic Energy Conversion During Subsurface Eddy Merging in the Northern South China Sea
content:
Abstract
Oceanic mesoscale eddy merging is critical for material transport, but subsurface (intrathermocline) eddy merging processes and mechanisms remain poorly understood due to limited observations. Using a 1/50° model with assimilation of underwater glider, satellite, and reanalysis data, we investigate a merging event of two subsurface anticyclonic eddies in the South China Sea (SCS). The potential vorticity (PV) was vertically redistributed during merging, with a minor rise in the upper layer, a pronounced reduction in the middle layer (eddy’s core), and a minor increase in the deeper layer. Based on energy diagnostics, we find that positive anisotropic barotropic instability (BTI) overwhelmingly governs the subsurface eddy’s core (30–150 m) during the merging event. The decomposition of BTI suggests that the normal strain component drives this forward kinetic energy (KE) cascade, which favors vertical turbulence and weakening of stratification, and causes a decrease in PV. These findings establish a link between eddy’s PV and energetic dynamics, advance understanding of the oceanic cross‐scale energy cascade, and are expected to provide critical implications for global ocean circulation and climate modeling.

title: Sources and Alterations to Trace Metal Distributions Through the Eastern Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Baffin Bay
content:
Abstract
On its way south to the North Atlantic Ocean, Arctic water of both Atlantic and Pacific origin is modified by sea ice and glacial melt, meteoric water (MW), and continental shelves. In the eastern Canadian Arctic, this modification occurs during transit through Nares Strait, Jones Sound, Barrow Strait, Lancaster Sound, and southward through Baffin Bay to Davis Strait. We sampled these key gateways in 2019, 2021, 2022, and 2024 for dissolved iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni), copper (Cu), zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), vanadium (V) and barium (Ba), and used a linear mixing model employing salinity, Ba, and Arctic nitrate‐phosphate endmembers to estimate water mass contributions. Pacific‐derived and Atlantic‐derived waters are strongly separated in several gateways, particularly Davis Strait, where Atlantic waters carry Mn, Fe, and V into Baffin Bay in the east, while Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd, and Ba are concentrated in Pacific outflow waters in the west. Elevated Pb in western Davis Strait likely reflects mobilization of legacy contamination from a former Distant Early Warning site. Cd:PO4 ratios, Cd* and N* identify Chukchi‐shelf modified Pacific waters through Parry Channel and northern Nares Strait, though mixing in the Canadian Arctic Archipelago (CAA) attenuates this signature before waters reach Baffin Bay. Trace metal supply to Baffin Bay, and ultimately to the North Atlantic, therefore depends on the balance of Pacific‐ and Atlantic‐origin water entering the bay and on local inputs from ice melt and legacy contamination, both of which are vulnerable to continued Arctic warming.

title: Vertical Compression of the Mesopelagic Deep Scattering Layer Associated With the Oxygen Minimum Zone in the Eastern Arabian Sea
content:
Abstract
The Deep Scattering Layer (DSL), formed as an antipredator refuge, shapes the ecology of the mesopelagic system. Despite its ecological importance and distinctive hydrography of the Indian Ocean, a comprehensive understanding of the determinants of its daytime residence depth is still lacking. We identify hydrographic and biological controls on the daytime vertical position of DSL by integrating shipborne ADCP acoustic backscatter, Multiple Plankton Net (MPN) tows, CTD profiles, and satellite‐derived products. The DSL became progressively thinner within the OMZ, with a deeper upper boundary and a shallower lower boundary, indicating compression of available daytime habitat under low‐oxygen conditions. Among the environmental variables examined, dissolved oxygen exhibited the strongest relationship with DSL structure, whereas indirect indicators suggested a secondary influence of ambient light conditions. Taxonomic and isotopic analyses revealed reduced abundance of several migratory taxa within the OMZ and indicated trophic variability among dominant migrators such as euphausiids, myctophid larvae, and Pleuromamma indica. These findings demonstrate that dissolved oxygen is a major control on DSL formation in the Arabian Sea and that OMZ conditions influence both the physical structure of the DSL and the ecological characteristics of its constituent organisms. The study provides a regional baseline for evaluating how future ocean deoxygenation and OMZ expansion may affect mesopelagic ecosystems and their contribution to carbon cycling.

title: Genomic Divergence and Variation in Developmental Plasticity Across Inselberg Populations of a Tropical Frog
content:
ABSTRACT
Understanding how phenotypic plasticity and local specialization are shaped by gene flow and environmental heterogeneity requires natural systems that vary in both spatial isolation and environmental conditions across the landscape, yet such systems are uncommon. Naturally discontinuous inselbergs may provide this opportunity. Here, using populations of the inselberg‐specialist frog Leptodactylus lithonaetes, we evaluated whether habitat discontinuity translates into restricted gene flow and genetic structure and then tested how variation in connectivity and environmental heterogeneity shapes the balance between phenotypic plasticity and local specialization. We predicted that populations with higher environmental heterogeneity and higher gene flow would evolve plasticity in growth and development, whereas populations in more homogeneous environments and more genetically isolated would exhibit reduced plasticity and increased specialization. Using > 11,000 SNPs, we showed that the apparent habitat discontinuity among nine inselbergs spanning 300 km was reflected in a strong population structure and varying levels of gene flow among inselbergs, in an isolation‐by‐distance pattern. We then tested whether tadpoles alter their size or timing at metamorphosis to pond‐drying risk, and whether these plastic responses vary among populations with environmental heterogeneity (seasonality). Although tadpoles did not plastically accelerate metamorphosis under pond‐drying risk, the magnitude of body mass reduction under desiccation stress differed among populations, indicating developmental plasticity in body mass. Northern localities, exposed to greater environmental heterogeneity, showed greater survival and less body weight loss, resulting in higher tolerance to environmental stress than southern localities. Even in the absence of developmental acceleration, population‐level variation in responses to environmental stress is congruent with reduced plasticity, or increased specialization, in isolated populations exposed to less heterogeneous environments.

title: Dietary Niches and Their Consequences for Five Insectivorous Passerines in a Seasonal Boreal Setting
content:
ABSTRACT
To understand the effects of climate change and other disturbances on ecosystems, methodologies capable of unravelling the complexity of biotic interactions are vital. Here, we present a dietary study on five passerines nesting in boreal forests: the crested tit Lophophanes cristatus, willow tit Poecile montanus, blue tit Cyanistes caeruleus, great tit Parus major, and pied flycatcher Ficedula hypoleuca. We used metabarcoding to describe their arthropod prey during the breeding season, and linked diets' properties with breeding success to understand birds' dependence on particular prey. The birds' diets contained hundreds of arthropod taxa, showing considerable richness and interannual variation. Most prey identities were resolved to species level. The most common prey were Lepidoptera, followed by Diptera, Coleoptera and Araneae. Dietary overlap was low to middling, conformed to temporal overlap, and fluctuated across the three studied years. Higher consumption of lepidopterans and their larvae was strongly associated with higher breeding success in blue tits and, to a lesser extent, great tits. In contrast, crested tits, willow tits and pied flycatchers had a more constant breeding success without relying on specific prey. The results suggest that the more recently settled blue tits and great tits are less capable of optimally utilizing the comparatively resource‐poor boreal environments. The apparent good adaptation to local foraging conditions contrasts to declining population trends in the Red‐Listed crested tits and willow tits. Our study highlights the complexity of arthropod communities and insectivore food webs, and showcase how molecular methods can be used to study ecological interactions.

title: The Influence of the Antarctic Circumpolar Deep Water on Deep‐Sea Eukaryotic Biodiversity and Distribution in the Western Pacific Ocean
content:
ABSTRACT
The Antarctic region, a centre of biodiversity origin, influences deep‐sea ecosystems by supplying species to distant regions. Understanding the influence of Antarctic Upper Circumpolar Deep Water (UCDW) on deep‐sea eukaryotic diversity is therefore essential for outlining global biodiversity patterns. Our results showed the UCDW community exhibited ~1.5‐fold higher taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity than the Caroline Basin control community and contained a substantial proportion of unique taxa across multiple eukaryotic lineages. Source tracking using the available Southern Ocean surface‐water reference detected a 4.42% Antarctic‐associated contribution to the UCDW community. Indicators and generalists of the UCDW community shared > 97% sequence identity with Southern Ocean samples. The community analyses suggested that the Yap‐Mariana Junction choke point did not constitute a strong barrier to connectivity between adjacent basins, consistent with UCDW‐mediated dispersal into the Philippine Basin. The UCDW microbial dispersal into the Philippine Basin occurs through two potential routes: directly through the YMJ at 2000–3000 m and via upwelling across seamounts at 500–750 m. Governed mainly by neutral, dispersal‐driven processes, the UCDW community showed strong genetic exchange and connectivity. These findings suggest a role for deep‐water circulation in shaping the diversity and distribution of eukaryotes detected in western Pacific deep‐water samples.

title: Cavity‐dwelling “acorn ants” nest in aborted red pine cones
Plant–hummingbird interactions, floral abundance, and floral traits for three altitudinal gradients in the Americas
content:
Abstract
Plant–animal interactions result in many ecosystem services, such as pollination. In the western hemisphere, and especially the Neotropics, hummingbirds are important pollinators for thousands of plant species, yet there is much to be learned about the spatial and temporal variation in mechanisms influencing these interactions. We collected an extensive dataset from 39 sites across elevation gradients spanning 4.7–3522 m above sea level in three regions: the Pacific slope of the Talamanca Mountain Range in central‐southern Costa Rica, the Chocó‐Andean region of northwestern Pichincha province in Ecuador, and the Atlantic Forest in southeastern Brazil. Because these regions have very different biogeographic histories, comparing them allows us to identify general patterns of interactions. Data on flower abundance and plant–hummingbird interactions were gathered monthly for 1.5–2 years along 1.5‐km transects situated along an elevation gradient in each country during 2017 and 2024. Trait data for flowers were also measured. This effort resulted in 95,824 pairwise interactions between 715 plants and 79 hummingbird species, and also 873 interactions with another 12 bird species in Ecuador. These data are being used to develop a predictive framework on species interactions necessary to understand and conserve biodiversity and ecosystem services. These data also provide detailed information on plants important for hummingbird conservation which have, for example, been used to guide restoration projects. The data are available for reuse under CC BY 4.0 licensing. Please cite the data release on Zenodo and this data paper when reusing the dataset.

title: Snapshot Europe 2021–2022: The first public dataset from a Europe‐wide camera‐trap survey of terrestrial vertebrates
content:
Abstract
Managing and conserving species in the face of the current biodiversity crisis requires consistent information on the status of wild animal populations across large spatiotemporal scales. Budgetary constraints, differences in national legislation, and the challenges of coordinating logistics transnationally often limit survey efforts to spatial extents that rarely encompass the full distribution of many species, and temporal extents that rarely exceed a few years. These limitations are particularly relevant in regions like Europe, where multiple countries often share and manage populations of the same wild species across national borders and under different legislative frameworks. Cooperation and collaboration can help overcome some of these challenges. Here, we present data from the first 2 years of Snapshot Europe, a collaborative, coordinated, and standardized European‐wide mammal survey conducted by camera‐trap experts working across the continent. Between mid‐August and mid‐November of 2021 and 2022, more than 160 researchers simultaneously collected camera‐trap data at 1198 and 967 locations across 81 and 55 arrays and 22 and 23 countries, respectively, for a total of 90,230 camera‐trap days (49,033 and 41,197 in 2021 and 2022, respectively), with 91% of the data collected in September and October. Thirty (28%) out of 106 arrays across the 2 years were sampled both in 2021 and 2022, allowing for comparisons of estimates over time. All data were managed and processed in Wildlife Insights (https://www.wildlifeinsights.org/); each record was reviewed by at least one participant who confirmed or edited the initial classifications provided by the AI model integrated into the platform. The final dataset contains a total of 94,441 observations of 63 species of mammals and 5024 detections of 78 species of birds. These data capture a subsample of the European wildlife community and can be used to explore ecological questions related to drivers of distribution, abundance, and activity across the continent. We envision repeating this effort annually for the foreseeable future. Data for Snapshot Europe 2023, 2024, and 2025 are currently being revised and will be made publicly available soon. Collated, all the annual datasets will enable estimates of trends over time. Additionally, four sister initiatives, Snapshot USA (2019‐ongoing), Snapshot Japan (2023‐ongoing), Snapshot Brazil and Snapshot Chile (both started in 2025), annually collect data based on the same sampling protocol, enabling a new era of global‐scale comparisons. The images associated with the data accompanying this publication are available in Wildlife Insights. The data are available for reuse under CC BY‐SA 4.0 licensing. Please cite this data paper when reusing all or part of this dataset.

title: Strong self‐limitation promotes the persistence of rare species: Comment
Bison grazing and prairie fire shape soil microbial community diversity and assembly
content:
Abstract
Soil microbes mediate ecosystem function in grasslands, but the impacts of megaherbivore grazing and fire on microbial community assembly are poorly understood, despite widespread changes in these drivers following bison extermination and fire suppression across North America in the 19th century. To better understand how grazing and fire influence microbial metacommunity assembly processes such as dispersal and environmental filtering, we analyzed five years of soil microbial community and soil chemistry data from a long‐term, landscape‐scale grazing and fire frequency field experiment. Bison grazing reduced soil microbial alpha diversity, while both drivers altered microbial composition. Grazing and fire interactively increased microbial community dissimilarity over distance, with the strongest distance‐dissimilarity patterns in grazed, 20‐year burn interval treatments, suggesting complex controls over microbial community assembly across large spatial scales. Increases in soil nitrogen and pH as a result of bison reintroduction, along with significant relationships between these factors and microbial composition, highlight environmental filtering as an important assembly process. Temporal patterns showed that grazing and fire effects on microbial composition did not covary with interannual differences in precipitation, but instead with soil environment differences, pointing again to the influence of the abiotic habitat on microbial community assembly. However, geographic distance and the soil environment independently influenced microbial composition, suggesting fire and grazing drive community assembly by influencing both local‐scale environmental filtering and regional‐scale dispersal processes. Notably, because bison grazing increases plant diversity at this experimental site while decreasing soil microbial diversity, our study reinforces how microbial communities can respond to the same drivers as plant communities, but with different patterns that reflect common ecological mechanisms operating at smaller spatial scales. Overall, this study shows that grazing and fire can shape soil microbiomes through multiple mechanisms, suggesting that soil microbial communities across the Great Plains shifted dramatically following bison extermination and fire suppression.

title: Additive mixed meta‐analysis with spline meta‐regression for nonlinear ecological trends
content:
Abstract
Ecologists use meta‐analysis models to propagate uncertainty from statistical models of independent datasets into a higher‐level analysis. Meta‐analysis can be used to combine independent studies or as a two‐stage method for hierarchical modeling of data components from a large‐scale or long‐term study that are impractical to analyze in a single statistical model. While linear meta‐regression against study‐level covariates is common, ecological patterns are frequently nonlinear. For such cases, meta‐analysis methodology lacks tools to estimate semiparametric smooth meta‐regression models. We propose new spline meta‐regression methods by melding meta‐analysis with additive mixed models, resulting in the class of additive mixed meta‐analysis (AMMA) models. In a simulation study, when first‐stage SEs are heterogeneous, meta‐splines perform better than naive approaches such as simple generalized additive models (GAMs). In a case study to investigate 43‐year patterns of seasonally averaged phytoplankton levels in San Francisco Bay, California, USA, meta‐splines give notably different results than naive methods in such heterogeneous cases. Seasonal averages and SEs are estimated annually, then combined with meta‐splines to investigate long‐term, nonlinear changes in the season‐scale averages. The meta‐analysis approach is practical, fully propagates the statistical information and uncertainties, and provides advantages for visualization. The methods are available in the R package splinemixmeta.

title: Assessing pulse–press interactions on semi‐arid grassland productivity: The role of timing and environmental context
content:
Abstract
Ecosystems are being altered by increasing nitrogen fertilization and deposition globally, representing a chronic resource “press.” In tandem, climate change is intensifying weather events, leading to more intense deluges (i.e., large rainfall events), which represent resource “pulses.” Nitrogen and water addition can independently limit aboveground net primary productivity (ANPP) in grasslands. When combined, their effects may be simply additive, or synergy may emerge, whereby chronic nitrogen addition and a pulsed deluge may cause an increase in ANPP that is greater than the sum of their separate effects. Furthermore, the magnitude of nitrogen addition and environmental context have been shown to differentially affect ANPP, so these factors may also influence the interaction of nitrogen and deluge. To test the role of nitrogen magnitude in moderating pulse–press interactions, we leveraged a long‐term nitrogen addition study in a shortgrass steppe of northeastern Colorado in which eight levels of nitrogen addition, ranging from 0 to 30 g m−2 year−1, have been added since 2014. Deluge events representing the 95th percentile of historic precipitation events were applied mid‐late season (late July to early August) in 2021 and early‐mid season (late June) in 2022 to separate subplots within each nitrogen addition plot. The 2021 mid‐late deluge did not significantly increase ANPP or interact with nitrogen addition. In contrast, the 2022 early‐mid deluge increased average ANPP by 300% and interacted synergistically with nitrogen addition, with ANPP response to deluge estimated to peak at ~17 g m−2 of nitrogen. The synergistic response appeared driven by fast‐growing, weedy forbs, which were abundant in the community in 2022 but not in 2021. These results highlight how increases in pulsed events, such as deluges, may generate unexpected impacts on a key ecosystem function in grasslands undergoing chronic alterations in nitrogen availability, but that these effects may be strongly moderated by environmental context.

title: The diversity of resilience patterns of natural populations decreases closer to human activities
content:
Abstract
Quantifying the resilience of wild populations is essential to predict their viability in the Anthropocene. Many species have become threatened and even gone extinct because they have failed to cope with human disturbances. We use demographic data for 956 plant and animal populations to assess their responses to increasing levels of human activities. We show that in areas characterized by high human activities, there is a smaller diversity of resilience patterns compared to areas with lower human activities. Furthermore, in plants, populations closer to human‐influenced habitats display the ability to experience a lesser decrease in population size after disturbances than populations in less anthropized habitats. Our results suggest that human activities might have eroded the diversity of resilience patterns of wildlife populations, with key implications for the future resilience of wild populations worldwide.

title: Accounting for spatial dependence in random forests improves ecological understanding and enhances prediction
content:
Abstract
Random forests (RFs) are widely used in ecology to model complex, nonlinear relationships among environmental variables and to summarize fitted relationships through variable importance and interactions. However, many ecological datasets, particularly observational data collected across space, exhibit spatial dependence. If this spatial dependence is ignored, RFs can incorrectly attribute importance to predictors that serve at least partly as proxies for spatial location. In this study, we evaluate how accounting for spatial dependence changes both predictive performance and ecological interpretation. Using simulations with known data‐generating mechanisms and an analysis of 1061 North American river catchments, we compare standard RFs, RFs with spatial residual modeling, and a model‐agnostic spatial decorrelation transformation. The simulations show that spatially structured noise variables and raw coordinates can receive inflated importance in standard RF workflows, whereas decorrelation reduces these artifacts and recovers the relevant predictors more consistently. In the river flow application, decorrelation improves held‐out prediction and shifts interpretation from broad spatially smooth gradients toward hydrologic and soil variables with more direct mechanistic links to flow seasonality.

title: Trophic highways and dead ends: Algal traits regulate nutrient flux and energy transfer in stream food webs
content:
Abstract
Primary producers supply energy to ecosystems, but their traits determine whether fixed carbon (C) and nutrients are retained or transferred to consumers. In nitrogen (N)‐limited rivers, N fixation can provide a critical nutrient input, yet its role in supporting food webs remains poorly constrained. We investigated how algal traits regulate the flux of newly fixed C and N to consumers in the South Fork Eel River, California, using stable isotope tracers to quantify nutrient flux and transfer to grazers (Gumaga nigricula). While several algal taxa exhibited high rates of nutrient fixation, trophic outcomes differed sharply. Assemblages dominated by Epithemia, a diatom genus with N‐fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts, supported disproportionately high trophic coupling. Conversely, cyanobacterial mats and mucilage‐rich green algae were highly productive but little consumed. This decoupling is driven by nutrient packaging: Epithemia diatoms provide accessible nutrients and high‐quality lipids, whereas cyanobacteria and filamentous green algae have traits that limit consumption. By quantifying variation in the flow of fixed nutrients into an algal‐based food web, we show that transfer to primary consumers is governed by producer functional traits, and that shifts from diatom‐dominated assemblages to cyanobacterial or green algal dominance will create trophic dead ends, limiting food supplies and top‐down impacts of algivores.

title: Discovery of mesophotic Sargassum forests within a possible depth refugium at Lord Howe Island
What goes up must come down: Using weather surveillance radar data to forecast migratory birds banded on the ground
content:
Abstract
Ecological forecasting is a powerful framework to predict future states of ecological systems, including species distributions and supporting proactive conservation, management, and policy decisions that exist in a rapidly changing world. Forecasting efforts span a diversity of systems and organisms, yet many ecological phenomena, especially those involving highly mobile species, remain difficult to predict. Migration, for example, shapes population dynamics, species interactions, ecological services, and disease spread across terrestrial and aerial environments. Migratory pulses of birds observed in airspaces and stopover habitats are often studied separately; however, the connection between these two phases of migration remains largely unquantified. Here, we evaluate whether weather surveillance radar (WSR) measures of nocturnal migration activity can predict the number of birds captured at a long‐term bird banding station, thereby bridging aerial and terrestrial perspectives of migration. Using data from two WSR sites—KBOX (Boston, MA) and KGYX (Portland, ME)—and bird banding records from Appledore Island, Maine (1996–2023), we examined how radar‐derived measures of aerial migration activity forecast terrestrial bird banding captures. Using leave‐one‐year‐out cross‐validation, generalized additive models incorporating radar measures, atmospheric conditions, and non‐environmental covariates produced skillful probabilistic forecasts of daily captures in both seasons, improving on a persistence baseline in 21 of 23 spring and 23 of 26 fall years (median CRPS skill 0.25 and 0.12). Including radar‐derived measures further improved forecasts beyond atmospheric predictors in the majority of years (spring: 18 of 23; fall: 21 of 26). The models explained 57.8% and 49.9% of the deviance in daily spring and fall captures, respectively. These findings show that linking aerial and terrestrial monitoring can enhance migration forecasts, with implications for conservation strategies such as targeted “lights out” initiatives and stopover habitat management. This approach offers a scalable pathway to forecasting the connection between large‐scale atmospheric data and ground‐level ecological processes.

title: Primary, ancient, or old‐growth? Navigating the dimensions of ecological continuity in forests
content: Ecological continuity is one of the key conditions for biodiversity conservation. However, concepts used to describe ecological continuity in forests remain poorly defined. To clarify ecological continuity, we present a framework with two temporal dimensions (ancientness and old‐growthness) and one spatial dimension (contiguity). Ancientness refers to a continued forested state and relates to undisturbed abiotic conditions of soil and microclimate. Old‐growthness relates to the continuity of late‐seral structural features in the forest, including the presence of large and old trees as well as dead wood. Contiguity refers to the spatial continuity and extent of the forest landscape. We highlight that these three dimensions may—but not necessarily—coincide, with each leading to distinct and prominent biodiversity values and having different conservation needs. In addition, we explain the different temporal dynamics resulting in development and loss of ancientness and old‐growthness as a function of land‐use change and forest management.

title: Ten simple rules for a department chair
content:
by Lubomir Tomaska

Department chairs occupy a pivotal position in the university. Teaching, research, graduate education, and much of the academic community's professional and administrative activity are organized at the departmental level. Yet, despite the importance of the position and the considerable challenges it entails, many scientists assume the role with little or no formal preparation for academic leadership. This paper is intended as a practical primer rather than a comprehensive guide to academic leadership. The proposed rules provide a framework that prospective and current department chairs can adapt to their own institutional circumstances, experience, and leadership style.

title: PINN-based functional inference in size-structured population models: Application to fish oogenesis
content:
by Louis Fostier, Manon Lesage, Violette Thermes, Frédérique Clément, Romain Yvinec

Early oogenesis in juvenile fish establishes the ovarian reserve, which conditions lifelong reproductive capacity. This process is regulated by local hormonal feedback mechanisms, mainly involving Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH). In this work, we develop a mechanistic size-structured population model describing an unstructured germ-cell compartment and a population of growing oocytes, with AMH feedback on the renewal of the precursor cells compartment. Using repeated cross-sectional observations of oocyte size distributions in fish ovaries, we formulate and solve a nonlinear inverse problem with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to infer three demographic functions: the size-dependent oocyte growth rate, the AMH-regulated net renewal rate of the precursor cells compartment, and the recruitment rate of new oocytes. We introduce an auxiliary PINN formulation to handle the nonlocal interaction term and jointly infer unobserved state variables and demographic functions. Our inference strategy combines non-parametric PINNs with a data-guided model-selection step: demographic functions are first inferred without prescribing their functional forms, and the learned profiles are then used to select parsimonious parametric laws, whose parameters are subsequently estimated within a parametric PINN. We investigate identifiability at both the functional and parametric levels, combining structural identifiability analysis with synthetic-data experiments assessing the practical recovery of functions and parameters. The inference procedure is embedded within an individual-level bootstrap framework to assess sensitivity to repeated-cross-sectional sampling and stochastic training. Applied to juvenile fish oogenesis, the framework recovers interpretable growth and renewal dynamics, provides access to unobserved quantities, and enables conditional in silico investigation. More broadly, this work provides a framework for functional and parametric inference in size-structured population models with nonlocal interactions from sparse cross-sectional data.

title: kinGEMs: A robust and scalable framework for resource-constraint models through stochastic tuning of deep learning-predicted kinetic parameters
content:
by Rana A. Barghout, Lya Chiñas Serrano, Benjamin Sanchez-Lengeling, Radhakrishnan Mahadevan

The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters (kcat) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework’s capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.

title: Sequence-based coevolutionary prediction of species-specific interactomes
content:
by Miguel Fernandez-Martin, Camila Pontes, Victoria Ruiz-Serra, Alfonso Valencia

Evolutionarily conserved protein-protein interactions (PPIs) reveal fundamental biological processes. However, predicting protein function solely from these interactions provides an incomplete picture of biological systems. Computational methods for predicting PPIs often struggle due to limited functional annotations in databases, making it difficult to fully understand unique biological systems. This study introduces ContextMirror2.0 (CM2.0), a coevolution-based method designed to address these limitations. Coevolutionary approaches, unlike supervised machine learning methods, do not rely on labelled datasets, proving valuable in addressing the scarcity of data for species-specific PPIs. Around 40% of CM2.0’s top-1000 predicted PPIs for E. coli, S. enterica, and S. aureus are supported by experimental PPI databases. However, comparative analysis of the resulting functional communities further revealed both highly conserved interaction patterns and species-specific interactions. CM2.0 leverages coevolutionary information at the phylogenetic level to explore protein interaction dynamics and understand the functional consequences of species-specific variations. This information can inform further studies on the emergence of novel functions, adaptation to specific environments, and the development of targeted therapies.

title: SwimmingIndividuals: A high-performance agent-based model for marine ecosystems
content:
by Matthew S. Woodstock, Jann Paul Mattern, Zhen Wu, Gregory L. Britten

Because they are based on established theory, mechanistic models are essential for projecting ecological responses to novel conditions. Yet mechanistic agent-based model (ABM) applications have often been limited by computational constraints. This paper introduces SwimmingIndividuals, an open-source ABM framework that advances our ability to simulate physiological processes, animal movement, higher trophic level marine ecosystem dynamics, and fisheries removals at large ecological scales. The software's key contributions are a suite of mechanistic sub-models governing the full life cycle of each agent, including visual prey detection, adaptive behaviors such as diel vertical migration (DVM), a flexible bioenergetics engine with three taxon-specific metabolic architectures, and a spatial pathfinding algorithm for habitat-seeking movement. These processes are made computationally tractable through a hybrid CPU/GPU architecture written in Julia. Unlike prior ABMs that use fixed perception radii or single-equation bioenergetics, SwimmingIndividuals enables emergent ecological dynamics across populations of superindividual agents. We demonstrate the framework through three Gulf of America simulations. The model reproduced DVM, cetacean diving patterns, size-based trophic shifts, and von Bertalanffy growth curves consistent with published King Mackerel stock assessments. Long-term simulations generated realistic population dynamics and quantified impacts of fishery harvest control rules across five fleets. SwimmingIndividuals provides a powerful, flexible, open-source platform for mechanistic marine ecosystem research and ecosystem-based fisheries management.

title: Sperm phospholipase C signaling via PLCζ1 and PLCδ4 is essential for Ca<sup>2+</sup> oscillations and fertility in mice
content:
by Neha Gupta, Lei Zhang, Hiroki Akizawa, Maria G. Gervasi, Darya A. Tourzani, Pablo E. Visconti, Ana Romarowski, Mariano Buffone, Wei Cui, Rafael A. Fissore

Fertilization-induced calcium (Ca2+) oscillations are essential for egg activation and embryonic development in mammals. The sperm-specific phospholipase C isoform, PLCζ1, is the primary trigger of these oscillations. Functional and clinical studies have linked mutations or reduced expression of PLCζ1 to male infertility. However, whether PLCζ1 alone accounts for Ca2+ release at fertilization in all mammals remains uncertain. Male mice lacking Plcζ1 exhibit subfertility and reduced litter sizes; their sperm induce delayed, low-frequency Ca2+ oscillations, indicating a compensatory mechanism. Notably, mouse sperm express high levels of PLCδ4, essential for completing the acrosome reaction (AR). In Plcζ1-null sperm, PLCδ4 is upregulated and retained post-AR. These observations suggest a secondary functional role for PLCδ4. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we generated Plcδ4 knockout (KO) mice. Plcδ4-null sperm trigger attenuated, delayed Ca2+ oscillations and significantly reduced fertilization rates, indicating that PLCδ4 contributes to but does not independently drive Ca2+ signaling. We therefore generated a Double Knockout (DKO) mouse line lacking both sperm-enriched PLCs. DKO males were sterile, with sperm failing to induce Ca2+ oscillations, and the isolated residual Ca2+ rise was insufficient to activate eggs. These findings reveal that PLCζ1, the primary oscillator, and PLCδ4, a compensatory factor, work cooperatively within a complex, multi-component PLC system that ensures robust fertilization. This work reveals molecular specialization among mammals in initiating the fertilization Ca2+ signals. It has implications for understanding male infertility, improving assisted reproductive technologies, and developing contraceptive strategies.

title: The resource elasticity of control
content: The ability to determine how much the environment can be controlled through our actions has long been viewed as fundamental to adaptive behavior. While traditional accounts treat controllability as a fixed property of the environment, we argue that real-world controllability often depends on the effort, time, and money we are able and willing to invest. In such cases, controllability can be said to be elastic to invested resources. Here, we propose that inferring this elasticity is essential for efficient resource allocation, and thus, elasticity misestimations result in maladaptive behavior. To test this hypothesis, we developed a novel treasure hunt game where participants encountered environments with varying degrees of controllability and elasticity. Across two pre-registered studies (N=514), we first demonstrate that people infer elasticity and adapt their resource allocation accordingly. We then present a computational model that explains how people make this inference and identify individual elasticity biases that lead to suboptimal resource allocation. Finally, we show that overestimation of elasticity is associated with elevated psychopathology involving an impaired sense of control. These findings establish the elasticity of control as a distinct cognitive construct guiding adaptive behavior and a computational marker for control-related maladaptive behavior.

title: The hypoxic response extends lifespan through a bioaminergic and peptidergic neural circuit
content: A coordinated response to stress is crucial for promoting the short- and long-term health of an organism. The perception of stress, frequently through the nervous system, can lead to physiological changes that are fundamental to maintaining homeostasis. Activating the response to low oxygen, or hypoxia, extends healthspan and lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans. However, despite some positive impacts, negative effects of the hypoxic response in specific tissues prevent translation of their benefits in mammals. Thus, it is imperative to identify which components of this response promote longevity. Here, we interrogate the cell-nonautonomous signaling pathway downstream of genetic activation of the hypoxic response. We find that HIF-1-mediated signaling in ADF serotonergic neurons is both necessary and sufficient for lifespan extension. Signaling through the serotonin receptor SER-7 in the GABAergic RIS interneurons is necessary in this process. Our findings also highlight the involvement of additional neural signaling molecules, including the neurotransmitters tyramine and GABA, and the neuropeptide NLP-17, in mediating longevity effects. Finally, we demonstrate that oxygen- and carbon-dioxide-sensing neurons act downstream of HIF-1 in this circuit. Together, these insights demonstrate a circuit for how genetic induction of the hypoxic response cell-nonautonomously modifies aging and suggests valuable targets for modulating aging in mammals.

title: Simple methods to acutely measure multiple timing metrics among the sexual repertoire of male Drosophila
content: Male Drosophila courtship behavior is a key model for studying temporal decision-making. While courtship index (CI) is widely used to quantify mating activity, other timing metrics like courtship latency, copulation latency (CL), and mating duration (MD) remain understudied. Traditional methods for quantifying these behaviors are often labor-intensive and prone to human error. In this study, we present a protocol combining a modular chamber system and automated software (DrosoMating) to quantify six key timing metrics during male courtship. Our image-based video analysis enables precise identification of courtship and copulation events, as well as quantification of their timing and duration under controlled conditions. Validation shows <0.05% error rates and 98–99% agreement with manual scoring for CL, CI, and MD. The protocol supports genetic and neural circuit manipulations, detecting subtle genetic, social, and environmental behavioral variations. By minimizing manual effort and standardizing data collection, this approach facilitates scalable, reproducible studies on adaptive trade-offs, learning, and neural mechanisms in mating behavior. This method streamlines timing analysis in male courtship, offering reproducible metrics for behavioral genetics.

title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention
content: The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

title: Historical Groundwater Memory Predicts Site‐Specific Persistence Horizons Across Germany
content:
Abstract
Groundwater levels retain memory of antecedent hydrologic conditions, but whether this memory defines a persistent timescale of later groundwater behavior remains unclear. We analyzed weekly records from 3207 wells across Germany, estimating groundwater memory during 1991–2005 and persistence during 2013–2022. Historical autocorrelation‐implied timescales strongly predicted later persistence horizons (Spearman ρ $\rho $ = 0.851; 95% confidence interval, 0.819–0.877), with a median absolute difference of 2 weeks. A well's own historical memory was much more closely related to later persistence than memory reassigned among hydrogeologically and spatially similar wells, indicating strong site specificity. Historical hydroclimatic–groundwater coupling was also associated with departures from the autocorrelation‐based expectation, and this relation persisted after removal of seasonal and trend components. These site‐specific timescales inform persistence‐based forecasting and provide a temporal perspective for groundwater resilience assessment and climate adaptation planning.

title: Submesoscale Thermal‐Feedback Coupling Coefficients in Intense Oceanic Boundary Current Systems Revealed by SWOT
content:
Abstract
Ocean motions at mesoscales (∼100 km) and below actively trigger air‐sea interactions by inducing anomalies of sea surface temperature (SST) and currents. Despite extensive research on oceanic submesoscale (O (0.1–10) km) processes, observational understanding of submesoscale air‐sea interactions remains limited. Using high‐resolution wind data from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography satellite and SST data from the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer, we investigate the wind response to submesoscale SST anomalies in five strong boundary current regions over the globe. Based on 3,054 samples obtained by identifying SST fronts and matching wind fields, we calculate and analyze the submesoscale coupling coefficient that measures the intensity of the response. The mean of the coefficients from the five regions is 0.51 m s−1 °C−1. Comparison shows a pronounced regional variability of the coefficient, with a factor of up to 1.56. This study provides an observational guide for high‐resolution coupled model simulation validation.

title: Differentiated Rift Rupture and Apparent Northward Earthquake Ordering in Southern Tibet Revealed by the 2025 Mw 7.0 Dingri Earthquake and Its Preceding Events
content:
Abstract
North–south‐trending rifts in southern Tibet accommodate active east–west extension, but how normal‐faulting rupture varies with rift development remains unclear. Here we use Synthetic Aperture Radar observations to investigate the 2025 Mw 7.0 Dingri earthquake in the southern Xainza–Dinggye rift. Our rupture model shows that the 2025 earthquake ruptured multiple segments and likely triggered three meter‐scale slope failures within surface‐rupture gaps at the rift margin. Together with preceding Dingri events, our results reveal contrasting along‐rift coseismic rupture behavior: larger, shallower, and more complex slip in the higher‐elevation, narrower northern Dengmo Co rift, but smaller, deeper slip in the lower, wider southern half‐graben. Combined with other geodetically constrained normal‐faulting sequences across southern Tibet, these observations show an apparent northward ordering along certain rift segments. Our study provides new insight into the relationship between long‐term rift development and earthquake rupture behavior in the southern Tibetan rift system.

title: Variations in dv/v Susceptibility to Earthquake Shaking Along the Alaska Subduction Zone
content:
Abstract
Earthquake‐triggered decreases in relative seismic velocity (dv/v) of the crust have been reported for many events, but regional variations in dv/v susceptibility to shaking are not well understood. Here, 14 Alaskan earthquakes with Mw 6.8–8.2 are consistently analyzed with single‐station coda‐wave interferometry. For peak ground velocities (PGV) >1 cm/s, significant dv/v drops are found for ∼40% of seismometers, with a moderate linear correlation coefficient of −0.3 between dv/v and PGV. Sites in the highest susceptibility decile, indicated by the largest dv/v drops per unit PGV, are all located near active volcanoes: Akutan, Makushin, Shishaldin, Pavlof, Katmai, and Augustine. Some Cook Inlet basin sites are among the largest decile of dv/v drops but have lower susceptibility due to amplified PGV. Frequency‐dependence of dv/v indicates concentration of velocity changes at <500 m depth, consistent with hydrothermal systems and weakly consolidated volcanic rocks influencing heterogeneous and high susceptibility near volcanoes.

title: Saltwater Intrusion Seasonality Under Climate Change: Interacting Effects of River Discharge, Sea‐Level Rise, and Bathymetry
content:
Abstract
Saltwater intrusion is a growing concern under climate change. Although previous studies emphasize intensified intrusion during low‐flow periods, changes in its seasonality remain understudied. We combine long‐term observations with coupled hydrologic–hydrodynamic modeling to examine how river discharge and sea‐level rise (SLR) affect intrusion seasonality in Pamlico River Estuary. We find that intensified discharge seasonality, with lower low flows and higher high flows, amplifies intrusion seasonality by driving landward salt‐front expansion during low‐flow periods and oceanward retreat during high‐flow periods, increasing its seasonal migration range. Moderate SLR increases intrusion magnitude while maintaining high seasonal variability. Under higher SLR, however, landward topography constrains low‐flow expansion and reduces seasonal migration. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding saltwater intrusion seasonality under climate change: river discharge and SLR determine how strongly the salt front tends to migrate, while its position relative to local topography determines whether that migration remains unconstrained or limited.

title: Seasonal and Interannual Variability of the Wind‐Driven Component of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation Transport at the Equator
content:
Abstract
The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) transport across the equator varies from seasonal to interannual timescales. Using ECCO v4r4 state estimates (1992–2017), the 26‐year mean transport is 12.8 Sv (1 Sv = 106 m3 s−1). The seasonal cycle peaks in February and reaches its minimum in August, with an amplitude of ∼8.5 Sv. The interior cross‐equatorial transport east of 37°W follows the Sverdrup balance on interannual timescales, correlating with the zonally integrated wind‐stress curl (r = 0.86). In contrast, the western boundary current changes include local compensating flows to interior wind‐driven transport and potentially contributions from extratropical regions that propagates equatorward along the boundary. Sensitivity experiments with a three‐layer primitive‐equation model show that remote extratropical forcing, rather than local equatorial wind, dominates interannual variability of the wind‐driven component of the equatorial AMOC transport.

title: Eddy‐Driven Upwelling of Heat and Salt in the Weddell Sea
content:
Abstract
In the Southern Ocean, upper ocean processes are important for water column stability, affecting air‐sea‐ice fluxes. Eddies can facilitate exchange with deeper layers, affecting heat and salt fluxes, though observations are lacking. New novel observations from an acoustically tracked profiling float, trapped within an eddy for 6 months, present the first direct vertical heat flux estimates due to eddy‐sea ice interactions. These observations revealed an increase in wintertime salt and heat fluxes to the upper ocean, resulting in a reduced mixed layer thickness at the end of winter and possible anomalous winter sea ice melt. Observational estimates of salt and heat fluxes were compared with those derived from eddies identified in a high‐resolution numerical simulation showing similar results. With the event based nature of eddies, this introduces highly variable salt and heat fluxes across the Weddell Sea, potentially impacting Winter Water evolution, spring time melt, and deep ocean convection.

title: Post‐Fire Surface Energy Partitioning and Thermal Responses in Arctic Boreal Forests and Tundra
content:
Abstract
Rapid Arctic warming intensifies wildfire activity across high‐latitude ecosystems, yet post‐fire surface responses of boreal forests and tundra remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate land surface temperature (LST) and energy partitioning responses during the first post‐fire summer across the pan‐Arctic using satellite observations and surface energy‐balance diagnostics. We find significant post‐fire warming in boreal forests and tundra, with mean LST increases of 0.53 and 0.44 K, respectively. Despite comparable warming magnitudes, energy redistribution pathways differ markedly. In boreal forests, post‐fire evaporative heat loss declines substantially. In contrast, tundra shows little latent heat flux change but a decrease in the residual sensible‐plus‐ground heat flux. Across both ecosystems, positive LST anomalies coexist with decreases in net radiation, while non‐radiative components exhibit different degrees of change. Our findings improve understanding of post‐fire thermal feedbacks in high‐latitude landscapes and highlight the importance of representing ecosystem‐dependent post‐fire energy dynamics in Arctic climate assessments.

title: Calibrating the Geomorphic Clock: Remote Sensing of Sediment Storage and Transit Timescales in Alluvial River Corridors
content:
Abstract
Constraining sediment and organic carbon storage duration in river corridors is essential for understanding terrestrial carbon cycling and interpreting the sedimentary record. However, existing methods rely on geochemical dating or theoretical models tailored to idealized meandering rivers, limiting their broader application. Here, we present a remote sensing framework using four decades of Landsat imagery and an area‐based mobility metric to quantify decadal‐scale channel mobility across diverse river planforms. We extrapolate these observations to millennial‐scale sediment storage and transit times using a bounded random‐walk model informed by remotely derived channel‐belt widths. Modeled storage and transit times reproduce independent geochemical benchmarks within a factor of three across four morphologically diverse rivers. River planform and channel mobility timescales independently govern sediment transit: multithreaded reaches transmit stored sediment faster than meandering reaches, and slower floodplain reworking prolongs transit. Our results provide a scalable foundation for quantifying fluvial sediment and carbon dynamics globally.

title: The Overlooked Role of Alongshore Beach Non‐Uniformity in Short‐Term Shoreline Variability
content:
Abstract
Long‐term beach monitoring and satellite‐derived shoreline products are typically validated, and shoreline models calibrated, along cross‐shore transects. Open sandy beaches, however, are rarely uniform alongshore, because crescentic megacusps migrate past fixed transects, and their effect on single‐transect records remains unquantified. We combine a 30‐year, daily‐to‐weekly single‐transect record with monthly surveys across 11 transects spanning 400 m at Hasaki Beach, Japan, and use the alongshore range (ΔY) $({\Delta }Y)$ of shoreline position as a proxy for megacusp magnitude. Between monthly surveys, 70%–76% of single‐transect observations lie within this range and cannot be distinguished from alongshore non‐uniformity at a single transect. The range shows no significant correlation with concurrent wave forcing, and the skill of wave‐driven equilibrium models declines as the range grows relative to the single‐transect variability. Densely spaced transects are therefore needed to isolate the forcing‐driven cross‐shore response from megacusp‐induced variability, in both in situ and satellite‐derived shoreline analyses.

title: Mountains Modulate the Response of Precipitation Flashiness to Warming in High‐Resolution Simulations Over the Western US
content:
Abstract
Global climate models (GCMs) robustly predict that precipitation will become flashier (i.e., more concentrated in time) as the climate warms, with extremely wet events accounting for a larger share of total precipitation at a given location. Here we test this prediction across the western United States, where precipitation is modulated by orographic mechanisms that GCMs do not resolve. Using the daily Gini index, we analyze the change in precipitation flashiness within an ensemble of high‐resolution regional climate model (RCM) simulations. In contrast to GCMs, which predict a widespread increase in flashiness, the RCMs indicate decreased flashiness in rain‐shadowed basins downwind of major mountain ranges. We show that this result follows from a weakening of orographic influence on precipitation as the climate warms. A widely used statistical downscaling method fails to capture this effect, and thus misses important features of the flashiness response simulated by RCMs.

title: Managing risk in carbon portfolios
content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02786-8

Carbon removal methodologies have different risks of stored CO2 leaking back to the atmosphere. Now a study provides a quantitative framework for comparison, a necessary tool for building carbon storage portfolios with improved delivery, valuation and cost.

title: The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02785-9

Carbon removal markets lack a standard metric for assessing permanence risk, limiting effective risk management and product development. Here researchers propose carbon at risk, a probabilistic measure, and calibrate it for forest carbon and geological storage projects, demonstrating the benefits of diversification.

title: Elevated early Eocene atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> tied to reduced Southern Ocean biological pump efficiency
content:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02142-7

Warming in the early Eocene reduced the efficiency of the Southern Ocean biological carbon pump, limiting carbon sequestration in the ocean interior and enhancing atmospheric CO2 levels, according to foraminifera-bound nitrogen isotope records.

title: Ettringite’s concrete contribution
content:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02132-9

Vincent Thiéry and Migueli Chedrewih discuss how studying ettringite’s natural, geologic occurrences can inform understanding of concrete’s material properties and ageing processes.

title: Sparing use of phosphorus in an acidifying ocean
content:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02133-8

Global cycles of carbon and phosphorus decouple under intensifying ocean acidification as marine diatoms restructure their lipid membranes and downregulate organic phosphorus scavenging to adapt to the decreasing pH.

title: Responsible use of artificial intelligence
content:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02149-0

AI is rapidly transforming geoscience research and publishing. To realize the benefits of AI while safeguarding scientific integrity, researchers, reviewers and editors must adopt transparent practices.
