Seasonal timing separates algal bloom records from marine heatwave exposure
content:
Abstract
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly invoked in explanations of coastal algal blooms, yet shared seasonality can confound apparent MHW–bloom coincidence. We assembled a source‐resolved catalogue of 48 algal bloom records and a satellite‐derived regional daily sea surface temperature series for Sansha Bay, China, to evaluate bloom‐record timing against MHW exposure during 2005–2020. Bloom records peaked in May–June, and regional MHW days peaked in July–September. The weighted circular seasonal centers were separated by 2.73 months, and the monthly overlap coefficient was 0.29. Event‐level classification identified 9 MHW‐related bloom records and 39 records without event‐period or pre‐start MHW exposure. Under the same‐calendar‐month null model, the observed count of 9 fell within the timing‐conditioned distribution centered at 10.84 records (95% interval, 6–16; one‐sided exact p = 0.799). The same‐year‐month, duration, source, and exposure‐window analyses placed the observed count within their respective timing‐conditioned distributions. Seasonal timing therefore provides the background needed to interpret MHW–bloom coincidence in Sansha Bay. This framework separates temporal co‐occurrence from enrichment above the expected timing of a historical bloom‐record catalogue.

title: Groundings of drifters in the Wadden Sea inform  the transport of floating macroplastic
content:
Groundings of drifters in the Wadden Sea inform the transport of floating macroplastic
Marc Emanuel Schneiter, Rolf Hut, and Erik van Sebille
Ocean Sci., 22, 3595–3617, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3595-2026, 2026
We study the transport and land-water transitions of 24 small floating position-trackers that are representative of plastic litter, which we released in the Wadden Sea, a region strongly influenced by tides and wind. We describe how to automatically identify from their tracks whether a tracker is afloat or not, and relate the transitions between afloat and beached to sea and wind conditions. Our method can be used in model simulations and in the planning of beach cleanups.

title: The Mediterranean observation systems: MonGOOS analysis  of present capabilities, weaknesses and perspectives
content:

Zarokanellos, George Zodiatis, and Vanessa Cardin

This work provides a comprehensive overview of the current marine observation capabilities in the Mediterranean Sea, making this information accessible to scientists, stakeholders and environmental policymakers. It supports initiatives such as the Copernicus Marine Service, European Marine Observation and Data Network, the European Ocean Pact and relevant European Union directives. It’s intended to be regularly updated, helping to identify strengths and gaps in Mediterranean observation systems.

title: stem.MAP: Identification of cell-type-specific protein complexes in mammalian embryonic stem cells.
content: Protein complexes carry out critical functions during development. Mapping cell-type-specific protein complexes in early embryogenesis is essential for uncovering the molecular mechanisms of embryonic development. We unfortunately currently lack a catalog of protein complexes specific for embryogenesis including embryonic stem cells. Here we develop a proteomics-based machine learning workflow to predict protein complexes present in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC). Our method integrates data from a cell-type agnostic protein complex resource with co-fractionation mass spectrometry (CF-MS) experiments on mESC. Our resource, stem.MAP, identifies 3,986 complexes encompassing ~133,000 unique interactions, and 8,616 proteins. stem.MAP captures variant complexes critical for stem cell function including the PRC2, BAF and NuRD complexes. stem.MAP also discriminates mutually exclusive interactions specific to embryonic stem cells (e.g. Eif4ebp2 - Eif4e). Finally we observe 1,388 high confidence stem.MAP interactions found only in mESC CF-MS data, many with support from AlphaFold modeling and a gastruloid coregulation network. We make stem.MAP protein complexes available through our web resource: stem.proteincomplexes.org. We anticipate stem.MAP will be beneficial to the study of early development and we expect our proteomics-based machine learning workflow to be applicable to the creation of any context-specific protein interaction network.

title: A three-factor model can explain symmetry breaking and the n-1 rule during X-chromosome inactivation
content: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is a mammalian gene regulatory process that via chromosome-scale transcriptional silencing, leaves active a single X chromosome per diploid genome complement. The mechanisms that enable cells to select the appropriate number of X chromosomes to inactivate while leaving others active remain unclear. We demonstrate that all known chromosomal counting scenarios during XCI can be accounted for by a three-factor mathematical model that includes (1) Xist, the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) responsible for gene silencing during XCI in eutherians, (2) an X-linked transcriptional activator of Xist, and (3) the autosomally-encoded SPEN, an Xist RNA-binding protein that is essential for gene silencing during XCI. In our model, symmetry between active X chromosomes is broken by stochastic differences in the number of Xist molecules that associate with the X chromosomes at the onset of XCI. Subsequently, integrated positive and negative feedback loops amplify then propagate superstoichiometric assemblies of SPEN complexed with Xist on the inactive chromosome(s), and select for levels of X-linked activator that enable only one X chromosome per diploid genome complement to remain active. Thus, asymmetric propagation of the SPEN-Xist ribonucleoprotein complex may play an essential role in symmetry breaking and chromosomal counting during XCI, independently of or in concert with cis-acting networks of DNA regulatory elements. Our results also have conceptual implications for gene regulatory circuits on autosomes.

title: LAP-TLR2 Axis Drives Inflammatory Pathology during Listeria monocytogenes Gastroenteritis
content: Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) causes acute gastroenteritis that precedes systemic invasive listeriosis, yet the molecular mechanisms coordinating bacterial virulence with host inflammatory responses during the enteric phase remain poorly understood. We show that Lm-associated gastroenteritis is dose-dependent, and a high infectious dose (~1x10^10 CFU/mouse), reflecting epidemic cases, recapitulates hallmark features of gastroenteritis in a mouse model, including early onset, epithelial erosion, and profound inflammatory cell infiltration. We identify Listeria adhesion protein (LAP), rather than classical virulence factors such as internalin A and listeriolysin O, as the primary mediator of enteric pathology, driving epithelial cell death and neutrophil recruitment. Transcriptomic (mRNA-seq) profiling implicates LAP-driven engagement of the TLR2-MyD88 pathway. Using the HEK-Dual hTLR2 (NF-kB) reporter cell line and TLR2 knockout mice, we show that LAP engages TLR2 to activate TNFalpha; NF-kB signaling and compromises the gut epithelial barrier. Disease severity correlates with myeloid hyperactivation and intestinal ion channel dysregulation, as CD11b-; mice exhibit attenuated diarrhea despite elevated bacterial tissue loads. Finally, studies in MLCK knock-out mice confirm that this myeloid-driven pathology requires MLCK-dependent tight junction opening for paracellular neutrophil migration, which works in concert with LAP-TLR2 signaling during Lm-induced gastroenteritis.

title: Metabolites cross the membrane, the transcriptome does not follow: co-localization is required for the cyanobacterial response to a yeast partner
content: Interactions between phototrophs and heterotrophs are usually explained by cross-feeding, yet whether that exchange alone accounts for the phototroph's response has rarely been tested. We grew the sucrose-secreting cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus with the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides as a synthetic community, either in mixed co-culture or in membrane-separated co-culture (0.22 m pore size), each with a matched axenic control. Metabolite exchange occurred in both configurations: sucrose reached the yeast and was consumed, and yeast-derived metabolites reached the cyanobacterium. The yeast reached a higher final density behind the membrane, whereas the cyanobacterium gained about 9% over its axenic control only in mixed co-culture. Yet the cyanobacterial transcriptome responded only with co-localization: expression of 51 genes changed consistently across time points (day-averaged q < 0.05), against one gene behind the membrane, and the number of differentially expressed genes rose from 20 on day 4 to 91 and 127 on days 6 and 8. Nine regulatory programs (iModulons), mainly nitrogen and photosynthesis, responded in mixed co-culture and none behind the membrane. Reactor configuration alone changed 40 genes in axenic culture. These results suggest that co-localization, in addition to metabolite exchange, was required for the heterotrophic partner to trigger a response in the phototroph. Co-culture studies that infer interactions from shared metabolites may miss effects that depend on spatial structure. Importance Partnerships between light-powered microbes and the heterotrophs living alongside them move large amounts of carbon in oceans and soils, and are now built on purpose to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals. Such partnerships are usually described by the chemicals the partners trade, so we asked whether those chemicals are enough. The cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus and the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides were grown together in one vessel, or in two chambers divided by a membrane that molecules cross but cells cannot. The yeast fed on cyanobacterial sugar in both, yet the cyanobacterium changed its gene activity only when the two shared a space. Partners in nature are usually clustered rather than evenly mixed, so closeness may contribute as much as the chemicals themselves. Keeping partners apart in engineered cultures can still deliver carbon to the heterotroph, but may not deliver the benefits of partnership to the phototroph.

title: The enemy of my enemy: A bacterial antagonist rescues Chlamydomonas by inactivating a toxin from a rival
content: Microbial interactions are shaped by multiple community members, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a tripartite interaction between the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and two Pseudomonas bacteria that coexist in the same soil habitat. In pairwise cultures, all three interactions are amensalistic (-like): Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5 antagonizes both C. reinhardtii and Pseudomonas fluorescens HKI0770 without benefit, while P. fluorescens inhibits C. reinhardtii without profiting from the alga. However, in a tripartite culture, P. fluorescens protects C. reinhardtii from P. protegens and promotes algal recovery. This protection is not stopped when the used carbon source, acetate, is supplemented. The P. fluorescens rescue effect is associated with reduced levels of the polyyne toxin protegencin produced by P. protegens. Protegencin levels, detected by Raman microspectroscopy, are decreased by application of spent medium or protein extracts from P. fluorescens, while heat- and protease-treatment abolish this activity. A heat-sensitive, proteinaceous factor, likely an enzyme(s), appears to contribute to protegencin inactivation. Our results show that P. fluorescens rescues C. reinhardtii by inactivating protegencin, despite being inhibited by P. protegens. These findings demonstrate the importance of investigating higher-order effects, since additional community members can transform pairwise antagonistic interactions into conditional protection through toxin inactivation.

title: Integrative identification of Tetratostichococcus sp. CCAH0201 (Trebouxiophyceae, Chlorophyta) from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam
content: A microalgal strain from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam, was examined by light microscopy and three molecular markers. Thirty-six cells from 22 micrographs measured 6.68-12.74 by 3.49-4.79 micrometres. Homologous phylogenetic windows comprised 550 nucleotides for SSU rDNA, 711 for ITS and 1,170 for rbcL. CCAH0201, P1 and Tetratostichococcus jenerensis SAG 2138 shared the SSU 3-prime sequence, whereas ITS and rbcL placed CCAH0201 with P1 (SH-aLRT/UFBoot 87/94 and 96.9/99). CCAH0201 differed from P1 at 22/711 ITS and 4/1,170 rbcL sites. Structure-guided ITS2 comparison identified one strict CBC, one two-sided change from a wobble pair and three hemi-CBCs relative to P1. CCAH0201 is thus identified as Tetratostichococcus sp. in a lineage close to P1.

title: CauloBrowser 2.0: an AI powered update
content: CauloBrowser is a systems-biology database for Caulobacter crescentus that organizes the largest repository of experimental data for this model bacterium. The original CauloBrowser provided a web interface for accessing these data, but the growing number of experimental datasets and advances in AI chatbots motivated an updated resource. We developed CauloBrowser 2.0 (CauloBrowser.org) as an open-source application that broadens access to RNA-seq, microarray, ribosome profiling, Tn-seq, ChIP-seq, and genome annotation data. The CauloChat AI interface allows users to query these datasets in natural language, generate visualizations, and achieve complex biological insights. While the database is hosted freely on the web, users may also download the database and run it locally, reducing dependence on the web-hosted service and allowing laboratories to use compatible unpublished datasets. Altogether, CauloBrowser 2.0 provides a significant update for exploring diverse systems biology data in C. crescentus.

title: Metatranscriptomic Profiling of Viral Diversity in Aquatic Environments with a Focus on Microalgal Viruses
content: Freshwater microeukaryotes contribute to aquatic productivity, yet the RNA viruses associated with these communities remain incompletely characterized compared with their marine counterparts. Here, we used metatranscriptomics to profile viral diversity across five Finnish freshwater sites (one river and four lakes) and one coastal marine sample from Hiroshima Bay in the Seto Inland Sea, Japan. We recovered 399 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), of which 285 (71.4%) represented RNA viruses distributed across five viral phyla and putatively associated with fungal, plant or algal, metazoan and bacterial hosts. DNA viruses formed a smaller component of the dataset, including bacteriophage-like vOTUs with transcripts encoding replication, structural, packaging, and lysis proteins. Two vOTUs, which were detected in the Vantaanjoki river sample, were putatively classified within the family Marnaviridae, which comprises RNA viruses that infect protists in marine and freshwater environments. Both vOTUs encoded conserved replication and picornavirus-like capsid domains, and one represented a near-complete dicistronic genome. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) -based phylogeny placed these vOTUs in a strongly supported lineage outside the currently recognized genera within the family Marnaviridae, supporting their provisional assignment to the candidate genus Vandarnavirus proposed here within Marnaviridae. Whole-genome comparisons using the IMG/VR v4 database revealed genetic similarities between the vOTUs representing the candidate Vandarnavirus genus and picorna-like virus sequences from freshwater, wetland, saltmarsh, and estuarine metatranscriptomes. These findings expand the known ecological range of marnavirus-like RNA viruses and identify freshwater habitats as under-sampled reservoirs of microalgae-associated viral sequences.

title: Evaluating non-oxidative glycolysis using 13C metabolic flux analysis
content: Non-oxidative glycolysis (NOG) converts glucose to acetyl-CoA without emitting CO2 during Escherichia coli bioproduction. Although 13C-metabolic flux analysis (13C-MFA) has the potential to evaluate NOG flux distribution in vivo, the precision of these estimates depends on the labeling patterns of glucose tracers. Because E. coli has multiple native glycolysis pathways, selecting the optimal glucose tracer is important for precise estimates. This study used simulations to evaluate the performance of 18 commercially available glucose tracers in precisely predicting NOG flux. We artificially generated flux distributions of central metabolic pathways, including three types of NOG pathways, and obtained 13C labeling patterns of amino acids metabolized from each glucose tracer. Using these data, we then calculated 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for NOG pathway fluxes. Comparing the sum of CI widths from three NOG fluxes showed that estimation with [1,3-13C]-glucose yielded the narrowest CIs. Several tracers, including [2,3-13C]glucose, were capable of determining fluxes with high precision, but [1-13C]glucose was not one of them, despite often being used for estimating glycolytic fluxes. We then experimentally evaluated [2,3-13C]- and [1-13C]glucose as tracers in E. coli strains with and without the expression of phosphoketolase, which is required for NOG pathways to function. The results suggested that [1-13C]glucose could not detect NOG fluxes, whereas [2,3-13C]glucose estimated the fluxes of all three NOG pathways with narrow CIs.

title: Visual surfaceomics reveals the substrate-scavenging cell surface of Asgard archaea
content: The emergence of eukaryotes from Asgard archaeal ancestors likely required a specialized cell envelope that enabled sustained physical and metabolic interactions with proto-mitochondrial symbionts. While the protrusion-rich cell architecture of Asgard archaea may enable such interactions, the molecular composition of their cell surface and its role in establishing cell-cell contacts remains unknown. Here, we developed a "visual surfaceomics" approach, integrating subtomogram averaging, predictive structural modeling, transcriptomics, proteomics, and expansion microscopy to identify surface proteins in situ. We show that Asgard cell bodies and protrusions lack an archaea-typical paracrystalline S-layer and are instead decorated by two main classes of surface proteins: subtilisin-like serine proteases (SubSs) and oligopeptide-binding proteins (OppAs). SubSs were detected as membrane-anchored dimers and were sparsely distributed across the surface. OppAs showed near-total membrane coverage but lacked any rigid, higher order assembly. Thermal shift assays and single particle cryo-EM showed that OppA binds oligopeptides in vitro. Comparative genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics suggest that this peptidophilic surface architecture is conserved across Asgard archaeal phyla. Finally, we discovered that the cell surface was remodeled at cell-cell contact sites. Altogether, our integrative approach revealed a metabolically specialized and structurally flexible cell surface that couples extracellular protein degradation with peptide capture and uptake, while potentially contributing to establishing and maintaining the symbiotic interactions of Asgard archaea.

title: Genomic signatures distinguish isolates of Salmonella Typhimurium from humans and livestock
content: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a major cause of human salmonellosis and livestock represent an important reservoir for human infection through the food chain. However, it remains unclear whether isolates recovered from human disease reflect the broader livestock population or constitute a subset of livestock-associated isolates characterized by specific genetic features. Here, we analysed 1,398 S. Typhimurium genomes from human, poultry, bovine and swine isolates to evaluate whether isolates associated with human disease can be distinguished from those circulating in livestock and to identify the genetic features underlying this discrimination. Whole-genome multilocus sequence typing profiles were converted into a gene presence/absence matrix and analysed using four machine-learning algorithms, which showed high and consistent discriminatory performance. Model performance was influenced by the phylogenetic structure of the population and by the variable distribution of human- and livestock-associated isolates across lineages of sequence type (ST) 19, the most prevalent S. Typhimurium ST. Nevertheless, within ST19, 97 genes were significantly enriched and 36 were significantly depleted in human-associated genomes relative to genomes from each of the three livestock sources. Human-enriched genes included 14 genes required for biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide core, the O-antigen, the T1 antigen, and six virulence factors. These genes were consistently absent from livestock-associated genomes across ST19 lineages. Conversely, human-depleted genes included the galactitol utilisation cluster and five virulence genes, which are predominantly absent in specific ST19 lineages. Overall, our findings support the existence of host-associated genomic signatures that distinguish isolates associated with human disease from those sampled from the livestock reservoir.

title: UVC Irradiation Induces Time-Dependent Proteomic Remodeling in Geodermatophilus obscurus G20
content: Geodermatophilus obscurus G20 is a multi-resistant extremophile observed to survive significant dosages of ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Despite previous work having measured G. obscurus G20s proteome in relation to its genome sequence, its proteomic response to stressors has yet to be explored. This study utilizes bottom-up proteomics with data independent acquisition to derive comprehensive proteomic measurements in both healthy and two UV-stressed conditions induced through 254 nm UV radiation administered at a median lethal dose. The first, an acute response treatment group, was recovered and flash-frozen immediately after UV radiation. The second, a recovery response treatment group, was allowed to incubate for 1 hour following UV radiation. Gene enrichment analysis revealed an increase in NADH dehydrogenase activity among both stressed treatment groups, however the recovery response treatment group experienced additional changes including reduced peptidoglycan synthesis and increased translational activity. Results suggest that the repair process undergone by G. obscurus G20 persists well after initial UV exposure and is likely to be inducing noteworthy energetic demands to facilitate UV induced genomic repair. Proteomic analyses revealed patterns that advance our mechanistic and temporal understanding of the G. obscurus metabolic response to UV irradiation.

title: The biochemical composition of coronavirus Nucleocapsid proteins drives the bicistronic properties of their sub-genomic mRNAs
content: The nucleocapsid (N) gene of coronaviruses (CoVs) encodes a structural RNA-binding protein required for viral assembly. In SARS- and MERS-CoV viruses, reading frame 2 of N contains an overlapping open reading frame (ORF) encoding an innate immune antagonist accessory protein. However, the extent of this dual coding capacity across the CoV family, and the genetic features driving overlapping ORF formation, remain unexamined. Here, we developed an in-silico tool (ORFan) to screen structural gene sub-genomic mRNA sequences from 152 species of coronavirus for the presence of overlapping accessory gene candidates. We found that frame 2 of the N gene in Alpha-, Beta- and Delta-CoVs frequently contains a potential accessory ORF (AcORF), conserved at the subgenus level, unlike the spike, envelope and membrane genes. We also show that CoV nucleotide biases in conjunction with codon biases integral to N protein function drive the relatively high abundances of start codons in frame two and stop codons in frame three, explaining the tendency towards frame 2 AcORFs. We further suggest that viral nucleotide biases and the codon composition required for RNA-binding function facilitate overlapping ORF formation in other virus families

title: Cell-scale confinement reorders bacterial speed rankings
content: Which bacterium swims fastest depends on where the race is run. Speeds are usually measured in open liquid, yet many bacteria live in pores, mucus and host passages no wider than a cell. Using a microfluidic device with eight channel widths (0.80-3.00 m) in one field of view, we tracked unlabeled cells of eight species spanning five motility systems. Chamber height, a polymer additive and channel width each reordered the ranking. Vibrio alginolyticus, the fastest in open liquid, slowed to ~4 m/s in 1.25-m channels, whereas Campylobacter jejuni and Bacillus subtilis kept 33-46 m/s. Open liquid speed did not predict robustness to confinement. In two unrelated lineages, host symbionts that pass through narrow passages during colonization, Caballeronia insecticola and Vibrio fischeri, outran their non-symbiotic relatives in the channels, and crossed them with flagella wrapped around the cell body at nearly the speed of unwrapped cells. Where space is tight, the ability to keep moving, not top speed, sets the ranking.

title: High reproducibility demonstrated in a direct-to-consumer microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions using fecal reference material
content: Recent studies have documented substantial variation in microbiome profiles recovered from identical biological samples across direct-to-consumer (DTC) gut microbiome testing providers and, in some cases, within individual providers. These reports underscore the need for transparent, published assessments of analytical performance from the companies offering these services. To assess analytical reproducibility in our own testing workflow, we processed 10 replicates of a homogenized National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) human fecal reference material (RM 8048) through our full sample processing pipeline, from sample collection to data generation. Replicates were shipped from five U.S. sites over a staggered 35-day window. They were processed amongst over 6,000 customer samples, batched for DNA extraction and sequencing based on their arrival in the lab in nine separate sequencing runs, and analyzed using our standard pipeline. The 10 reference material replicates yielded highly concordant community profiles regardless of shipping time or temperature. Technical variability was minimal (median Bray-Curtis dissimilarity = 0.04) compared with the variation observed in samples from the same Tiny Health customer collected the same day (median Bray-Curtis: 0.08), within one week (0.25), one to two weeks apart (0.28), and between unrelated individuals (0.88). When evaluated using NIST's Coefficient of Disagreement (COD) metric, our workflow yielded a maximum pairwise COD of 0.045, well below NIST's published upper bound of 0.073 for this reference material. All three spike-in control strains were successfully recovered from every sample. These results demonstrate the reproducibility of our DTC microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions, with robust consistency across sample collection, shipping, laboratory processing, and bioinformatics analysis. They also highlight the value of RM 8048 and similar reference materials for evaluating and transparently reporting analytical performance in DTC microbiome testing.

title: Examining urban weed response to elevated salt levels
content: Stressors from the urban environment cause adverse effects on city-dwelling organisms. While there is evidence that some species are adapting to urban stressors, such as the urban heat island and impervious surfaces, other stressors such as road salt are less studied. We investigated whether plants are adapting to elevated salt concentrations with two common garden experiments using three common weed species: Veronica arvensis, Stellaria media, and Lamium purpureum. We collected plants from parks around Baltimore, MD, USA, collecting plant maternal lineages from roadside soils (i.e. higher soil salinity) and inner park soils (i.e. lower soil salinity). We hypothesized that roadside lineages would tolerate salt treatment better than park lineages. In our germination experiment on wild-collected seeds, we observed a non-significant trend where the germination rate of roadside L. purpureum lineages was reduced less by salt treatment than for park genetic lineages, while S. media had similar declines between groups. In our greenhouse experiment on the F1 generation, roadside V. arvensis lineages displayed a less adverse reaction to salt treatment than park V. arvensis lineages. L. purpureum did not display this difference, but roadside lineages of both species exhibited less tissue damage overall. The results of our experiments were likely influenced by the maternal environment, and work on F2 generations is required to confirm them. Our findings show some support for urban salt tolerance adaptation, and point to the heterogeneity of the urban environment and the complexity of plant reactions to salinity.

title: Invasion analysis for structured populations: analytical principles and numerical workflows
content: All real populations show some form of structure--differences among individuals, such as life stage or physiological condition, that shape a species' ability to persist. Yet it remains challenging to incorporate population structure into models of species interactions. We provide a general framework for studying competition in structured populations by quantifying species' invasion growth rates. The crux of our approach is separation of timescales: the initial dynamics of a structured population depend on how exactly it is introduced, but these transient differences do not affect long-term invasion success. Depending on the research question, the relevant long-term growth rate when rare may equivalently be derived using analytical separation of timescales, matrix population theory, or numerical simulations. Using case studies spanning developmental stage, environmental state, and infection status, we illustrate how our methodology derives simple, ecologically meaningful invasion conditions for a variety of systems. Finally, we extend the approach to fluctuating resident dynamics, showing how to use simulations or a general mathematical framework known as Floquet theory to correctly quantify invasion growth. By unifying the quantitative methods of population biology and community ecology, our framework will allow ecologists to study species persistence and coexistence across a greater variety of demographically complex systems.

title: Primary vitamin B12 limitation and widespread stress in Antarctic phytoplankton
content: Iron is considered the dominant limiting or colimiting nutrient for phytoplankton growth in the Southern Ocean. However, strong competition and limited biosynthesis capabilities for vitamin B12 (cobalamin) within the microbial community creates conditions suitable for cobalamin limitation. Through a nutrient enrichment experiment in the Amundsen Sea, we show that growth in a phytoplankton community comprising diatoms and prasinophytes was limited primarily by cobalamin and secondarily by iron. Protein biomarkers across a broad area of the Southern Ocean further indicate widespread cobalamin stress within diatoms and Phaeocystis. As warming-induced melting of ice-shelves increases iron supplies in the coastal Southern Ocean, shifts from iron to cobalamin limitation favor mixotrophic flagellates with low cobalamin requirements, altering community composition and function.

title: Interspecific social contacts spread gut microbiota in wild rodent communities
content: Background: The mammalian gut microbiota influences a wide array of host phenotypes and varies substantially among individuals. Among conspecifics, microbiota composition is strongly shaped by microbial transmission through social interactions, yet the extent to which such transmission also occurs across species boundaries remains poorly understood. Here, we combine high-resolution tracking data collected over more than 10 months with gut microbiota profiling to examine social associations, space use, and microbiota similarity among individuals of three sympatric rodent species - wood mice (Apodemus sylvaticus), yellow-necked mice (A. flavicollis) and bank voles (Myodes glareolus), in two woodlands. By integrating multi-species social networks and spatial overlap with individual microbiota data, we test how both conspecific and interspecific interactions shape gut microbiota composition. Results: At both study sites, social associations strongly predicted microbiota similarity among conspecific individuals, whereas spatial proximity consistently predicted microbiota similarity among interspecific pairs. In addition, social associations between mice of different species predicted microbiota similarity, although this effect was weaker than that observed within species and was asymmetric, with evidence for stronger microbial transmission from wood mice to yellow-necked mice than vice versa. By focusing on species-indicative bacterial taxa, we further show that wood mice with more social connections to yellow-necked mice harboured a greater richness of gut bacteria typical of yellow-necked mice. Conclusions: Together, these results demonstrate that individual-level social behaviour can influence gut microbial transmission across species boundaries, particularly among closely related species with overlapping ecological niches. Interspecific social interactions may therefore represent an underappreciated pathway for the acquisition of novel gut symbionts in multi-species communities.

title: Microscale nonrandomness revisited: An overlooked predictor of ecological change
content: Abrupt ecological transitions have driven the development of early warning signal metrics that track how ecological systems respond as external conditions gradually change and systems approach transitions between states. However, their generality and applicability remain uncertain, particularly for short-term ecological dynamics that can occur without directional external change. To address this gap, we propose a general framework based on the hypothesis that microscale nonrandomness, quantified from frequency distributions or spatial patterns, predicts subsequent short-term rates of change in populations and interactions, as well as current macroscale ecosystem states. We applied the framework to four datasets: time series from an incubation experiment of phytoplankton-parasitic chytrid interactions; spatiotemporal field observations of leaf beetles on willow trees and aphids in a crop system; and spatial snapshot data linking soil surface characteristics with aboveground and soil ecosystem properties in a forest vegetations-soil system. We quantified microscale nonrandomness using Morisita I_{delta} from frequency distributions and Moran's I and SADIE from spatial patterns. Across all systems, models incorporating microscale nonrandomness metrics consistently showed greater cross-validated predictive performance than those based on macroscale variables or spatial averages alone. Although their relative performance varied among systems, frequency-based metrics performed as well as or better than spatially explicit metrics in some cases. The consistent improvement across contrasting systems supports the broad applicability of this framework, including under limited data conditions. This framework broadens ecological forecasting to short-term, continuous dynamics beyond those associated with directional environmental change.

title: Elevational filtering reshapes mountain understory communities through diversity decline, functional shifts, and species replacement
content: Mountain understory communities are structured along elevational gradients, as environmental constraints filter which species and ecological strategies can persist and where. Yet, how community differentiation, local diversity, functional strategies, and species replacement are shaped by elevational gradients remains poorly resolved. Here, we examine 107 herbaceous species across 27 sites spanning 2,202-3,696 m a.s.l. and three elevational zones. We determine how elevation reorganizes multiple dimensions of community assembly. We hypothesize that increasing elevation differentiates community composition, reduces -diversity, favors persistence-oriented strategies, and drives {beta}-diversity primarily through species turnover, rather than nestedness. We test our hypotheses by integrating taxonomic, functional, and {beta}-diversity patterns across the elevational gradient. A coherent pattern of community reassembly emerges as elevation increases: communities become increasingly distinct with elevational separation and locally less diverse toward higher elevations. Functional composition changes concurrently, with perennial and chamaephytic groups increasing as annual and therophytic groups decline. We find that increasing community differentiation primarily reflects species replacement rather than progressive species loss. Species turnover accounts for 97.95% of total Sorensen {beta}-diversity and increases with elevational separation, whereas nestedness declines. Our findings therefore show that elevation reorganizes herbaceous understory communities through linked changes in diversity, functional strategies, and species identity. Indeed, environmental filtering favors persistence-oriented strategies while progressively replacing species across elevations, linking taxonomic and functional differentiation within a common process of mountain understory community assembly.

title: Polymerase and primer biases in eukaryote ultra-long-read metabarcoding
content: Ultra-long-read metabarcoding is a recently developed method for biodiversity monitoring that enables both high-accuracy species-level identification and reliable phylogenetic placement of taxa. Ultra-long-read analyses require high-processivity DNA polymerases for amplicons and primer pairs that fully cover the targeted taxonomic groups. So far, there is no published information on the relative suitability of commercial high-processivity polymerase kits and on the relative performance of primer pairs targeting a DNA fragment spanning much of the 18S, ITS and 28S rRNA gene regions in eukaryotes. Using PacBio sequencing, we assessed the performance of five commercial high-processivity DNA polymerases and three ultra-long marker primer pairs relative to a commonly used full-ITS primer pair on producing artefacts and recovering biodiversity in two mock communities and 10 soil samples. Our analyses revealed great differences in both polymerases and primer pairs in data quality and biodiversity. For testing evolutionary hypotheses, we recommend using the Solis or Fusion polymerases and the Euk575F-21Rngs primer pair in ultra-long-read metabarcoding analyses of soil eukaryotes. Compared with a previous study using the same DNA samples, the ultra-long amplicons revealed substantially lower biodiversity than medium-sized, full-ITS amplicons across taxonomic levels, suggesting that medium-sized amplicons may be better suited for routine soil eukaryote biodiversity monitoring than ultra-long amplicons.

title: The game-theoretical analysis of multiple Nash equilibria of a cholera epidemic model with non-exponential distributions
content:
Publication date: Available online 6 November 2026

Source: Journal of Theoretical Biology

Author(s): Junyuan Yang, Yiqian Bai, Shasha Gao

title: Divergent Responses of Bacterial and Microeukaryotic Diversity to Water‐Level Fluctuations in a Lake‐Floodplain System
content:
Water‐level fluctuations deliver soil‐derived taxa into the water column, yet bacteria and microeukaryotes respond divergently to flooding. This asymmetry leads to inconsistent diversity trends, with microeukaryotic richness increasing with water levels while bacterial richness remains unchanged. This pattern challenges the classic diversity pattern associated with water‐level fluctuations.

ABSTRACT
Water‐level fluctuations (WLF) are widely accepted as key drivers of aquatic species diversity in lake‐floodplain systems, with diversity increasing as water levels rise. However, microorganisms may challenge this pattern that their richness does not necessarily increase with water levels. To resolve this inconsistency, we applied 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to bacterial and microeukaryotic assemblages in Dongting Lake, China, during the low‐water (LWP; January 2024) and high‐water periods (HWP; August 2024). Microeukaryotic richness was higher during HWP than LWP (p < 0.01), whereas bacterial richness remained comparable (p = 0.96). Habitat‐of‐origin annotation indicated that terrestrial‐derived microeukaryotes contributed to this increase (p = 0.02), whereas terrestrial bacterial inputs did not (p > 0.3), consistent with their divergent fates in the water column: soil microeukaryotes are more likely to persist after flooding than soil bacteria. Co‐occurrence networks evidenced substantially stronger bacteria‐microeukaryote associations at high water and partial least squares path modelling resolved a DOC‐to‐bacteria‐to‐microeukaryotes pathway activated only during the HWP. These signals suggest that enhanced hydrological connectivity promoted community coalescence, possibly through intensified trophic coupling, although this interpretation requires experimental verification. This study highlights that natural WLFs reshape microbial richness by intermittently reconnecting terrestrial and aquatic microbial species pools.

title: Rapid Downward Propagation of Wind‐Generated Near‐Inertial Waves Within a Cyclonic Eddy in the Northern South China Sea
content:
Abstract
Wind‐generated near‐inertial waves (NIWs) are important pathways for transferring wind energy into the ocean interior, yet their propagation is strongly modulated by mesoscale eddies. The classical view suggests that cyclonic eddies (CEs), with positive relative vorticity, tend to repel NIWs and inhibit local downward propagation. Based on subsurface mooring observations in the northern South China Sea during six typhoon passages, we show that typhoon‐generated near‐inertial energy within a CE can follow both near‐surface‐confined and deep‐propagating pathways. Several NIW packets are confined to the upper approximately 150 m, consistent with the classical view. In contrast, energetic near‐inertial motions also occur in the deeper CE layer, including a separated deep energy patch after Typhoon BUALOI and a coherent downward‐propagating packet after Typhoon MATMO. The MATMO‐induced packet propagates from the near surface to 650 m in approximately 9 days. Ellipse analysis indicates that this packet has a large vertical wavelength of 1439.0 ± 199.3 m and a fast vertical group velocity of 76.0 ± 6.2 m/day. Modal decomposition shows low‐mode dominance, with modes 1–3 accounting for 64% of modal near‐inertial kinetic energy. Energy diagnostics indicate that the packet is primarily powered by wind input rather than eddy‐to‐wave energy transfer, with downward energy flux accounting for 23%–28% of the wind‐generated near‐inertial energy input. These observations demonstrate that CEs do not uniformly suppress near‐inertial energy penetration. Low‐mode NIWs can provide a pathway for wind‐generated near‐inertial energy to enter the deep layer of a CE, providing new insight into the pathways of wind energy penetration in eddy‐rich oceans.

title: Dissolution and Heterotrophy at a Florida Coral Reef One Year After Severe Bleaching
content:
Abstract
Net ecosystem calcification (NEC) and net ecosystem production (NEP) are key metabolic indicators of reef functioning that underpin habitat formation and biomass assimilation, providing insight into ecosystem responses to environmental stressors. We employed a gradient‐flux approach at a shallow inshore reef in the Florida Keys to measure hourly NEC and NEP one year after the 2023 coral bleaching event. In situ chemical sensors and a current profiler were deployed from June 26 to August 28, 2024, a period that included two episodic disturbances: Tropical Storm Debby (TS Debby) and a biogeochemical pulse. Despite relatively high coral cover (∼33%), the reef was in a state of net dissolution and heterotrophy, consistent with prolonged functional impairment from the bleaching event. NEC tracked changes in seawater carbonate chemistry, with the highest rates of dissolution coinciding with periods of reduced ΩArag. NEP was linked to temperature and salinity, with elevated heterotrophy measured when both parameters were depressed. Light availability was not a strong driver of reef metabolism, suggesting that the stimulating effects of light may be weakened for functionally compromised reefs. The two disturbance events suppressed NEC and NEP, masking normal biogeochemical signals. This was particularly evident during TS Debby, reflecting altered metabolic activity in response to rapid cooling, depressed ΩArag to near undersaturation levels, and low light availability. Our study reveals that despite visual coral recovery, cryptic metabolic impairment can persist 1 year after severe bleaching, highlighting the value of metabolic assessments for evaluating reef condition.

title: Drivers of Ocean pH Variation in Front of Dotson Ice Shelf, West Antarctica
content:
Abstract
The highly productive Amundsen Sea Polynya in West Antarctica is bounded in the south by rapidly‐melting ice shelves, including the Dotson Ice Shelf (DIS). We present a high‐resolution, full‐depth pH data set within 10 km of DIS using a Lab‐On‐Chip (LOC) spectrophotometric pH sensor on an ocean glider. The LOC performs well with a 0.01 difference in pH between sensor measurements and discrete samples. Over 19 days in January–February 2022, the pH sensor captured the variability resulting from summertime biological and physical processes. At depth, modified Circumpolar Deep Water entering the DIS cavity exhibited a relatively low pH (7.91). The outflow had a higher average pH (7.94) as a result of dilution by glacial meltwater, but its pH was 0.01 lower than that of surrounding water at the same density. The Antarctic Coastal Current transported unventilated surface water with a low pH emerging from below fast ice east of Bear Island, westward to the eastern side of DIS. Net primary production increased pH in the upper 50 m in front of DIS, whilst temperature change was responsible for 5% $\%$ of the change in pH. This study provides the first direct measurements of pH in the Amundsen Sea capable of deducing the impact of glacial meltwater on pH. It demonstrates the value, particularly in remote regions, of LOC pH sensors that have the longevity and stability to measure ocean pH without sensor drift.

title: Evidence for Local Adaptation Associated With Temperature Despite Weak Latitudinal Structure in a Temperate Seagrass
content:
ABSTRACT
Understanding genetic diversity and structure in natural populations is important for conservation and developing resilience into restored populations for the future. Populations at the lower latitude (or northern) range edges tend to have lower levels of genetic diversity and are poorly connected, although they may be locally adapted to warmer environments. The temperate seagrass, Posidonia sinuosa, occurs across a latitudinal gradient along the Western Australian coastline. Some meadows have experienced significant decline due to industrialisation and urbanisation of coastal areas. We investigated spatial genetic diversity, structure, and local adaptation using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). All meadows had similarly low levels of genetic diversity with high levels of inbreeding, despite high clonal diversity. Weak genetic structure was consistent with genetic connectivity, enabled by sea‐surface seed dispersal. Approximately 6.1% of SNPs were identified as putatively adaptive and most were associated with temperature variables. Allelic turnover was associated with < 1.4°C temperature change, suggesting plants may be sensitive to small temperature changes. Meadows are currently growing in temperatures below their thermal optima, so may tolerate future projected temperatures up to a point. Importantly, this temperature increase is below the 1.5°C–2.0°C goal of the Paris Agreement and plants are unlikely to tolerate current projections for 2100, which equate to +3.2°C, in addition to extreme heatwave events. Conservation of fragmented, northern, warmer‐adapted meadows will be important to assist recovery and persistence of damaged meadows into the future, as translocation of putatively warmer‐adapted genotypes that have exhibited historic connectivity may be a viable strategy for restoration of impacted higher latitude meadows.

title: Symbiont‐Derived Key Innovations Across the Diversity and Diets of Herbivorous Insects
content:
ABSTRACT
With prodigious biomass and diversity, herbivorous insects are among the world's most successful animals. It is widely believed, however, that some plant‐based diets do not meet the needs of insect metabolism. Microbial symbionts may balance such deficits through diverse biochemistry. Here, we consider whether obligate nutritional symbioses between insects and microbes support large portions of insect herbivore diversity. In doing so, we assess the evidence that these highly integrated relationships are key innovations, circumventing nutritive shortfalls within particular plant tissues. Toward these ends, we compile nutrient data for 20 plant‐ and non‐plant foods, plus data on diet and symbiosis across 874 families of insects—both herbivorous and non‐herbivorous. Our results reinforce widely believed, but often uncited evidence that several insect taxa have long‐consumed plant tissues with low concentrations of B‐vitamins, nitrogen, or accessible carbon. Emerging as symbiont‐enriched are seed‐feeders, which face insufficient quantities of several B‐vitamins in their food. Experimental and genome assessments show how symbionts surmount these B‐vitamin shortcomings, showing also where this same challenge, and those of high fibre or low amino acid content are surmounted through symbiosis on other diets. We thus show where symbiont services are key innovations. Over half of the world's insect herbivores persist without nutritive assistance from obligate symbionts. This is largely because many consume leaves, which are reasonably good sources of amino acids and B‐vitamins. Lateral transfer of microbial genes encoding plant cell‐wall degrading enzymes has helped to overcome high fibre content, defusing the most challenging nutritive aspect of leaf‐chewing diets.

title: Chromosome Evolution in Amniote Vertebrates: A Comprehensive Atlas of Karyotypic Diversity From Ancestral States to Rapid Turnover
content:
ABSTRACT
The evolution of the amniote genome is characterized by a striking dichotomy between extreme karyotypic stasis and rapid structural innovation. To identify the mechanisms governing this variation, we provide a comprehensive synthesis of chromosome number and karyotype data across non‐avian reptiles, birds and mammals, integrating a century of classical cytogenetics with modern chromosome‐scale genomics. Amniote chromosome numbers span a range from 2n = 6 to 142 and have been shaped primarily by chromosomal fusions and fissions rather than by polyploidization common in non‐amniotes. Recent ancestral state reconstructions suggest a highly fragmented ancestral amniote karyotype of 2n = 88 with a bipartite organization of macro‐ and microchromosomes. They also support environmental sex determination as the plesiomorphic state. We explore the evolutionary mechanisms facilitating chromosomal turnover, including lineage‐specific transposable element activity, hybridization‐driven genomic instability and genetic hitchhiking, alongside the canalization model and the position‐effect hypothesis as primary responses to environmental transitions. Social structure, such as polygynous harem systems, can further contribute to rearrangement fixation via genetic drift in some, but not all, lineages. Chromosomal divergence across these lineages serves as a useful cytotaxonomic marker and, in some cases, a barrier to gene flow, as in the postzygotic incompatibility of equid and cervid hybrids. In contrast, introgression persists across karyotypically divergent rock‐wallabies and crocodilians, indicating that the reproductive consequences of karyotypic divergence are lineage‐specific rather than a fixed function of karyotypic distance. This synthesis presents an updated atlas of amniote chromosomal evolution and provides a conceptual framework for understanding how molecular mechanisms, ecological shifts and behavioural factors interact to shape genomic structure.

title: SNPs in Copy Number Variants Play a Key Role in Local Adaptation to Climate in Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera)
content:
ABSTRACT
Copy number variation (CNV) constitutes a major source of adaptive genetic variation, yet its relative contribution to climate adaptation compared to non‐CNV (single‐copy) variants remains unresolved. Using whole‐genome sequencing of 125 Nelumbo nucifera (sacred lotus, a common aquatic vegetable) wild accessions spanning tropical‐temperate gradients, we distinguished 388,600 CNV‐derived SNPs from 485,982 SNPs of single‐copy regions. Latent factor mixed models (LFMM) revealed that CNV‐SNPs appear to drive adaptation to temperature extremes and precipitation seasonality, whereas non‐CNV SNPs dominate humid thermal adaptation. NnPAL2, a homologue of a drought‐related gene in Arabidopsis, shows a recent selective sweep in temperate N. nucifera, with reduced copy number and expression associated with lower precipitation in the warmest quarter. Our results suggest that CNV SNPs and non‐CNV SNPs contribute to distinct environmental axes, but the heterogeneous CNV effects across bioclimatic variables largely reflect ecotype‐specific copy number backgrounds rather than intrinsic differences in selective pressures. CNV therefore plays a disproportionate role in coping with abiotic extremes. Discriminating CNV‐derived SNPs from those derived from single‐copy genomic regions is essential for accurately understanding the genetic basis of climate adaptation, with potential applications for crop improvement.

title: Species Identification in Drosophilids; the Utility of k‐mer Characters
content:
ABSTRACT
Over 14,900 COI DNA sequences of drosophilids were used to build a character‐based diagnostic system for the identification of genera and species in the group. This approach uses aligned COI sequence characters, k‐mer characters and applies a hybrid approach that combines the two. To assess the efficacy of the diagnostics, accuracy versus coverage plots were used and resulted in the observation that practical rules (allowing 5% leakage [misidentified assignments]) perform much better than strict rules (no leakage). In addition, k = 10 was determined as the optimal k value for k‐mer character analysis. Hybrid methods incorporating both k‐mer characters and aligned DNA sequence characters outperform the individual approaches. Finally, unnamed drosophilid accessions were compiled and tentatively assigned taxonomy based on the diagnostic system developed here.

title: A novel strategy for estimating subsurface dissolved oxygen from surface ocean parameters
content:
Publication date: Available online 6 November 2026

Source: Deep Sea Research Part I: Oceanographic Research Papers

Author(s): Bo Ping, Ruiting Yang, Yunshan Meng, Cunjin Xue, Zhi Li

title: Evaluating the Impact of Multiscale E‐Region Turbulence on HF Scintillation
content:
Abstract
Ionospheric scintillation driven by plasma irregularities disrupts radio propagation across frequencies from HF to L‐band. While phase‐screen methods dominate scintillation modeling, they can be inadequate in the E‐region where irregularity scales can be comparable to the radio wavelength or Fresnel scale and span orders of magnitude. Here we quantitatively evaluate scintillation with a new full‐wave methodology coupling particle‐in‐cell simulations of the gradient drift (GD) and Farley‐Buneman instabilities with finite‐difference time‐domain electromagnetic propagation. Using a frozen‐in approximation and spatial filtering, we evaluate the contributions of various turbulence scale sizes to HF (6–24 MHz) phase and amplitude scintillation. Long‐wavelength GD waves dominate the modeled amplitude scintillation through diffractive scattering, while Farley‐Buneman turbulence contributes negligibly. Amplitude spectra closely follow irregularities near the Fresnel scale, demonstrating a direct correspondence between scintillation and plasma structuring. These results demonstrate full‐wave scintillation modeling and provide a framework for investigating scintillation across a wide range of spatial scales.

title: Fluid‐Controlled Tidal Modulation of Aftershocks Following the 2022 M6.8 Luding Earthquake
content:
Abstract
Aftershock sequences record how fault zones recover and weaken after earthquakes, but the roles of fluid migration and stress heterogeneity remain difficult to isolate. Earth tides impose predictable stress perturbations and thus provide a natural probe of faults near failure, although their signals are often obscured by aftershock clustering. Here we apply bootstrap‐based spatial spectral analysis to the 2022 M6.8 Luding earthquake sequence to resolve tidal sensitivity. We identify a systematic shift from a fluid‐rich region before the mainshock to the margins of the high‐slip zone, bypassing the rupture core. This pattern suggests coupled interaction between coseismic stress heterogeneity and postseismic fluid redistribution. Elevated pore pressure enhances sensitivity to weak tidal stress in high stress‐gradient regions, whereas permeability contrasts promote localized fluid accumulation and triggering. Our results show that tidal forcing can reveal where postseismic faults are closest to failure, offering an indirect window into fluid migration and fault‐zone weakening.

title: Desert Lakes Nasser–Toshka: A Novel Site for Satellite Gravimetry Validation
content:
Abstract
Validation results for mass estimates measured by GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) and GRACE‐FO (GRACE Follow‐On) currently hold uncertainties exceeding 10 gigatons (Gt), due to errors in auxiliary models and leakage noise from surrounding hydrological signals. Here, we propose the Lakes Nasser–Toshka in the Sahara Desert as an easily accessible benchmark that could remarkably reduce the validation uncertainty to several gigatons. We evaluate the 2002–2025 GRACE(‐FO) line‐of‐sight gravity difference (LGD) record against water storage derived from satellite altimetry and optical imagery. The results show that the measurement uncertainties for GRACE KBR (K‐band Ranging), GRACE‐FO KBR and GRACE‐FO LRI (Laser Ranging Interferometer) are 7.76 Gt, 5.46 Gt and 4.35 Gt, respectively. The GRACE‐FO LRI LGD interquartile range (0.166–0.493 nm/s2) establishes a performance benchmark for future LRI‐based missions. Lakes Nasser–Toshka offer a rare natural benchmark for in‐orbit commissioning and evaluating future satellite gravimetry missions.

title: High‐Resolution Discharge Inversion in a Small Alpine Watershed: Combining Monitoring Images and Triaxial Seismic Data
content:
Abstract
In small alpine watersheds, abrupt rainfall‐ or meltwater‐driven runoff leads to dramatic variations in flow width over uneven channel beds, thereby complicating discharge monitoring. Using a typical watershed near the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon as the study area, we presented a workflow combining imagery and seismic data to estimate the instantaneous discharge with machine learning. Results show that image‐based flow width correction effectively improved discharge records to provide a better basis for modeling. For hourly instantaneous discharge estimation, the machine learning model achieved good performance, with mean coefficients of determination of 0.77 for the training, 0.68 for the validation, and 0.66 for the independent testing, and corresponding mean Kling–Gupta efficiency values of 0.83, 0.79, and 0.75, respectively. Using minute‐level seismic data, we further detected 179 suspected flood events between July and October 2025 and analyzed their hydrological characteristics. In general, this proposed framework could address the limitations of traditional monitoring approaches and support water resources management in similar small watersheds.

title: Plasma and Electric Environment Within Lunar Pits and Caves Exposed to the Solar Wind
content:
Abstract
We have assessed the plasma and electric environment within a lunar pit and its connected subsurface cave utilizing plasma simulations. It is shown that adjacent illuminated and shadowed regions along the interior walls of the pit induce differential charging, exceeding the levels typically observed on open planar surfaces. Within the illuminated sectors, the incident solar wind (SW) proton flux dominates over the electron counterpart. In this regime, photo‐emitted and secondary electrons imported from adjacent illuminated surfaces suppress excessive positive charging by acting as negative charge carriers to compensate for the scarce SW electrons. Deep inside the cave, a residual population of SW electrons induces significant negative charging despite their small flux. The relative significance of minor current components, such as ion‐induced secondary electrons and protons scattered off the lunar regolith, is also enhanced therein. The local equilibrium potential is thus governed by the current balance of these multi‐species particle populations.

title: Strengthened Central Pacific ENSO Variability With Reduced Asymmetry Modulated by Upper‐Ocean Salinification Since the Late 1990s
content:
Abstract
Central Pacific (CP) El Niño‐Southern Oscillation (ENSO) variability has intensified since the late 1990s. Existing literature has emphasized the role of upper‐ocean stratification in modulating ENSO, primarily focusing on decadal thermal changes. This study further demonstrates that the regime shift of ENSO is modulated by the increasing salinity in the CP region. This decadal salinification enhances near‐surface density and weakens static stability, facilitating stronger vertical entrainment and a warmer subsurface at the base of the mixed layer. Consequently, thermocline feedback responsible for the growth of ENSO is reinforced during El Niño but weakened during La Niña, favoring stronger CP El Niño and weaker La Niña. Then the negative skewness of CP ENSO asymmetry is reduced. The CP salinification is primarily linked to a decadal intensification of the Walker circulation and reduced freshwater flux. Understanding these salinity‐driven processes is essential for improving ENSO predictions and mitigating climatic impacts on decadal‐to‐multidecadal timescales.

title: Transformational Faulting: The Case of Quartz‐Coesite
content:
Abstract
Transformational faulting in olivine has been widely invoked as a possible triggering mechanism for deep‐focus earthquakes, yet its dynamics remain debated. It is unclear whether it requires the combined effects of heat release, volume change and mechanical strength contrast, or whether it can be triggered by any one of these alone. Here, we tested if transformational faulting can be caused solely by a large volume change, through deformation experiments on novaculite during the quartz‐coesite transition. Under sluggish reaction kinetics, acoustic emissions and microstructural observations indicate strain localization and fault plane formation. Under fast kinetics, deformation was distributed and associated with fewer, lower‐magnitude events. b‐values of ∼1 and ∼3 reflect these two regimes. Our results provide the first evidence of transformational faulting during the quartz‐coesite transition, suggesting that volume change is the primary driver of brittle failure at high pressure, broadening the range of mineral transitions generating deep and intermediate‐depth earthquakes.

title: Enhanced Surface Coupling but Suppressed Convective Triggering During Humid–Hot Extremes in the Yangtze River Basin, a Major Humid‐Heat Hotspot in China
content:
Abstract
Compound humid‐hot extremes bring growing threats to human society, yet land–atmosphere feedbacks regulating these events remain insufficiently understood. Using high‐resolution observational and reanalysis data, we reveal that the Yangtze River Basin (YRB) is a prominent hotspot for humid‐hot extremes, with rare hot‐only events. Comparing humid‐hot and non‐humid‐hot days, we find that humid‐hot extremes are sustained by positive feedbacks involving a high‐pressure anomaly, suppressed clouds and precipitation, drier soils, enhanced evapotranspiration, and lower relative humidity—mutually reinforcing the extreme state. Land–atmosphere coupling strengthens substantially for near‐surface variables, indicating stronger land surface control. Yet this enhanced coupling does not extend to cloud development: elevated lifting condensation levels and reduced relative humidity inhibit cloud formation, leading to a decoupling between convection and cloud development and allowing humid‐hot extremes to persist. Our findings highlight the role of land surface processes in modulating compound extremes and provide a foundation for improving their prediction.

title: Water Vapor Buoyancy and the African Easterly Jet
content:
Abstract
The African easterly jet (AEJ) is a prominent circulation feature in the tropical atmosphere. It transports mineral dust and affects easterly waves that serve as seeds for hurricanes. Conventional wisdom holds that the AEJ is in thermal wind balance with the positive meridional temperature gradient over North Africa. Here, using reanalysis data, we show that the negative meridional moisture gradient partially counteracts the effect of the temperature gradient on density in that balance, diagnostically accounting for a 30% reduction in the AEJ magnitude. Using CMIP6 data, we further show that this effect of the moisture gradient on the AEJ strengthens under global warming, highlighting the critical role of the moisture distribution in large‐scale circulation. Analysis of the AEJ in CMIP6 models confirms that some models neglect the effect of the moisture gradient on the AEJ, raising questions about the relevance of their projections of climate change in that region.

title: Record‐Shattering Winter “Heatwave” Over the Antarctic Peninsula in 2026, Associated Primarily With Tropical East Indian Ocean Surface Temperature Anomalies
content:
Abstract
Extreme winter warming events over the Antarctic Peninsula (AP) have potential impacts on ice‐shelf stability, but their mechanisms and teleconnections remain poorly studied. Using multi‐station observations, we report several warm extremes during May–June 2026, with early–June temperatures exceeding 0°C and peak anomalies reaching +22.32°C. These extremes were primarily driven by a pressure‐dipole pattern, featuring an enhanced Amundsen Sea Low and Drake Passage blocking, which directed frequent atmospheric river landfalls. The resulting moisture‐heat advection, alongside enhanced downward longwave radiation, dominated the rapid warming over the AP. Notably, record‐high sea surface temperatures in the tropical eastern Indian Ocean played a key role in this anomalous circulation, whereas the concurrent El Niño (still developing) had minimal direct impact. Our findings enrich the rare wintertime cases and identify the tropical Indian Ocean as a key precursor for improving projections of such events, which is also essential for estimating their impact on ice‐shelf stability.

title: Tree Rings Indicate Potential for Severe Soil Moisture Drought in California Is Much Greater Than Observations Suggest
content:
Abstract
Tree rings reveal that 1579–1580 was by far the driest pair of years across California since at least CE 1100. Here we produce a gridded tree‐ring reconstruction of summer soil‐moisture anomalies for California and perform a peaks‐over‐threshold extreme value analysis on statewide mean drought severity from CE 1100–2025. Results indicate marginal annual exceedance probabilities (AEP) of ∼0.24% for 1579 and ∼0.04% for 1580, with a two‐year block EP of ∼0.05% for 1579–1580. Considering only the instrumental record (1901–2025), AEPs for the drought severities reconstructed for 1579 and 1580 cannot be robustly estimated and, for 1580, the reconstructed severity appears essentially impossible. Our findings demonstrate that including tree‐ring reconstructions meaningfully changes the expected frequency of droughts on realistic planning horizons, such as a 1% AEP (100‐year) event. Modern risk assessments based solely on observations likely underestimate the true probability of extreme drought events, even without accounting for anthropogenic climate change.

title: Pore‐Scale Segregation and Enrichment of Polydisperse Colloids via Transverse Migration in Porous Media
content:
Abstract
Understanding transport of anomalous colloids and contaminants requires partition of polydisperse colloids at the pore scale. Using a high‐resolution dual‐mode microscopy system, we directly visualize cross‐sectional concentration profiles. Furthermore, we identify a previously overlooked phenomenon: the occurrence of persistent transverse concentration heterogeneity and centerline enrichment above the injected concentration (C/C0 > 1) during transport. Observations at different spatial and temporal scales reveal transverse colloid migration during anomalous segregation and enrichment of colloids. These observations revealed that colloid transport results in the formation of distinct concentration‐defined regions that cannot be inferred from conventional solute transport behavior. We establish a double‐erf logarithmic‐gradient criterion to delineate the main‐flow and diffusion zones and quantify the main‐flow ratio (β $\beta $). This criterion defines transport zones directly from the observed concentration gradients, avoiding the nonuniqueness of conventional inversion‐based two‐zone models. Our results provide direct pore‐scale evidence and a quantitative framework linking pore‐scale transport structure to macroscopic behavior.

title: Accelerated Atmospheric Drying in Neighboring Rural Areas Across China Associated With Urban Warming
content:
Abstract
Neighboring rural areas (i.e., rural zones surrounding cities) experience strong urban–rural interactions and provide critical ecosystem services, yet their responses to atmospheric drying remain poorly understood. Here, we quantify urban impacts on vapor pressure deficit (VPD) in neighboring rural areas across China by comparing station observations from neighboring rural stations (NRS) and remote rural stations (RRS, stations located in rural regions far from urban influence). During 1985–2019, 69% of cities exhibited faster VPD growth in their NRS than in their RRS, with a mean drying rate 27.5% higher than that of RRS. This disparity was more pronounced in summer, particularly within urban clusters. The NRS‐RRS temperature difference dominated VPD variations, likely attributable to the urban‐rural temperature gradient, whereby temperatures gradually decline outward from urban cores. These results reveal potential urban influence on rural atmospheric drying, highlighting ecosystem risks in neighboring rural areas and targeted adaptation needs in sustainable urban development.

title: Observation of Return‐Stroke Current Wave Speed in a Long Channel Formed by Preceding Upward Connecting Leader
content:
Abstract
Direct measurements of return‐stroke current propagation speed inside lightning channels remain extremely challenging, so the propagation speed of return‐stroke luminosity is widely used as a proxy. We present the first direct measurement of return‐stroke current propagation speed along a natural lightning channel, using synchronized lightning current, electromagnetic field and optical observations. The return‐stroke current propagated downward along an unusually long preceding upward connecting leader (UCL) channel before reaching the top of Canton Tower. The average three‐dimensional (3D) downward propagation speed of the return‐stroke current wave is estimated to be approximately 2.4 ± 0.4 × 108 m/s across a roughly 870 m propagation path. The rising edge of the initial peak of return‐stroke current measured at the channel base is morphologically similar to that of the initial electromagnetic field peak at return‐stroke initiation.

title: The Scale Length of Electron Cyclotron Harmonic Wave Power by MMS Satellites
content:
Abstract
Using four MMS satellites from 2015 to 2021, we statistically investigate Electron Cyclotron Harmonic (ECH) wave power scale lengths. These waves are categorized into three distinct populations based on the background magnetic field topology: equatorial, off‐equator, and near the magnetopause. Generally, the observed scale lengths range from several kilometers to 100 km, with a typical value of ∼10 km. For the equatorial population, the typical parallel and perpendicular scale lengths are ∼14 and 24 km, respectively. For the off‐equator population, the parallel and perpendicular scale lengths are typically 20.8 and 19 km, respectively. For the population near the magnetopause, the parallel and perpendicular scale lengths are 19 and 13.7 km, respectively.

title: Intrinsic Backflow in Heterogeneous Aquifer During Electrokinetic Remediation: A Challenge in Field‐Scale Application
content:
Abstract
Electrokinetics is a remediation technology applying direct‐current voltage across soil to mobilize solutes. It induces electromigration whereby ions migrate toward electrodes of opposite charge, and electroosmosis whereby water flow is engendered because of surface charges in soils. As confirmed by various experiments, electroosmosis has the advantage of mobilizing non‐ionic solutes especially in low permeability clay. We argue herein that due to subsurface heterogeneity, the upscaling of electroosmosis may not be always achievable under normal conditions, mainly because of backflow in regions outside of clay. In this study, analytical solutions derived in periodic heterogeneous system demonstrate how nonuniform electroosmosis induces local hydraulic‐head gradient and backflow. Application in standard lognormal heterogeneity system produces limited backflow due to smoothly varying zeta potential, whereas discrete high absolute zeta potential lenses generate more extensive backflow. These findings highlight the importance of spatial organization (or lacunarity), especially lens size, spacing, for applications of field‐scale electrokinetic remediation.

title: Convective Vertical Velocities of Dust Devils in Gale Crater, Mars
content:
Abstract
Dust devils are believed to be a significant contributor to the martian global dust cycle, supplying as much as 50% of dust to the atmosphere annually. However, their in situ meteorological properties remain poorly known, specifically horizontal and vertical wind speeds. We use Mars Science Laboratory Curiosity rover Navigation Camera images to track image‐to‐image changes in dust devil heights as a proxy for their vertical wind speeds. Across 54 dust devils, we find an average vertical wind speed of ∼1.79 m s−1 with a standard deviation of 0.39 m s−1, nearly identical to the 1.8 m s−1 found in Gusev Crater by the Spirit rover (Greeley et al., 2006, https://doi.org/10.1029/2006je002743). Using typical dust devil opacities and occurrence rates in Gale Crater, we find the areal dust mass flux into the atmosphere in Gale Crater to be 3.5*10−11 kg s−1 m−2, 1–2 orders of magnitude below that of other regions on Mars.
